title: Thematic Investing on Steroids
abstract: Investors love to focus. We focus on the latest macro-event, the market that has delivered stellar returns or the theme that is capturing everyone’s attention. The problem is that this focus tends to lead to bad things happening – performance chasing, market timing, injudicious portfolio concentration. A flurry of blockbuster IPOs is giving investors the chance to turn our focus towards a selection of individual companies. This is unnecessary and potentially dangerous. An IPO in an in-vogue area like AI creates the opportunity for thematic investing on steroids. Not only do we gain narrow exposure to an industry that has fared spectacularly well in recent years, but – even better – a specific stock able to capture the AI zeitgeist in an incredibly focused fashion. Thematic investing always leaves us subjected to an exceptionally wide range of outcomes (many negative); expressing a thematic view through an individual stock takes this to the extreme. The fervour around investing in such powerful themes, and the stocks within it, often seems related to a profound fear of missing out – the idea that unless we invest directly in the theme we won’t have any or enough exposure. This is puzzling. Any sensibly diversified investor will have some allocation to whatever theme or stocks are exciting markets at any given time. And, if these areas turn out to be genuine long-term winners backed by fundamentals, then the exposure will naturally grow. The problem is that this sense of not having enough of whatever is performing well and capturing investor attention leads us inexorably towards taking concentrated bets that give us a ‘pure’ version of the theme. High-profile IPOs can seem like a theme captured in its most distilled form. In the midst of IPO hype and the temptation to take oversized positions in individual stocks, it is worth remembering Hendrik Bessembinder’s research on the concentration in stock market returns. Over the long-term the majority of stocks underperform cash and, since 1926, 46 out of nearly 30,000 stocks accounted for more than half of the total wealth created in the stock market. There were very few winners and lots of losers. Some people may read this and decide that the right approach is to try and pick the select group of winners that will dominate returns in advance. This is the wrong conclusion. Bessembinder’s work shows that being concentrated in individual stocks has been a strategy with terrible odds – the chances of finding and holding just the right stocks is incredibly slim. The better answer is diversification – spread our bets so we will own some of the companies that do come out on top. Deciding to take concentrated positions in individual stocks is a particular type of overconfidence – overprecision. This is where we make choices and judgements that suggest we know precisely how the future will play out. finding: Over the long-term the majority of stocks underperform cash and, since 1926, 46 out of nearly 30,000 stocks accounted for more than half of the total wealth created in the stock market.

title: The downside of AI for investment analysis
abstract: Yesterday , I wrote about how AI can enhance investment analysis. But I also promised that today I would write about the drawbacks of using AI for investment analysis. So, here we go, the stage is yours, Andrew Lo . Andrew Lo is a professor at MIT who is legendary in the quantitative finance space. He also founded the hedge fund Alpha Simplex Group, so when he does research, he usually puts it in practice. Together with a team of researchers , he analysed what could happen when more and more investors use generative AI to make investment decisions. Now, normally, I would not write about simulations in a model environment, but alas, in this case I have no choice since we don’t really live in a world where AI-driven investments have taken on a major share of market action. But what happens when they do? Or rather, what is likely to happen as AI-driven investment becomes more popular? Let’s do a little thought experiment. Assume there is one dominant frontier model that has become the standard model for most investors, just like Google Search has become the dominant search engine ( and let’s ignore for a moment that I think that the future of AI will not be in large language models but many small local models ). If everybody uses the same tool to ask whether to buy or sell shares of company X, one would expect that they all get more or less the same answer. That is, the more investors use the same LLM the more they buy or sell the same stocks and that not only ruins the diversification effect, but makes markets overall riskier. But what if people use different models? Shouldn’t that give more variety in the answers? Well, not really. After all, the models use the same input data, so they tend to give the same answer, whether you use ChatGPT, Claude or DeepSeek. So again, no luck. The more people use AI, the more they will act in similar ways and create riskier markets and reduced diversification in their own portfolios. But what if the inputs change? If, for example the views of analysts change or the valuation changes, wouldn’t the AI models give different recommendations? This is what Lo and his colleagues simulated. They asked 7 LLMs 64 scenarios that differed in the fundamental and price inputs about a stock. They varied things like analyst consensus view, price momentum, valuation, and the volatility of the stock. Then they asked these models what to do with the stock and let them evaluate the fair value vs the current share price. This fundamental gap between the fair value and the current share price was then used to measure the correlation between different analyses of the same model with different input data for the stock. Sounds complicated, but look at the two charts below and I will explain. title: Which Quality Signal Works in India? A Horse Race of Four Quality Measures
venue: American Journal of Financial Technology and Innovation
abstract: Quality as in investment style focuses on identifying companies with superior quality characteristics that tend to outperform the relatively low quality companies selected on the basis of certain fundamental criteria. The present study attempts to compare the risk and return performance of four widely used quality measures, namely: gross profitability, the Piotroski F-score, Greenblatt’s Magic Formula, and the quality-minus-junk (QMJ) score. The study has selected NSE-listed firms excluding financial firms as universe and covers period starting from October 2002 to December 2025. Equi-weighted quintile based portfolios were formed on quarterly basis for each quality measure and evaluated on return, risk and the Carhart four-factor model. All four high-quality portfolios outperform the NIFTY 500, but only the Piotroski F-score separates high- from low-quality firms: its high-minus-low spread earns 0.82% per month (t = 3.69) with a Sharpe ratio of 0.23, and a Carhart alpha of 0.92% (t = 4.33) with modest factor loadings. Gross profitability, the Magic Formula and QMJ produce no raw spread; also their positive Carhart alphas arise because the high-quality firms they comprise of tilt towards large and growth stocks, which underperformed small and value stocks in India over the period.

title: Fintech Expansion
abstract: Abstract I study credit market outcomes with different competing lending technologies: a fintech lender that learns from data and can seize on-platform sales, and a banking sector that relies on physical collateral. Despite flexible information acquisition technology, endogenous fintech learning is surprisingly coarse, with a single threshold that screens out low-quality borrowers. As fintech lending technology improves, better enforcement harms, while better information technology benefits traditional banking sector profits. Big data technology enables the fintech to leverage data from its early-stage operations in unbanked markets to develop predictive models that support expansion into wealthier markets. (JEL G21, L13, L52, O33, O36)
summary: I study credit market outcomes with different competing lending technologies: a fintech lender that learns from data and can seize on-platform sales, and a banking sector that relies on physical collateral.

title: The upside of AI for investment analysis
abstract: I came across two really nice research papers that both look at the impact AI has on investment research. If you read the first one, it will lift your spirits, but if you read the other one, it is going to be a bit anticlimactic. Today, then, let me start with the positive news. Tomorrow, I will discuss the other study that shows us the flip side. The first study used Factset’s integration of Generative AI in 2023 as a natural experiment to examine what happens when analysts have access to AI. I can already hear my readers complain about how FactSet is not the best provider of financial data, and they would never use it, but instead prefer Bloomberg, LSEG Workspace or whatever data provider they use. Other readers will comment that Bloomberg’s data is not the same quality as FactSet, and a third group will claim that nothing is as good as IBES, which you can only get through Datastream, and so on. Truth is, I don’t use FactSet and am partial to Bloomberg (I clearly have expensive tastes), but in the end, it boils down to what you are used to and which provider and system you trust and can use best for your purposes. So, let’s move on from that debate and focus on what happens when FactSet introduced AI support in its tools. Apparently, the introduction of AI support was a success for FactSet. The chart below shows the percentage of analyst reports that quote a specific data provider as a source. In the third quarter 2023, Factset was a source in roughly 25% of all analyst reports, but by the end of 2024, that had risen to 50%. Analysts clearly loved the new feature in FactSet and switched from Refinitiv to FactSet. Data provider sourced by analysts Source: Xue et al. (2026) Closer inspection of the data shows that usage increased, particularly with smaller firms and larger teams, which indicates that it is likely that users didn’t cancel one subscription to switch to FactSet, but that users who already have FactSet used it more frequently. And the users of FactSet clearly found tremendous value in the AI feature. The second set of charts shows how the number of third-party sources changed for users of FactSet vs users who did not cite FactSet (Panel A). Thanks to the introduction of the AI feature, the users of FactSet found sources that they probably wouldn’t have found otherwise. The number of sources quoted in FactSet-supported research reports rose by roughly 26% after the AI feature was launched. Panel B below shows the number of topics covered in analyst reports. Because AI makes it easy to analyse topics influencing a stock, the number of topics covered in analyst reports that used FactSet rose by roughly 24%. Finally, AI allows for deeper quantitative analysis, and the number of analyses and tools used in analyst reports also rose by 21%. Plus, the reports produced with the help pf Factset were on average released quicker than reports from analysts that did not use Factset. Data provider sourced by analysts Source: Xue et al. title: Is It Better to Rent Forever?
abstract: With nominal U.S. home prices near record highs and 30-year fixed-rate mortgages exceeding 7%, many prospective homebuyers are debating: should I buy a home or keep renting? I know this because I'm one of them. Back in 2024, I ran the numbers on buying vs. renting and concluded that I would "remain a renter for the foreseeable future." Well, it's been two years and I'm still renting. Though U.S. home prices are technically 3.9% below their 2022 peak (after inflation) , nominal prices remain high and rates have gone up slightly since 2024. The math says I should keep renting based on my local housing market ($4,650/month to rent vs. ~$10,000/month all-in to buy). But I've started to wonder: can I do this forever? It's easy to justify renting when the circumstances make sense. Maybe rates are too high or prices have gotten a little ahead of themselves. But what if things never revert? What will I do in that scenario? Though the math suggests that I should be better off financially as a renter, what kind of risks does this entail? Renting for a few years is one thing, but what are the tradeoffs of renting for the long haul? Let's find out. The Case for Renting Forever Before we look at the downsides of being a forever renter, let's examine some of the primary benefits. Most of these benefits hold in any housing market, but the first one is based on today's higher rates and prices: More Wealth : All else equal, you would expect to end up with more wealth over the next few decades by being a renter (and investing the excess cash you save) versus borrowing and buying at today's rates and prices. This is because the money you save on your mortgage, taxes, insurance, and maintenance (relative to your rent) can compound over time and build more overall wealth. The best way to check, though, is to run the numbers . More Predictability : Even without running the numbers, renting has another clear advantage over buying—predictability. As the saying goes, "Rent is the most you’ll pay for housing. A mortgage is the least you’ll pay." Renters know how much they will pay for housing through the end of their lease term. Homeowners have no such assurances. While a mortgage is a predictable expense, property taxes, insurance, and maintenance are anything but. Property taxes and insurance tend to rise over time, sometimes sharply. And while many experts recommend budgeting 1% of your home's value annually for maintenance, such costs are rarely linear. For example, one year you may spend almost nothing on home maintenance while in another you spend a few percent of your home's value on a new roof or A/C unit. So while the average cost is around 1% (of home value) per year, you can't predict how much you might spend in any given year. Less Hassle : When you're a renter, you don't have to worry about fixing anything on the property. That's your landlord's responsibility. Collateral Demand in Wholesale Funding Markets
abstract: Abstract Repo markets are systemically important funding markets, but are also used by firms to obtain the assets provided as collateral. We build and structurally estimate a model of trade between heterogeneous firms in the sterling gilt repo market, and show that this collateral demand depresses repo market activity and can impede the transmission of monetary policy. We quantify how well-designed central bank repo facilities can improve outcomes: if the central bank were to lend out the assets on its balance sheet following quantitative easing, transmission and total firm surplus would improve by 20% and 38%, respectively.
summary: Repo markets are systemically important funding markets, but are also used by firms to obtain the assets provided as collateral.
finding: We build and structurally estimate a model of trade between heterogeneous firms in the sterling gilt repo market, and show that this collateral demand depresses repo market activity and can impede the transmission of monetary policy.

title: How the media treats climate change and other ‘crises’
abstract: Two months ago, I wrote about the way the German tabloid Bild undermined the German heating law with an emotionally charged campaign . In the meantime, I came across a study from the University of Lancaster that did something very similar, but on a broader basis and with UK newspapers. The researchers analysed the language used in ten UK newspapers in articles written about specific topics between 2015 and 2024. The five left-leaning newspapers are the Guardian, the Independent, iNews, the Mirror, and the Observer. The five right-leaning newspapers were the Express, the Mail, the Sun, the Telegraph and the Times. What is really interesting to see is what topics the newspapers on different ends of the political spectrum focus on and what they call a ‘crisis’. The analysis showed that there are plenty of crises in the world; it’s just that we can’t seem to agree on what is a crisis and what is not. The chart below shows the percentage of times a paper called something a ‘crisis’. Clearly, left-leaning papers emphasise climate change as a climate crisis, while right-leaning papers focus more on the energy crisis and the cost-of-living crisis after the 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Crisis, what crisis? (sorry, I couldn’t resist) Source: Tao and Ryan (2026) Similarly, when papers focus on the damage done by different events, they seem to agree on one thing: That there is a lot of damage done everywhere. They just can’t seem to agree on which damage is important. Left-leaning papers focus on environmental damage and damage to lifestyle and property, while right-leaning papers focus on damage to infrastructure (e.g. the potholes on roads) and the financial and business damage from different events and developments. Damage, what damage? Source: Tao and Ryan (2026) And of course, what the papers focus on shapes what their readers perceive as important. And thus, the political debate and the actions taken by the government and in Parliament.
summary: Two months ago, I wrote about the way the German tabloid Bild undermined the German heating law with an emotionally charged campaign .

title: Financial Performance and Cost Efficiency in the Textile Industry: Analysis of Square Textile PLC and Paramount Textile PLC
publisher: Academic Journal of Digital Economics and Stability
venue: Academic Journal of Digital Economics and Stability
abstract: The textile industry plays a significant role in the economic development of Uzbekistan, contributing to industrial production, employment generation, export diversification, and the development of value-added manufacturing. However, increasing competition in international markets, fluctuations in raw material prices, high energy consumption, inefficient resource utilization, and rising production expenses create considerable challenges for textile enterprises. Therefore, the implementation of modern cost optimization strategies has become an essential condition for improving financial performance and ensuring long-term competitiveness. This comparative analysis utilizes Cost-Volume-Profit (CVP) analysis to examine the cost structures and financial performance of Square Textile PLC and Paramount Textile PLC within the textile industry in Bangladesh. The study is based on secondary data from the company's FY 2022-23 annual report. Researchers found that Paramount Textile PLC demonstrates superior cost efficiency and profitability potential across multiple financial metrics compared to Square Textile PLC. Paramount Textile PLC exhibits a lower variable cost percentage, higher contribution margin ratio, and more efficient management of fixed costs relative to its contribution margin, leading to higher operating profit percentages and lower break-even sales levels. Both companies maintain a high margin of safety percentages. Still, Paramount Textile PLC's slightly higher margin of safety suggests a stronger financial position, potentially due to more efficient cost management or higher profit margins. These findings underscore the significance of cost efficiency and effective financial management in driving longterm profitability and economic resilience in the competitive textile industry. The study suggests that Square Textile PLC should focus on optimizing variable and fixed costs, improving operational efficiency, and reviewing its pricing strategy to enhance profitability and competitiveness in the market. Paramount Textile PLC should continue its focus on maintaining cost control, optimizing product mix, investing in innovation, and further exploring opportunities for market expansion to strengthen its position and profitability in the industry.
summary: The textile industry plays a significant role in the economic development of Uzbekistan, contributing to industrial production, employment generation, export diversification, and the development of value-added manufacturing.

title: Social Media Hype, Investor Sentiment and Retail Investor Participation in the Nigerian Capital Market: A Systematic Literature Review
publisher: International Journal of Modern Science and Research Technology
venue: International Journal of Modern Science and Research Technology
abstract: The use of social media as platforms for communicating financially has increased the avenues through which retail investors obtain investment information, share market views, and react to investment chances. Nevertheless, the dissemination of investment advice, speculation, and market narratives via social media may affect the sentiment of the investor and the behavior traits like herding and Fear of Missing Out (FOMO). This research aims at examining the connection between social media hype, investor sentiment, and participation of retail investors in the Nigerian capital market. The research focuses on the effects of social media hype on investor sentiment, the connection between investor sentiment and retail participation, the behavioral effects of social media hype, herding and FOMO on investment decisions, and digital financial communication and its role in developing investment sentiments. A systematic literature review based on the PRISMA 2020 guidelines was employed. Articles written in the English language from January 2021 to 2026 were obtained using Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar, complemented by a manual search of reference lists. Among the 232 references obtained from the search process, 19 studies were noted as meeting the inclusion requirements and were included for analysis. The literature reviewed suggests that studies from Nigeria provide insights into social media sentiments, stock market behavior, investor sentiments, and other forms of digital financial transactions. Studies from other countries, on the other hand, can contribute theories and additional comparisons. Evidence connecting social media exposure and investor sentiment to retail investors' participation in the Nigerian stock market, especially in IPOs, is lacking. This study aims to contribute through the synthesis of available evidence and identification of gaps in theory, methodology, and context. There is a need for contextspecific empirical evidence using accurate measurement of investment social media exposure and investor sentiment, as well as longitudinal approach and transaction data.
summary: The use of social media as platforms for communicating financially has increased the avenues through which retail investors obtain investment information, share market views, and react to investment chances.
finding: There is a need for contextspecific empirical evidence using accurate measurement of investment social media exposure and investor sentiment, as well as longitudinal approach and transaction data.

title: Reinforcement Learning-Based Stock Selection and Trading Using KOSPI 200 Constituents
abstract: Equity-market trading systems must account for constraints such as integer-share trading, transaction fees, and taxes. This study proposes a reinforcement learning-based trading system (RLTS) for strategy-based stock selection and subsequent trading simulation in the Korean stock market. Daily price data for stocks included in the Korea Composite Stock Price Index 200 (KOSPI 200) from 2011 to 2021 were used to generate technical-indicator inputs. An asynchronous advantage actor–critic (A3C) algorithm was used to train a shared network across stocks, and stocks with positive mean excess training returns relative to contemporaneous short-term benchmark rates were selected as the selected stock set. Stocks selected using 3-, 6-, 9-, and 12-month training windows were evaluated during subsequent testing periods, and their trading performance was compared with that obtained using the implemented deep Q-network (DQN) and policy-gradient (PG) baselines. The A3C-based configuration achieved positive average trading returns and positive annualized Sharpe ratios based on three-month out-of-sample returns across all training-window widths. The 9-month configuration produced the highest average return (11.43%), whereas the 12-month configuration produced the highest annualized three-month out-of-sample Sharpe ratio (0.57). The A3C-based configuration showed higher observed average trading returns than the implemented DQN and PG baselines across the evaluated training-window settings. Relative to the KOSPI 200 buy-and-hold benchmark, A3C produced higher average returns for the 9- and 12-month configurations but lower average returns for the 3- and 6-month configurations. These findings indicate that the relative performance of the RLTS depends on the evaluated configuration and should not be interpreted as uniform superiority over the market.
summary: Equity-market trading systems must account for constraints such as integer-share trading, transaction fees, and taxes.
finding: Relative to the KOSPI 200 buy-and-hold benchmark, A3C produced higher average returns for the 9- and 12-month configurations but lower average returns for the 3- and 6-month configurations.

title: Intelligent When Sold, Mechanical When Sued: The Strategic Ontology of Artificial Intelligence
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Contemporary legal, philosophical, and policy debates surrounding artificial intelligence frequently stall on an abstract metaphysical question: whether machine-learning systems are genuinely intelligent, creative, or autonomous. This paper shifts the inquiry from intrinsic ontology to *strategic ontology*—the patterned institutional practice of assigning shifting, context-dependent identities to the same technical artifact across commercial, contractual, judicial, and regulatory domains. Drawing on science and technology studies, tort and copyright jurisprudence, and comparative corporate discourse from 2023 through 2026, we identify eight recurring ontological registers grouped across four structural polarities: creative partners versus mere statistical systems, independent agents versus neutral tools, controllable products versus unpredictable emergent phenomena, and humanity-level technologies versus uncontrollable geopolitical forces. While complex sociotechnical systems can legitimately exhibit heterogeneous functional properties, ontological switching demands institutional scrutiny whenever its asymmetries run in one direction—concentrating revenue, equity valuation, intellectual property, and cultural prestige inside model-deploying firms while dispersing verification burdens, psychological labor, and failure costs across creators, annotators, employees, users, and third parties. Through a seven-stage lifecycle ledger, an examination of five governing industry abstractions, a reflexive methodological protocol treating the large language model as an "industry-made mirror" with explicit epistemic limits, and three primary-source legal and regulatory case studies, we develop a seven-part interrogative audit framework and propose the legal principle of *ontological estoppel*. Rather than presuming hidden corporate conspiracy, the paper demonstrates that the most revealing dynamics of contemporary artificial intelligence are public contradictions awaiting precise shared vocabulary. Keywords: Strategic Ontology, Artificial Intelligence Governance, Anthropomorphism, Moral Crumple Zones, AI Liability, Copyright and Fair Use, AI Alignment, Open-Washing, Reflexive Methodology, Ontological Estoppel, Sociotechnical Imaginaries, Accountability
summary: Contemporary legal, philosophical, and policy debates surrounding artificial intelligence frequently stall on an abstract metaphysical question: whether machine-learning systems are genuinely intelligent, creative, or autonomous.

title: Behavioural Insights into Investment Analysis: Understanding Investor Perception in Contemporary Stock Markets
authors: CH V L L Kusuma Kumari
abstract: This paper examines the behavior motivators of investment decision in modern stock markets with the focus on how, investor perception and emotions and biases and thinking process affect market operations. Although traditional finance focuses on rational decision-making models, the concept of irrationality, and psychological factors which largely influence the results of the stock market are presented by behavioral finance. This paper illuminates how these psychological biases influence the strategy of both individuals and groups when investing, and therefore by exploring investor sentiment, herd behavior, overconfidence, loss aversion, and framing effects, we can understand the influence of these biases on their behavior in the market. The study combines both the empirical and theoretical data to learn the interaction between psychological factors and fluctuations in the market and points out the consequences of the research to the retail and institutional investors. The paper also contains implications that can be of use to investors and policy makers and gives strategies to alleviate the effects of the cognitive biases and make better decisions during the event of uncertainty.
summary: This paper examines the behavior motivators of investment decision in modern stock markets with the focus on how, investor perception and emotions and biases and thinking process affect market operations.
finding: The paper also contains implications that can be of use to investors and policy makers and gives strategies to alleviate the effects of the cognitive biases and make better decisions during the event of uncertainty.

title: Trust and Lottery-Related Anomalies
abstract: We examine whether social trust shapes the pricing of lottery-like stocks by influencing investors' beliefs regarding optimistic information associated with extreme future payoffs. We argue that higher social trust reduces investors' skepticism toward optimistic information associated with extreme future payoffs, increasing demand for lottery-type stocks and leading to overpricing and lower subsequent returns. Using a sample of 8,875 firms across 49 US states over the period 1996-2018 and MAX as a proxy for lottery-like characteristics, we show that the MAX effect is concentrated in regions with relatively high trust and is weak or absent in regions with relatively low trust. We further find that this trust conditioning is stronger in regions with lower education or income levels, consistent with social trust playing a relatively more important role when investors have more limited access to private information. The results are robust to alternative lottery proxies and a range of robustness checks. Our findings identify social trust as a novel determinant of the pricing of lottery-like stocks and provide evidence that social capital may amplify belief-driven mispricing in assets with highly skewed payoffs.
summary: We examine whether social trust shapes the pricing of lottery-like stocks by influencing investors' beliefs regarding optimistic information associated with extreme future payoffs.
finding: We further find that this trust conditioning is stronger in regions with lower education or income levels, consistent with social trust playing a relatively more important role when investors have more limited access to private information.

title: When Will Buy the Dip Stop Working?
abstract: Ten years ago Nvidia was a $50 billion company. Heading into the 2020s, the market cap was $150 billion and video game GPUs were its main business line. title: Taylor Swift kills people
abstract: [Warning: Satire] And so do other megastars, but only on certain days. Using the phone while driving is so distracting that most countries have outlawed it because it creates increased risks of car accidents. But you know what else causes a lot of distraction for drivers? A brand-new album by their favourite musician. After all, if you are a Taylor Swift fan and she drops her latest album, you may want to listen to it on your drive to work, for example. But because it is a new album, you probably pay more attention than usual to the music and less to the traffic around you. In other words, you get distracted. A group of researchers wanted to test this hypothesis that new albums cause traffic accidents. To do this, the researchers analysed the traffic accidents in the US between 2017 and 2022 and compared them to the days when the most successful new records were released. The table below shows the days and who the culprit is, I mean, who released the album. Top 10 most streamed albums in a single day from 2017 to 2022 Source: Patel et al. (2026) On the days of these album releases, online streaming of music increased typically by 43%, but unfortunately, so did traffic accidents. On average, distracted drivers caused about 20 more fatalities on the day the albums were released compared to the ten days before or after the release. In conclusion, Taylor Swift kills people, and so do Drake, Bad Bunny and all the superstars who release albums. When will insurance companies hold them to account? When will the government prohibit driving on days of major album releases? When will streaming providers introduce driver safety features that block new albums from being streamed in a car? Important questions to ponder while we head into the weekend. Change in traffic fatalities around major album release dates Source: Patel et al. (2026)

title: Weekend Reads – 11/20/26
abstract: Quote for the Week The popular view of diversification is not putting all your eggs in one basket. If you place all your bets on one holding, you can win big or lose big, but the possible range of outcomes is wide. If you spread your bets across a number of holdings, the odds are that you will not be wrong on all of them or right on all of them. Then the range of outcomes will be narrower. Or will it? Suppose all those holdings you bet on move in sympathy with one another. If you had held all 50 of the “favorite fifty” in the early 1970s, your portfolio would not have been diversified at all: Those 50 stocks went merrily up together and horrifyingly down together. The 50 holdings acted like one holding. The first lesson of Modern Portfolio Theory is that diversification has more to do with seeking assets whose prices move in different kinds of rhythms than it has to do with proliferating the number of baskets in which you carry your eggs. A few holdings with radically different types of market behavior will do more to smooth out the pattern of portfolio returns than 50 or 100 holdings that move up and down together. — Peter Bernstein ( source ) From the Archives Asset Allocation Drives Returns When Investment is Most Businesslike Last Call Vaguely Right > Exactly Wrong – Net Worthwhile 30 Things I Know about Money at 30 – Your Brain on Money Investor Misbehavior: Recency Bias is the Investor’s Worst Enemy – L. Intellectual capital efficiency and operating performance in ASEAN pharmaceutical firms: the moderating role of R&D intensity
abstract: This study examines whether R&D intensity moderates the relationship between intellectual capital efficiency and operating performance among publicly listed pharmaceutical firms in six ASEAN countries. The sample comprises 596 firm-year observations from 70 firms over the 2015–2024 period and is analysed using a two-way fixed-effects model. Intellectual capital efficiency is measured using the Value-Added Intellectual Coefficient (VAIC), operating performance by return on invested capital (ROIC) and R&D intensity by R&D expenditure relative to sales. The baseline results show a positive but statistically insignificant association between VAIC and ROIC. Contrary to the hypothesised positive moderation, the contemporaneous VAIC–R&D interaction is negative and statistically significant in the combined sample. The marginal effects remain positive at the three evaluated R&D levels, namely 0%, the sample mean and the 90th percentile, suggesting attenuation rather than reversal at these levels. Component-level analysis reveals heterogeneous patterns, with positive interactions for HCE and CEE but a negative interaction for SCE. Although the negative interaction is retained under several alternative specifications, the lagged interaction is not statistically significant, and excluding Singapore reverses the contemporaneous interaction to a positive coefficient. The contribution centres on a weakening contemporaneous VAIC–ROIC association whose generalisability is limited by sensitivity to predictor timing and country composition. Unresolved endogeneity further precludes interpreting this association as a causal mechanism.
summary: This study examines whether R&D intensity moderates the relationship between intellectual capital efficiency and operating performance among publicly listed pharmaceutical firms in six ASEAN countries.
finding: Although the negative interaction is retained under several alternative specifications, the lagged interaction is not statistically significant, and excluding Singapore reverses the contemporaneous interaction to a positive coefficient.

title: The Cost of Human Frailty: Nvidia's Jensen Huang Test!
abstract: In a month full of big stories, perhaps the biggest business story was the fall from grace of Jensen Huang and the consequences for Nvidia, investors, and the rest of the AI trade. The initial story, with its potent mix of personal fallibility and security concerns, related to Jensen’s affair with Alice Huang, who news stories labeled a Chinese spy, though the evidence on the ground is still thin. I had planned to write about the story then, but on the road in Asia and with teaching commitments, I put it off for a few days, and over those days, the story took a turn, with stories of dalliances with Nvidia employees. Last week culminated with Nvidia’s board asking Jensen to step down, and his agreeing, perhaps bringing to an end one of the more eventful and productive stints as a CEO in corporate history. I have no desire or standing to debate the moral aspects of this story, and I will let others take sides on whether the board should or should not have fired Jensen. In this post, I will focus on the question of what Jensen stepping down as CEO might mean for Nvidia’s value, and whether after the market correction over the last three weeks, the market has overreached. What does a CEO do? What does a CEO do for a business? Given the many tasks that go into creating, building, and running a business, it should come as no surprise that the list is long, but I will classify them broadly into groups: Storyteller: Every business is built around a story, and that story drives its valuation and sometimes its pricing. While that story is grounded in the company’s products and the markets that it seeks, it is the top manager’s job to craft and tell the story to investors, employees and to consumers. Clearly, the significance of this component of a CEO’s story will shift, depending on where the company is in its life cycle, with its importance being greatest at either end of the life cycle. B usiness manager: It is of course CEO’s job to manage the business that they are put in charge off, but that can span the spectrum from building a business model, for young companies, to working on ways to scale up a business for high growth firms to defending a business model for mature businesses to scaling down the model, as the company enters the declining phase. People leader: Organizations are composed of people, including suppliers, employees and customers, and it is the top management’s job to lead these people, though the nature of that leadership will also shift as a company ages. Early on, when a company is still seeking out a business model and faces failure risk, it is to inspire people with vision and direction. As companies grow and mature, it is to create a corporate culture that retains employees, as competitors try to lure them away. In decline, when a company is shedding employees and shrinking, it is finding a way to do so as humanely as possible and find a soft landing, without destroying morale. title: What happens when a country increases taxes on the rich?
abstract: The UK used to be a popular place to live for billionaires because the resident-non-domiciled tax regime meant they only had to pay tax on their UK income, not their foreign income. However, successive governments in the UK have cracked down on that tax advantage while countries across Europe have introduced reduced tax regimes for rich people. The result is that we are witnessing a steady flow of super-rich leaving the UK, most notably hedge fund manager Chris Rokos, who moved to Greece , which means he will not pay the UK government £330m annually in taxes going forward. I did not know this, but apparently in 2012, the Netherlands experienced an exodus of highly paid people itself after it changed the eligibility rules for its so-called ‘30% ruling’. Ok, my readers in the Netherlands, hopefully forgive me when I try to summarise a tax change that I have no clue about. But as far as I understand, the Netherlands had a special tax regime for people moving to the Netherlands from abroad. In 2001, that scheme was modernised, and it allowed people from abroad to move to the country and pay a maximum 30% income tax rate for up to ten years as long as they were employed by a Dutch company and possessed special skills that were in demand in the Netherlands. After the ten-year grace period, the employees would pay normal tax rates in the Netherlands, so it was a time-limited incentive scheme for expats. Ok, so far so normal. Many countries have this kind of incentive scheme for highly skilled workers. But there were unintended consequences. For example, Dutch workers who spent more than ten years abroad could move back home and use this tax incentive scheme. And in companies close to the border, native workers were crowded out by foreign workers from across the border because these guys could benefit from the 30% ruling, while domestic Dutch workers could not. So, in 2012, the Dutch government changed the rules. From then on, only workers with a wage above a certain threshold were eligible for the scheme, and people who lived within 150km of the Dutch border were no longer eligible for the tax break. People who came to the Netherlands after 1 January 2007 and did not meet these criteria were only entitled to a five-year tax break, and new arrivals were not entitled to the tax break unless they met the new criteria. In essence, some of the roughly 55,000 people who used the tax scheme in 2012 suddenly saw their tax rates go up much sooner than they expected. So, what did they do? The chart below shows the change in population as a function of income. People who used the tax scheme but had incomes below the 90% threshold did not move away. They simply stayed and paid higher taxes when the scheme ran out. But the top 5% and top 1% income earners moved away. After the reform, these individuals were some 10% less likely to stay in the Netherlands, according to a study by Jose Giarola and his colleagues . Policy response to tax change Source: Giarola et al. (

finding: After the reform, these individuals were some 10% less likely to stay in the Netherlands, according to a study by Jose Giarola and his colleagues .

Green Value Investing in the Banking Sector: The Effectiveness of a Green F-Score Strategy in Poland as a CEE Case Study
abstract: The banking sector serves as a critical transmission belt for capital allocation toward renewable energy (RE) projects, yet traditional equity valuation models fail to capture banks’ exposure to energy transition risks. To bridge this gap, this paper develops a novel fundamental–environmental indicator—the “Green F-Score”—tested on 10 major commercial banks listed on the Warsaw Stock Exchange (WSE) between 2023 and 2025. By synthesizing classical financial efficiency criteria with EU Taxonomy disclosures (Green Asset Ratio), the portfolio sorting methodology reveals how capital markets price sustainable energy financing in Central and Eastern Europe. The empirical results indicate that portfolios with high environmental–fundamental readiness (“Green Leaders”) generate a higher mean annual return of 60.43% and a higher price-to-book (P/B) premium than laggards (15.41%), although inter-group ANOVA differences are not statistically significant (p = 0.215) given the small sample (N = 30). Correlation analysis indicates that the market premium is significantly associated with the ESG sub-score (r = 0.40, p = 0.028), rendering traditional financial metrics an operational hygiene factor. Consequently, the Green F-Score emerges as a promising exploratory tool for institutional investors assessing transition readiness in commercial banks.
summary: The banking sector serves as a critical transmission belt for capital allocation toward renewable energy (RE) projects, yet traditional equity valuation models fail to capture banks’ exposure to energy transition risks.

title: The Rocky Road from Aggregate to Per Share Value: Anthropic's IPO update
abstract: I valued Anthropic in a post on November 2, 2026, and while estimating a value of $1.475 trillion for the equity in the company, I noted that the share count was a placeholder, while we waited for bankers to make a final judgment on how many shares would be outstanding in the company. I promised that I would return to complete the per share valuation, when the details were made available, and an updated prospectus filed last week filled that gap. The world has not stayed still in the fifteen days since my original valuation, and both company-level and macro developments require an update to my valuation. The prospectus was updated to include third quarter numbers, and the midterm elections have potentially altered the economics of the AI business, as data centers may become more difficult and expensive to build and AI regulations may become more stringent. In this post, I will start with a general discussion of how share count is complicated by the existence of multiple classes of shares and stock-based compensation, and argue that the absence of standardization has made share count the Wild West in investing, with consequences for both intrinsic valuation and pricing. I will then update my valuation of Anthropic and assess the per share value, based on the prospectus that was just filed. The Elusive Share Count When I first started valuing companies, getting from aggregate value to equity value per share was a trivial exercise, where you divided the aggregate value by the number of shares outstanding. This was, of course, a period when almost every US company had only one class of shares and stock-based compensation was still in its nascent stages, and lightly used. That is no longer the case, and while tedious, I think that the process of understanding share count has to start with the basics of what goes into that number for publicly traded companies. Primary share count : The primary share count is obtained by looking at the shares in the company, across all classes of shares. That information is usually embedded in the balance sheet or in the footnotes, but with different numbers usually for authorized, issued and outstanding shares. The authorized share count is the least relevant of the numbers and is just a measure of the total number of shares that the company can issue, with an increase beyond it requiring a fresh authorization. The shares issued are a measure of the shares that the company issued to the market and while shares outstanding match shares issued for most firms, the presence of treasury stock (stock acquired back by a company, but held by the company) can cause outstanding shares to be lower than issued shares. Restricted shares : Restricted shares comprised shares that have been issued by the company to its employees, though in rare cases, they can also be issued to the public. The restrictions take two forms. With employee issuances, there can be a vesting requirement, where an employee has to work for a specified period

title: What the last two bubbles tell us about the AI boom
abstract: My latest piece for Reuters is out this morning and I talk a little bit about whether this bubble will pop or just slowly deflate. I am particularly chuffed with my charts about the analyst recommendations at the start of each bear market in 2000 and 2008. As you might imagine, they didn’t warn investors to sell their stocks, but the lopsidedness of their recommendations is something to behold. What the last two bubbles tell us about the AI boom LONDON, Nov 18 (Reuters) - Wall Street analysts were overwhelmingly bullish at the peak of the 1990s tech bubble and on the eve of the 2008 global financial crisis. The same is true of AI stocks today even as bad news accumulates. The question now may ​be whether the current stock boom ends with a bang or a whimper. title: The changing stock market reaction to inflation surprises
abstract: I keep coming back to this post on why I think working in finance is so fascinating and never boring. Things change all the time. And even if the same thing happens again and again, stocks, bonds and other assets react differently to the same event all the time. That post looked at stock market reaction to economic surprises from the 1990s to the 2010s, but since the pandemic, things have changed yet again. A team from the Bank of Italy has analysed how stock markets in the US and Europe react to inflation surprises. Admittedly, we had rather a lot of surprises in inflation over the last five years. The chart below shows the surprises in US inflation vs the expectations in inflation surveys among economists and investors. Obviously, we had particularly large surprises after the war in Ukraine started, but what is notable is how big the cumulative surprises were over time. US inflation surprises Source: D’Andrea et al. (2025) Now, traditionally, we finance professionals are trained to think about higher-than-expected inflation as a negative thing for stocks because it increases costs, thus reducing profits. And higher inflation, if it persists, increases the cost of capital and the discount rate for future cash flows. The effect is more pronounced for stocks with a lot of debt and financial leverage because for them the impact on the net present value of future cash flows is larger. Ok, so what really happened? The chart below shows the price action of stocks on the day of the inflation surprise. The independent variable is the size of the inflation surprise times the financial leverage of the company, measured as the ratio of debt with more than five-year maturity divided by total assets. That’s all very technical, but the bottom line is that before 2020, a positive inflation surprise was negative for the share price, and it was more negative for companies with higher financial leverage on the balance sheet. Just as we knew it would happen. But look at the share price reaction since 2020. All of a sudden, it is in the opposite direction. Higher inflation is positive for the share price, and it is even better for highly levered companies. Huh? The answer lies in the type of inflation shock we experienced since 2020 vs the 2010s. In the 2000s and 2010s inflation shocks were mostly demand-driven, i.e. inflation rose because the economy was growing hot. In this environment, the central bank can cool inflation by hiking interest rates and reducing economic growth. But since the pandemic the inflation shocks have been supply-driven shocks similar to the 1970s. In this environment, the central bank is powerless to reduce inflation because hiking interest rates is not going to move more tankers through the Strait of Hormuz. So, the inflation shock from supply-side disruptions tends to be more persistent and effectively creates a devaluation of nominal debt companies own. Hence, from the perspective of a company, such an inflation shock is great for their
summary: I keep coming back to this post on why I think working in finance is so fascinating and never boring.
finding: Higher inflation is positive for the share price, and it is even better for highly levered companies.

title: Wise Words on Handling Market Gyrations
abstract: Market volatility always picks up at random moments every year and somehow investors seem surprised about it. Being less surprised is one of the keys to investment success. In fact, it’s so important that Ben Graham dedicated a chapter to handling market fluctuations in his classic The Intelligent Investor . His parable of Mr. Market has been retold by others ( here , here , and here) over the years for the same reason. Mr. Market has a crazy streak. He also happens to be your partner in a number of business ventures. Mr. Market shows up day after day quoting a price to buy your shares or sell you his. And every so often, his craziness peaks and he rattles off some ridiculous prices for those shares. Sometimes those price quotes are much higher than they were the week before. Sometimes they’re much lower. And since Mr. Market is so unpredictable, there’s no telling what prices he’ll offer up next week. Now, it’s up to you to decide if you want to listen. You can take advantage of the offer or you can do nothing. But whatever you do, never get caught up in Mr. Market’s mood swings. You see, Mr. Market’s singular goal in life is to get you to buy his shares or sell him yours. He doesn’t care if you make money or lose it. He doesn’t care if he does either. To him, it’s all about the transaction. Day after day he does whatever he can to get you to act. The risk is in succumbing to his wishes too often. Now, investors have a few defenses against Mr. Market’s temptation to do something. First, know yourself. It’s key to investing. If you understand your temperament and tolerance for market swings, you can create a plan around it and build a portfolio you can stick with in good times and bad. The plan doesn’t have to be perfect. It only has to fit within your own constraints. Do that and you shouldn’t worry about the day-to-day moves in the market. The plan will take care of itself. This is especially true if your time horizon is measured in years. The short-term swings become less important the longer your time horizon stretches out. Second, study market history. You’ll quickly learn that Mr. Market’s current craziness is nothing new. He’s been acting up for centuries. The entirety of market history is an endless stretch of crazy volatility broken up by brief moments of calm. If you view it from that perspective, then volatility is normal. Finally, it never hurts to remind yourself of this either. Getting caught up in market gyrations has been an ongoing problem for investors for as long as stock markets have existed. Much ink has been spilled about it too, but the message is the same. Market gyrations may be normal but it’s best to be prepared for it just in case. *** The only significance of stock market gyrations to the true investor is that they give him an opportunity to buy good common stocks when they are cheap — or at least reasonably priced — and at times offer him an invitation to sell out at temptingly high levels. — Benjamin Graham *** The

abstract: The present study entitled “A Study on Retail Investors’ Investment Preferences, Stock Market Awareness and Participation Barriers in the Stock Market” examines the investment preferences and awareness of retail investors. The study is based on primary data collected from 125 respondents. A structured questionnaire was used to collect the required data. The collected data were analysed using percentage analysis. The study examines the preferred investment avenues of the respondents. It also studies their level of awareness and knowledge about the stock market. The findings show that equity shares are the most preferred investment avenue. Most respondents have a moderate level of stock market awareness. Self-learning and digital platforms are important sources of investment knowledge. Financial literacy is essential for improving investor knowledge. Proper investment guidance can help new investors make better decisions. Simple trading platforms can encourage greater participation. Greater transparency and investor protection can improve investor confidence. The study concludes that awareness, knowledge, and proper guidance are important for stock market participation. Improving these factors can encourage informed and confident investment decisions.
summary: The present study entitled “A Study on Retail Investors’ Investment Preferences, Stock Market Awareness and Participation Barriers in the Stock Market” examines the investment preferences and awareness of retail investors.
finding: The findings show that equity shares are the most preferred investment avenue.

title: Do venture capitalists beat a random benchmark?
abstract: No. I could leave it at that, but since some venture capitalists have annoyed me terribly in 2026, let’s embarrass them a little bit with the results of a study by Max Sina Knicker, Jean-Philippe Bouchaud, and Michael Benzaquen. Of course, this is not to say that all venture capitalists are unskilled, but when venture capital funds are being quoted in an article in the New York Times arguing that a bubble in AI is a good thing because how else would we be able to fund all those great ideas, then you deserve some ridicule. I mean, isn’t it the job of venture capital to allocate scarce capital to the best ideas? And didn’t we have a process called ‘due diligence’ to determine which ventures are most likely to succeed? It seems that in 2026, the philosophy among some venture capital funds is to fund everything and see what survives. Anyway, you get my annoyance with the profession. So, what the researchers did was to look at thousands of deals of US venture capital funds and then compare their performance (measured as money multiple at exit) with a benchmark where these funds simply chose investments at random. The charts below show the money multiples of the venture capital funds in coloured lines vs the random benchmark in black. If you can’t see the black line; that is the point. There is no statistical difference between the investments of venture capital funds and a monkey throwing darts on a list of potential ventures. Performance of venture capital investments vs random benchmark Source: Knicker et al. (2026) But it gets better. As in listed equity markets, the investments where you overpay the most tend to do the worst. The second chart today shows the rank of the investments made by venture capital funds, ranked from highest (rank=1) to lowest multiple. For each investment, the researchers calculate a z-score with the performance at exit and compare that to the average performance of a random investment made with a similar entry multiple. Performance vs random benchmark as function of entry level multiple Source: Knicker et al. (2026) The negative z-scores for investments with a low rank indicate that venture capital funds tend to perform worse with investments where they pay high multiples on entry. The z-scores close to zero or above zero for higher-ranked investments indicate that venture capital funds tend to perform as expected or better than expected for investments made at lower multiples. Just like many investors in listed stock markets, venture capital funds tend to overpay for trophy assets with high growth prospects, and in the process of doing so reduce the performance of their funds. So maybe it would be better to replace some venture capital fund managers with a random number generator (or trained monkeys throwing darts)? It probably would save investors a lot of fees and improve performance at the same time…
summary: I could leave it at that, but since some venture capitalists have annoyed me terribly in 2026, let’s embarrass them a little bit with the results of a study by Max Sina Knicker, Jean-Philippe Bouchaud, and Michael Benzaquen.
finding: The z-scores close to zero or above zero for higher-ranked investments indicate that venture capital funds tend to perform as expected or better than expected for investments made at lower multiples.

title: How Much Should You Have Saved for Retirement by Age?
abstract: One of the most common questions around saving for retirement is: Am I on track? While it's a good question to ask, there are a lot of factors that influence the answer. Between your future spending, your age, your family situation, and your financial goals, knowing whether you're saving enough is harder than it looks. But what if there was a better way? What if we could find a good enough answer rather than trying to chase the perfect one? What if we relied on data instead of guesswork? That's what this post is about. There have been a lot of articles on how much you should have saved for retirement by age. But I haven't seen one that does a deep dive on how much Americans actually have saved for retirement and what this means for your retirement savings. So let's get started. What the Traditional Retirement Savings Advice Says The traditional retirement savings advice says that you should have a certain amount saved for retirement by a given age. For example, Fidelity argued that you should have a certain multiple of your salary saved based on your age: Age 30 = 1x Age 35 = 2x Age 40 = 3x Age 45 = 4x Age 50 = 6x Age 55 = 7x Age 60 = 8x Age 67 = 10x So if you were 30 and making $100k/year, you would need to have $100k [1x income] in retirement savings. If you were 45 and making $100k/year, you would need $400k [4x income] in retirement savings. And so forth. Below is a chart showing how much you would need to have saved by age for a $50k, $100k, and $200k income using the benchmark above: This isn't a bad rule to follow, but it isn't a great one either. One of the problems with income-based savings guidelines is that income can be quite volatile. For example, if your income doubles within a decade, should we also double what you need to save for retirement? What if you work a commission-based role and have a killer year? Do we use that year of income to determine how much you need to save for retirement, or do we use an average of your income? What if you have a high-paying job, but then get laid off? If you take a new role that is much lower paying, do we revise your retirement needs downward to reflect your new (lower) income? I understand that these are rough guidelines, but they can be hard to follow if your income is even slightly unstable. But the other big problem with income-based savings guidelines is that most U.S. households aren't meeting them. Let's look at how much Americans actually have saved for retirement to see why. How Much Do Americans Actually Have Saved for Retirement? Unfortunately, the data on retirement savings in America isn't great. The median retirement account balance among all U.S. households is just $5k (from the 2025 SCF data ). There are two reasons for this. First, there's a large variation in retirement savings by age cohort. For example, the youngest households and the oldest households tend to have less retirement savings than everyone else: Why is this the case? For the youngest, they haven't had as much ti
summary: One of the most common questions around saving for retirement is: Am I on track?
finding: If you take a new role that is much lower paying, do we revise your retirement needs downward to reflect your new (lower) income?

title: Dimensional Expands Australian ETF Offering with Two New Strategies
Beyond Bitcoin - The Allocator Perspective: Why Digital Asset Benchmarking Is Entering a New Era
Simulation-Based Strategy Valuation Under Uncertainty: Risk Aggregation and Liquidity Constraints in a Manufacturing SME
venue: Journal of risk and financial management
abstract: Strategic valuation in financially constrained SMEs requires the joint consideration of expected value, operational performance, working-capital exposure, and liquidity risk under uncertainty. This study develops a simulation-based strategy valuation framework for an Ecuadorian manufacturing SME by integrating commercial, operational, logistics, working-capital, and financing variables within a dynamic operational-financial model. Monte Carlo simulation propagates uncertainty over a 36-month horizon under multiple environmental regimes and generates distributions of net present value (NPV), free cash flow (FCF), return on invested capital (ROIC), EBITDA margin, cash conversion cycle (CCC), and cash-stress indicators. The current analysis shows substantial heterogeneity across strategic configurations in both value creation and liquidity exposure, with working-capital conditions materially influencing the conversion of operating improvements into cash and economic value. The results also indicate that expected financial performance alone is insufficient for strategy evaluation when liquidity constraints and downside exposure are considered. The revised framework therefore complements primary financial metrics with scenario, distributional, and multicriteria robustness analyses rather than treating a single composite ranking as conclusive. The study contributes to decision-oriented corporate valuation by integrating operational and financial risk aggregation with strategic choice in an SME setting and provides a reproducible framework for examining how working-capital and financing constraints shape firm value under uncertainty.
summary: Strategic valuation in financially constrained SMEs requires the joint consideration of expected value, operational performance, working-capital exposure, and liquidity risk under uncertainty.
finding: The current analysis shows substantial heterogeneity across strategic configurations in both value creation and liquidity exposure, with working-capital conditions materially influencing the conversion of operating improvements into cash and economic value.

title: Determinants of Share Price Movement: A Comparative Study of Fundamental and Sentimental Factors in the NSE
publisher: International Journal of Research Publication and Reviews
venue: International Journal of Research Publication and Reviews
abstract: This study investigates the relative impact of fundamental and sentiment-driven factors on share price appreciation within the National Stock Exchange (NSE). Utilizing primary data collected from 60 active investors in Malappuram district through purposive sampling and secondary quarterly time-series data across six prominent Indian equities (Tata Power, Adani Green Energy, NTPC, Amara Raja Energy & Mobility, Sona BLW, and Servotech Power Systems), the research evaluates structural valuation anchors against behavioral sentiment spikes. The findings establish that while long-term fundamental metrics (EPS, P/E ratio, ROE, and earnings growth) dictate intrinsic value, short-term volatility and acute price deviations are governed by market speculation, investor psychology, and news flow.
summary: This study investigates the relative impact of fundamental and sentiment-driven factors on share price appreciation within the National Stock Exchange (NSE).
finding: The findings establish that while long-term fundamental metrics (EPS, P/E ratio, ROE, and earnings growth) dictate intrinsic value, short-term volatility and acute price deviations are governed by market speculation, investor psychology, and news flow.

title: The relationship between Twitter uncertainty measures and stock market returns during the COVID-19 crisis
abstract: Purpose This paper aims to explore how uncertainty captured through social media, particularly Twitter, affects global stock markets during the COVID-19 crisis. It focuses on whether the Twitter economic uncertainty (TEU) and Twitter Market Uncertainty (TMU) indices contain information that helps explain market behaviour in periods of stress. Design/methodology/approach The analysis relies on daily data from January 2007 to May 2023. This paper combines linear and nonlinear Granger causality tests (Diks and Panchenko, 2006) with the BDS nonlinearity test, and a Dynamic Conditional Correlation-Generalized Autoregressive Conditional Heteroskedasticity (DCC-GARCH) connectedness framework is used (Gabauer, 2020) to capture the dynamic transmission of volatility between Twitter-based sentiment indicators and 13 international financial markets. Findings The results highlight strong nonlinear causal effects from Twitter-based uncertainty measures to market returns. TEU and TMU indices appear to drive fluctuations in stock returns, particularly during episodes of heightened uncertainty. The DCC-GARCH analysis shows that TEU-ENG and TEU-USA act as net transmitters of volatility to markets such as Japan, Ukraine, China, Germany and even Bitcoin. Research limitations/implications As the study focuses mainly on the COVID-19 crisis, future research could extend the analysis to other stress periods or explore alternative sentiment measures such as the volatility index. Practical implications The findings suggest that social media sentiment can serve as a timely indicator for risk managers and investors, complementing traditional uncertainty measures. Social implications The results highlight how collective behaviour on social networks can amplify uncertainty and market reactions, underscoring the need for responsible communication and better public understanding of financial information online. Originality/value This study offers fresh evidence on how Twitter-based uncertainty indices interact with market dynamics, combining behavioral–finance insights with nonlinear econometric techniques.
summary: This paper aims to explore how uncertainty captured through social media, particularly Twitter, affects global stock markets during the COVID-19 crisis.
finding: Practical implications The findings suggest that social media sentiment can serve as a timely indicator for risk managers and investors, complementing traditional uncertainty measures.

title: Why Clearer Loan Disclosure Beats a Standardized Contract
abstract: In a 2018 Consumer Reports survey of U.S. adults, about two-thirds (64%) said they thought they were paying more in unexpected or hidden fees than they had five years earlier. Regulators have traditionally addressed this problem in two ways: requiring lenders to provide clearer information or encouraging them to offer standardized financial products. Both approaches aim to protect consumers, but which one actually improves financial outcomes? Better loan disclosure may help borrowers understand what they are signing. Standardization, meanwhile, may simplify decisions by reducing the complexity of available products. Yet neither approach guarantees that consumers will make better choices. The U.S. survey is about fees on services, not loans, but a new Journal of Financial Economics study tests both approaches using Chilean bank consumer loans. Removing the fine print: Disclosure, standardized products, and consumer outcomes Sheisha Kulkarni, Santiago Truffa, Gonzalo Iberti Journal of Financial Economics, November 2026, Vol. 185, Article 104353 A version of this paper can be found here Want to read our summaries of academic finance papers? Check out our Academic Research Insight category Key Academic Insights Better Disclosure Can Significantly Reduce Loan Delinquency The authors examine Chilean consumer lending regulations introduced in 2011 and 2012. The first reform introduced standardized loan contracts with improved disclosure, while the second extended the disclosure requirements to all consumer loans. Using administrative lending data and a regulatory loan-size threshold, the authors compare borrowers exposed to different requirements. They find that improved disclosure reduced delinquency by 13.7 percentage points, a 40% reduction relative to an average delinquency rate of about 34%, and reduced default by 1.68 percentage points, or 98%. Standardization, by contrast, had no overall effect. The results suggest that making financial information more accessible can materially improve borrowers’ ability to meet their repayment obligations. Disclosure Matters More Than Standardization for Many Borrowers One of the paper’s central contributions is separating the effects of disclosure from those of standardized financial products. By exploiting the timing of the two reforms, the authors find that improved disclosure accounts for nearly all the reduction in delinquency around the regulatory threshold. Standardized contracts, by contrast, do not generate a significant additional improvement for borrowers near that threshold. This distinction matters because simplifying financial products and improving financial information are not necessarily equivalent interventions. For relatively sophisticated borrowers, understanding the terms of an existing product may be more valuable than being offered a standardized alternative. title: About those net zero targets
abstract: Last Monday , I wrote about how companies have dialled down their public communication on DEI programmes. Another big topic of the post-pandemic years was net zero targets. What was the impact of these targets on emissions so far? The proliferation of net zero targets started in earnest after the pandemic. The chart below, taken from a study by Simon Dietz and Nikolaus Hastreiter, shows that of roughly 2,000 global large-cap companies, only 70 had committed to long-term net zero targets at the end of 2019. By the end of 2024, this had risen to more than 1,200 companies, accounting for two-thirds of the combined market cap of the sample. Number of companies with net zero targets Source: Dietz and Hastreiter (2026) Of course, many of these net zero targets are far in the future (typically between 2040 and 2050), but at least we can measure the progress so far. And that doesn’t look too convincing. The charts below show the change in absolute emissions and emissions intensity after a company adopted net zero targets. On the positive side, we can see a trend towards lower emissions, with an average emissions reduction of about 15% and an average emissions intensity reduction of nearly 10% three years after a company adopted net zero targets. So the trend goes in the right direction. But it is not strong enough to be statistically significant. Now that may change as emissions reductions increase, but at least for now, we cannot say that the adoption of net zero targets has significantly reduced greenhouse gas emissions. Greenhouse gas emissions after the adoption of net zero targets Source: Dietz and Hastreiter (2026)

title: Global Stocks Are Expected to Rally in 2027 Even as Earnings Growth Slows
Structural Alpha: A Missing Category in China's Index Enhancement Market — A Three-Layer Attribution Framework for Futures-Based Index Enhancement Products
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: China's index enhancement market, with over RMB 3 trillion in quantitative strategy AUM, implicitly equates "index enhancement" with "factor-based stock selection enhancement." The standard evaluation tool—Barra multi-factor analysis—assumes that excess returns originate from cross-sectional factor exposures in equity portfolios. However, a subset of index enhancement products uses stock index futures (rather than stock portfolios) as their base position, deriving excess returns from futures discount capture, arbitrage convergence, and options enhancement—sources entirely outside the cross-sectional factor domain. When evaluated through Barra analysis, these products exhibit near-zero factor exposure—a result typically interpreted as "unexplainable" by investment committees, effectively rendering them "unevaluable" and therefore "uninvestable." This paper argues that the near-zero factor exposure is not an evaluation failure but evidence that these products' alpha sources are structurally different from factor-based products. We define this category as "Structural Alpha Index Enhancement" and propose a three-layer attribution framework: (1) Discount Carry, (2) Arbitrage Enhancement, and (3) Options Enhancement Alpha. We introduce corresponding metrics—Discount Capture Ratio (DCR), Arbitrage Information Ratio (AIR), Options Enhancement IR (OIR), and Crowding Immunity Score (CIS)—designed to evaluate what Barra cannot capture. The framework's practical implication is significant for FOF portfolio construction: the near-zero Barra factor exposure of Structural Alpha products implies genuinely low correlation with factor-based index enhancement products, offering real diversification value—particularly during factor crowding events such as Q1 2024 and October–November 2026.
