title: An integrated financial statement analysis and valuation method for stock investment decisions: Evidence from PT Bank Syariah Indonesia
venue: MUQTASID Jurnal Ekonomi dan Perbankan Syariah
abstract: This study aimed to examine the role of financial statements in supporting stock investment decisions by integrating financial performance analysis with Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) valuation method. Focusing on PT Bank Syariah Indonesia (BSI) during the period from 2020 to 2023, the study adopted a quantitative descriptive method using financial ratios and valuation analysis. The results showed consistent growth in assets, revenue, and net profit, as well as improvements in profitability ratios such as Return on Assets (ROA) and Return on Equity (ROE), reflecting enhanced operational efficiency. The valuation results further indicated that the Bank’s stock was undervalued, as the estimated intrinsic value exceeded market price, suggesting potential investment opportunities. These results outlined the importance of applying an integrated analytical method that combined fundamental and valuation analysis to support moreeffective and informed investment decision-making.
summary: This study aimed to examine the role of financial statements in supporting stock investment decisions by integrating financial performance analysis with Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) valuation
finding: The results showed consistent growth in assets, revenue, and net profit, as well as improvements in profitability ratios such as Return on Assets (ROA) and Return on Equity (ROE), reflecting enhanced operational efficiency.

title: Credit Rating Changes and Stock Market Reaction:The Impact of Investor Sentiment
abstract: This paper explores the impact of firm-specific investor sentiment (henceforth FSIS) on stock market returns around the announcement of credit rating changes. We find that FSIS modulates the relative impact of credit rating downgrades on stock returns. A negative FSIS exacerbates the impact of a downgrade, while a positive FSIS attenuates it. Consistent with behavioural explanations, we find the effect to be concentrated in firms that are more prone to investor sentiment biases, such as low-rated firms. Consistent with over-(under-) reaction, we also find evidence of reversals in the longer post-announcement windows.
summary: This paper explores the impact of firm-specific investor sentiment (henceforth FSIS) on stock market returns around the announcement of credit rating changes.
finding: Consistent with over-(under-) reaction, we also find evidence of reversals in the longer post-announcement windows.

title: LLM-Based Pure Management Sentiment in Earnings Communication Conferences and Stock Returns
venue: Advances in economics, business and management research/Advances in Economics, Business and Management Research
abstract: This study focuses on the impact of pure management sentiment on short-term stock returns. Using A-share listed companies in China from 2014 to 2023 as the research sample, this study employs the Qwen large language model to analyze textual information from earnings communication conferences and conducts an empirical analysis using the pure management sentiment indicator constructed by stripping out firm fundamentals and stock performance. The results indicate that pure management sentiment significantly boosts short-term stock returns. This positive impact is further strengthened by the quality of interactions and the level of industry competition, and is more evident in private companies and those with smaller market capitalizations. Furthermore, the results show that pure management sentiment influences short-term stock returns by increasing investors’ sentiment.
summary: This study focuses on the impact of pure management sentiment on short-term stock returns.
finding: Furthermore, the results show that pure management sentiment influences short-term stock returns by increasing investors’ sentiment.

title: Dangerous Liaisons? Debt Supply and Convenience Yield Spillovers in the Euro Area*
abstract: Abstract The literature established that a sovereign bond’s “convenience yield” premium diminishes when that country issues more debt. But how is this convenience yield affected when another country issues sovereign debt? Using high-frequency identification and debt management offices’ communication, we find that an increase in German or French debt reduces convenience yields across the eurozone. Spillovers to low-risk countries are one-for-one while those to riskier countries are smaller. To rationalize these findings, we develop a model with heterogeneous credit risk. Safe sovereign bonds are close substitutes to hedge against idiosyncratic risk, explaining large spillovers, while risky bonds are poor substitutes.
summary: The literature established that a sovereign bond’s “convenience yield” premium diminishes when that country issues more debt.
finding: Using high-frequency identification and debt management offices’ communication, we find that an increase in German or French debt reduces convenience yields across the eurozone.

title: Huge If True: Learning from the Size of the Surprise
abstract: Responses to earnings surprises depend on an unknown multiplier mapping earnings to value. Investors, however, learn about the news and the multiplier from the same number. Large surprises may indicate small multipliers and tiny surprises large ones. We model how greater uncertainty about the multiplier attenuates responses on average but makes them steeper near zero surprises. In an incentivized experiment, we find that greater processing constraints lower average sensitivity but raise it near zero. We confirm this with real-world earnings announcements: stocks with higher valuation uncertainty, our proxy for multiplier uncertainty, respond less on average but more steeply near zero.
summary: Responses to earnings surprises depend on an unknown multiplier mapping earnings to value.
finding: In an incentivized experiment, we find that greater processing constraints lower average sensitivity but raise it near zero.

title: INVESTMENT MANAGEMENT
abstract: This book discusses investment management. It covers the basic concepts and scope of investment management, the investment decision-making process, risk and return analysis in investments, investment instruments in financial markets, the role of fundamental analysis in investment decisions, and the role of technical analysis in investment planning. Investment is a crucial activity in financial management because investment decisions determine how available resources are allocated to generate future economic benefits. From a management perspective, investment is more than simply purchasing stocks, bonds, mutual funds, or other assets. It is a process that includes goal setting, identifying needs and constraints, analyzing opportunities, measuring risk and return, forming a portfolio, implementing, monitoring, evaluating, and continuously adjusting decisions. Developments in financial markets have expanded investment options for individuals and organizations. Investors now have access to a variety of asset classes, capital market instruments, collectiveinvestment products, and technology-based strategies. In Indonesia,developments in investment management have also been accompanied by a strengthening of the regulatory framework. In 2025, the Financial Services Authority (OJK) emphasized the development and strengthening of investment management in the capital market, while the 2025 Capital Market Pocket Book updated its material with market developments through 2025, including carbon trading and financial derivatives with underlying securities (OJK, 2025; OJK, 2026). In addition to technical and financial aspects, this subchapter also highlights the role of management accounting information in providing relevant differential data and sensitizing readers to the influence of behavioral finance, which often traps investors in decision-making. By understanding all elements of this process,readers are expected to be able not only to make more rational and measured investment decisions but also to develop a disciplined and adaptive mindset to the ever-changing dynamics of the capital market.
summary: This book discusses investment management.
finding: By understanding all elements of this process,readers are expected to be able not only to make more rational and measured investment decisions but also to develop a disciplined and adaptive mindset to the ever-changing dynamics of the capital market.

title: Climate Risk Disclosure and Risk Sharing in Financial Markets
abstract: Abstract In this paper, I model how climate risk disclosure impacts climate risk sharing among investors. I show that this disclosure can improve risk sharing by helping investors identify stocks that effectively hedge climate risk, and I analyze the disclosure’s impact on investors’ equilibrium portfolio choices. I then study firms’ voluntary disclosure incentives and analyze when disclosure mandates enhance risk sharing. Finally, I demonstrate that, by facilitating risk sharing, climate risk disclosure reduces the climate risk premium among stocks held by climate-focused investors. Hence, disclosure can lower the valuations of firms with low climate exposures and the overall market. (JEL: D82, D84, G12, G14)
summary: In this paper, I model how climate risk disclosure impacts climate risk sharing among investors.
finding: Hence, disclosure can lower the valuations of firms with low climate exposures and the overall market.

title: Government Guarantees and Dynamic Debt Runs
abstract: Abstract This study quantifies the impact of public guarantees on the stability of bank wholesale funding. We study the Chinese market for negotiable certificates of deposit (NCDs) around the first bank failure in two decades, the Baoshang event, which struck investors’ belief in government guarantees on wholesale bank debt. We document a sharp increase in NCD spreads, issuance failures, and runs, with weaker banks becoming more exposed to rollover risk after the event. Using a model of dynamic debt runs, we estimate that the perceived guarantee fell from 54% of creditor losses before the event to approximately zero after the event. The decline is largest for small banks, low-rated banks, and rural commercial banks. Our structural model also allows us to compare alternative policies aimed at stabilizing creditors’ willingness to roll over short-term debt.
summary: This study quantifies the impact of public guarantees on the stability of bank wholesale funding.
finding: Our structural model also allows us to compare alternative policies aimed at stabilizing creditors’ willingness to roll over short-term debt.

title: Is the Illiquidity Premium Really Gone?
abstract: Greg Leonard, author of the August 2026 SSRN working paper “ Revealing the Illiquidity Premium: The Role of Short Sale Constrained Stocks ,” argues that the apparently weak illiquidity premium in U.S. equities is partly a measurement problem. The premium may not have disappeared; rather, it can be obscured by stocks that are both illiquid and expensive to short. It is a working paper that has not been peer reviewed, so the figures may change. The central implication is important for investors and researchers: illiquidity and short-sale constraints should not be treated as separate effects. Stocks with high borrowing costs tend to be illiquid, but they also tend to have low expected returns. Combining them indiscriminately with other illiquid stocks can make the measured illiquidity premium look smaller than it is. What the paper examined Economic theory predicts that investors demand higher expected returns to hold illiquid assets—if it is costly or difficult to sell a security quickly without moving its price, an investor should require compensation for bearing that implementation risk. This relationship has appeared in many markets. Yet, recent work has suggested that the equity-market illiquidity premium—the excess return of illiquid stocks over liquid stocks—has weakened (see for example research about the illiquidity premium and illiquidity and stock returns ) markedly or even vanished. Leonard re-examines that conclusion. He studies U.S. common stocks listed on the NYSE, Amex, and Nasdaq, using: Amihud’s illiquidity measure , which approximates price impact by dividing absolute daily returns by dollar trading volume. Equity loan fees , or the cost of borrowing shares to establish and maintain a short position. Monthly portfolio sorts that go long the most illiquid quintile of stocks and short the most liquid quintile—an illiquidity-minus-liquidity, or “IML,” portfolio. His data sample spans the period July 1964-March 2022 for the broad illiquidity-premium analysis, with equity-loan-fee data available from July 2013 through March 2022. The paper labels stocks in the highest quintile of loan fees as “special,” meaning they are relatively costly to borrow and therefore more short-sale constrained. The other 80% are described as general collateral stocks. The core argument Leonard’s argument is straightforward: Illiquid stocks should earn higher expected returns , because investors require compensation for greater trading costs and price impact. Hard-to-short stocks tend to earn lower expected returns , consistent with the idea that pessimistic investors have difficulty expressing negative views through short selling. High-loan-fee stocks are disproportionately found among illiquid stocks. Therefore, an illiquid-stock portfolio can be contaminated by hard-to-short stocks whose low expected returns offset the conventional illiquidity premium. In the paper’s recent sample, 28% of stocks in the illiquid leg of the IML portfolio were short-sale con
summary: He studies U.S. common stocks listed on the NYSE, Amex, and Nasdaq, using: Amihud’s illiquidity measure , which approximates price impact by dividing absolute daily returns by dollar trading volume.
finding: High-loan-fee stocks are disproportionately found among illiquid stocks.

title: Meetings are a waste of money
abstract: I think I don’t have to belabour the point that many (most? all?) meetings are a waste of time. The very fact that there is a standing expression, ‘this meeting could have been an email,’ tells us that there are too many meetings that are. But did you know that they are likely also a gargantuan waste of money? About four years ago, I wrote a note on what makes a good meeting where I quoted some baffling statistics. Now, I came across a new survey of the time spent in meetings. They used data from more than 9,000 workers in the US to check how much time they spent in meetings, and how many meetings they had. The added bonus of this survey was that the researchers also knew which industry they worked in and what rank, age, gender, etc. they had. It won’t surprise you when I tell you that managers spend waaayyy more time in meetings than non-managers and that in this post-pandemic world, there are far more meetings held online than in person. Men, older workers, and workers with a college degree tend to spend somewhat more time in meetings than women, younger workers, and workers without a college degree. I think these small differences are, however, simply a reflection of the manager vs non-manager gap, since managers tend to be, on average, more male, better educated and older. What surprised me to see, however, were the graphs below that show the average number of meetings per week (left-hand chart) and the average number of hours spent in a meeting per week (right-hand chart). They show the differences by sector, and I will ignore for the moment that, apparently, most people have blissfully few meetings each week and somehow spend less than five hours a week in them. Meeting intensity by sector Source: Deming et al. (2026) What surprised me is that, on average, people who work in finance or IT have more meetings per week than people who work in public administration. Apparently, the private sector is as good at wasting time in meetings as the public sector is. And someone, please tell me what all these miners are doing in meeting rooms??? But here is the kicker. Because managers tend to spend more time in meetings than non-managers and because people in finance and IT tend to be better paid than people who work in retail, the cost of meetings in different industries can be quite high. The authors of the study estimate that in finance and IT, some 20% of the wage bill is paid to people attending a meeting, while in retail that is just 10% of the wage bill. I used to joke that in previous jobs, half my salary was punitive damages for having to deal with idiots in useless meetings. Given that I had jobs where I sometimes spent 30 to 40 hours a week in meetings, I think I was still underpaid. Wage bill spent on meetings by sector Source: Deming et al. (2026)
summary: I think I don’t have to belabour the point that many (most? all?) meetings are a waste of time.
finding: They show the differences by sector, and I will ignore for the moment that, apparently, most people have blissfully few meetings each week and somehow spend less than five hours a week in them.

title: Weekend Reads – 11/13/26
abstract: Quote for the Week In the stock market, the most important organ is the stomach. It’s not the brain. On the way to work, the amount of bad news you could hear is almost infinite now. So the question is: Can you take that? Do you really have faith that 10 years, 20 years, 30 years from now common stocks are the place to be. If you believe in that, you should have some money in equity funds. It’s a question of what’s your tolerance for pain. There will still be declines. It might be tomorrow. It might be a year from now. Most people do really well because they just hang in there… You’ve got to look in the mirror every day and say: What am I going to do if the market goes down 10%? What do I do if it goes down 20%? title: Concentration of Investments by Berkshire Hathaway in Alphabet: Evaluation of its Business and Corporate Cultures
abstract: Traditionally, value investing has been distinct from volatile tech stocks. In its latest moves, however, Berkshire Hathaway has made a departure from that distinction by making an unusually fast move into Alphabet, the corporate parent company of Google, starting from the third quarter of 2025. This paper employs the value principles followed by Berkshire as the criterion and subjects the position to rigorous scrutiny through a comprehensive analysis of holdings data, financial figures, and governance characteristics. We find an initial investment of around 17.85 million shares valued at about $4.3 billion, followed by further development in the first quarter of 2026 in which the position grew 204 percent. Continuous buying occurred until the aggregate position reached 106 million shares valued at approximately $38 billion, making it the third largest holding in the equity portfolio. Furthermore, the forward price to earnings ratio of around 17, a free cash flow of $72.8 billion in 2024, and a buyback exceeding $200 billion over a four-year period make the company more than fit into the criteria set forth by the firm. Ultimately, the paper argues that Alphabet's platform business model and innovating organizational culture provide the company with the necessary earning capacity and strategic flexibility to justify crossing the traditional sector border. This strategic shift highlights a broader evolution in modern portfolio management, where traditional value metrics are increasingly adapted to accommodate high-growth technology enterprises.
summary: Traditionally, value investing has been distinct from volatile tech stocks.
finding: We find an initial investment of around 17.85 million shares valued at about $4.3 billion, followed by further development in the first quarter of 2026 in which the position grew 204 percent.

title: The Horizon of Investors’ Information and Corporate Investment
abstract: Abstract The quality of investors’ information across different horizons has real effects. When managers care about the effect of investment on their stock price, a decline in the informativeness of investors’ signals about long-term cash flows leads firms with long-term projects to cut investment more than firms with short-term projects. Using a novel, hand-collected measure of project horizons, we confirm this hypothesis: relative to firms with short-term projects, the investment of firms with long-term projects decreases by 3.7% following a 1-standard-deviation drop in the quality of investors’ long-term information. This effect becomes larger when managers prioritize current stock prices. (JEL D84, G14, G17, M41).
summary: The quality of investors’ information across different horizons has real effects.
finding: This effect becomes larger when managers prioritize current stock prices.

title: The Sky’s the Limit: Asset Price Spirals When Margin Traders Are All In
abstract: Abstract We analyze a setting in which some investors are all in and buy as much of a risky asset as their margins allow. A higher price of the asset increases all-in investors’ wealth, against which they borrow to buy more shares. If all-in investors have enough wealth and access to at least 2:1 leverage, then prices can spiral upward indefinitely. This is true even if there exist deep-pocketed investors with no explicit limits to arbitrage. Increasing access for retail investors to leverage through leveraged ETFs, derivatives, and margin suggests increasing opportunities for price spirals and collapses. (JEL G12, G30)
summary: We analyze a setting in which some investors are all in and buy as much of a risky asset as their margins allow.
finding: A higher price of the asset increases all-in investors’ wealth, against which they borrow to buy more shares.

title: The start-up challenge in Europe: Part Deux
abstract: On Tuesday , I wrote about a study by the OECD that compared start-up financing in the EU and the US. That study emphasised that while growth-oriented firms in Europe get on average the same funding as in the US, rising superstars (future unicorns) can accumulate much more funding in the US than in the EU. But the supply of funding is one thing; the cost of it is an entirely different story. I admit, the study by Bo Becker, Efraim Benmech, and Joao Monteiro looked at listed companies only, but something tells me the same issue applies to private companies before they list. Their original research question was to explain why the largest global megacaps are almost all in the US. There isn’t a single trillion-dollar company in Europe. The gap between the US and Europe is not due to fundamentals. Instead, there are fewer new companies, and newly listed firms are worth less than their newly listed US peers. And once they are listed, European companies often don’t grow that much. The main answer they gave came as a major surprise to me: the cost of capital. Naively, I thought the cost of debt in Europe is lower than in the US because interest rates (which are the foundation of corporate loan rates) are lower. And the cost of equity seems to be roughly the same in Europe and the US, according to the annual survey by Pablo Fernandez . But apparently, I was wrong because the cost of capital is higher for European firms, and the gap increases the smaller the firms are. Cost of capital by firm size Source: Becker et al. (2026). Note: Firms are ordered by percentile of market value, with the smallest firms to the left. If you look at the cost gap between the firms with below-median market cap and above-median market cap, you see that smaller firms in Europe face a much higher ‘size premium’ in their cost of capital than the US. And in the second half of the 2010s, this gap seems to have widened, making it even harder for European small caps to get the capital necessary to grow. One discussion we should thus have in Europe, and in the UK, is how to make capital cheaper for small companies so they can invest in their growth. Size premium in cost of capital Source: Becker et al. (2026).
summary: On Tuesday , I wrote about a study by the OECD that compared start-up financing in the EU and the US.
finding: Naively, I thought the cost of debt in Europe is lower than in the US because interest rates (which are the foundation of corporate loan rates) are lower.

title: Investors’ perceived value of founder CEOs: evidence from natural experiments
abstract: Almost all firms start with founder(s); however, only 11% of S&P 1500 firms retain founders as CEOs. Although extant literature documents superior firm performance in founder-led U.S. public firms, recent studies find that founder CEOs are more likely to face forced turnover than their counterparts. In this context, we investigate investors’ perceived value of founder CEO leadership by analyzing stock price reactions around the sudden and unexpected deaths of 177 CEOs from 1960 to 2019. If founder CEOs are valuable to investors, stock prices should fall around their sudden departure. We document several novel results. First, the cumulative abnormal return (CAR) from one day before to two days after a CEO’s sudden death is -0.81%, suggesting CEOs are, on average, valuable to investors. Second, CAR (-1,2) % increases by 1.48% upon the death of a founder CEO and 2.11% for descendant CEOs; however, it decreases by 2.67% upon the death of a professional CEO. Third, investors’ perceptions of founder CEOs vary over time. The perceived value of founder CEOs declines during the 1980s and 1990s, a period marked by increased scrutiny of anti-takeover provisions, managerial performance, and entrenchment. Fourth, younger founder CEOs add significant firm value, whereas older founder CEOs do not add value for shareholders. Finally, founder CEOs’ services are considered valuable in small and medium-sized firms; however, they are less valuable in complex and large firms. The findings have implications for CEO turnover, stock market participation, and capital allocations in the economy.
summary: Almost all firms start with founder(s); however, only 11% of S&P 1500 firms retain founders as CEOs.
finding: First, the cumulative abnormal return (CAR) from one day before to two days after a CEO’s sudden death is -0.81%, suggesting CEOs are, on average, valuable to investors.

title: The Omitted Sector: Factor Investing in Financials
Resolving the Factor Zoo Conundrum for US Industry Portfolios
Global Seasonality Factor Investing
abstract: We study seasonality as a factor for predicting risk-adjusted returns across global futures markets. We document five seasonality anomalies that, in aggregate, are pervasive across bond, commodity and equity markets. We demonstrate that each seasonality factor produces excess returns that are not reasonably explained by established global time series carry, momentum and skewness factors. We apply recent innovations in statistical learning and fit nonlinear seasonality models at the individual market level, thereby allowing each feature-market pair to express its unique seasonal prediction pattern. We discuss candidate economic rationales for the existence and persistence of each seasonality anomaly. Walk-forward out-of-sample testing demonstrates that fast-moving seasonal patterns, such as day-of-week and day-of-month, produce strong gross performance but with extremely high turnover, resulting in negative performance net of transaction costs. In contrast, slower-moving seasonal patterns, such as day-of-quarter, day-of-half-year and day-of-year, produce positive gross performance and, with the exception of day-of-quarter, positive net performance. An equal-weight ensemble of seasonality models produces an out-of-sample Sharpe ratio that is competitive with, and uncorrelated to, established global time series factor portfolios. Empirical results demonstrate that adding seasonality to a global factor portfolio increases the out-of-sample Sharpe ratio by approximately $30\%$ over the full evaluation period.
summary: We study seasonality as a factor for predicting risk-adjusted returns across global futures markets.
finding: Empirical results demonstrate that adding seasonality to a global factor portfolio increases the out-of-sample Sharpe ratio by approximately $30\%$ over the full evaluation period.

title: Treasuries lose their haven status
abstract: In March, I wrote a post titled ‘Trust the dollar, not the Treasury’ where I argued that investors are increasingly losing trust in the US Treasury and the paper it issues, but retain faith in the US dollar. A new study by the Banque de France measured correlations between assets during periods of heightened risk aversion to assess which assets really act as safe havens. They examined the behaviour of government and corporate bonds, currencies and a number of alternative assets like gold, silver, oil, and Bitcoin. And to pre-empt the question that many readers will have: While Bitcoin, oil and silver have no safe haven characteristic, gold does. But gold ranks well below most government bonds or the US dollar as a safe haven asset. Ok, with that out of the way, let us look at the ranking of government and investment-grade corporate bonds. The chart below shows the average safe haven score for these assets together with their score in individual risk aversion episodes. Safe haven score of bonds Source: Burban et al. (2026) Swedish government bonds have overtaken US Treasuries, followed by Norwegian government bonds. In general, the less indebted a country is, the more its government bonds are treated as safe-haven assets – with US Treasuries the notable exception to the rule. At the bottom of the government bond ranking, we find French, Korean and Belgian government bonds, which behave as much like safe-haven assets as Japanese corporate bonds. Note that when it comes to corporate bonds, Swedish, Norwegian, and Australian investment-grade bonds behave much the same way as a safe haven as German Bunds or Swiss Eidgenossen. But these are long-term averages. Over time, the risk perception of investors changes, and that leads to shifts in the ranking of securities. And this is where it gets interesting for the US. The second chart shows the changing ranking of the US dollar and US Treasuries among all assets the researchers considered. And while the US dollar remains on top as the asset with the most pronounced safe haven characteristics, Treasuries are increasingly falling behind, just like they did during and after the Global Financial Crisis. Safe-haven score of the dollar and Treasuries Source: Burban et al. (2026)
summary: In March, I wrote a post titled ‘Trust the dollar, not the Treasury’ where I argued that investors are increasingly losing trust in the US Treasury and the paper it issues, but retain faith in the US dollar.
finding: The second chart shows the changing ranking of the US dollar and US Treasuries among all assets the researchers considered.

title: The Portfolio Decisions that Matter
abstract: When the market gets crazy, you’re itching to trade your portfolio, or just want to act on the latest breaking news, the decisions you weigh matter in the long run. Of course, not all portfolio decisions are equal. Sometimes it’s the decisions you don’t make that matter most. In fact, Charley Ellis made this case two decades ago. He broke down portfolio decisions into five categories: In making investment decisions, there are five separate levels of decisions for each investor to make individually: Level One : Asset mix — The optimal proportion of, e.g., equities, bonds, private equity, for the policy normal of the investor’s portfolio. This is where investment counseling usually concentrates. Level Two : Equity mix — Policy normal proportions in various types of stocks: e.g., growth versus value; large-cap versus small-cap; domestic versus international. Level Three : Active versus passive management — Deciding on the appropriate method of implementation for the policy normal mix of investments. Level Four : Specific manager selection (where most investors and most investment committees concentrate their time and effort) — Deciding which firms will manage each component of the overall portfolio, firing the most disappointing, and hiring the most promising. Level Five : Active portfolio management — Changing portfolio strategy, security selection, and trading. Investors should recognize that the game of investing is not necessarily a single, bundled package, but can be divided into separate parts or levels and that investors can engage in or ignore each level of the game. And investors are free to choose. Ellis ranks the levels by order of importance. Levels one and two are the most important, levels four and five the least. Yet, thanks to innate biases like overconfidence and overoptimism, many investors prioritize the opposite. The active part of investing, levels four and five, receive the most time and attention, with levels one and two getting the least. Investors have it backwards and it’s costly. Each level also comes with a cost, not just in fees but potential mistakes. Levels four and five being the costliest. Choosing active funds that underperform an index, chasing returns, trading your account, and other active decisions increase the chance of underperforming a simple portfolio with the appropriate asset mix to fit your goals, objectives, and risk tolerance. Choosing to put all your time and attention into levels one and two, while avoiding levels four and five is Ellis’s key to winning the loser’s game. A focus on asset allocation while minimizing costs and mistakes means winning at investing. How do investors avoid the mistakes that result from the active decision levels? You can choose to be less active in your portfolio. A low-cost passive approach has proven results, but even it can be difficult to stick with at times. Of course, not everyone wants to be purely passive either. The simple solution, for both cases, is to have an in
summary: When the market gets crazy, you’re itching to trade your portfolio, or just want to act on the latest breaking news, the decisions you weigh matter in the long run.
finding: Choosing active funds that underperform an index, chasing returns, trading your account, and other active decisions increase the chance of underperforming a simple portfolio with the appropriate asset mix to fit your goals, objectives, and risk tolerance.

title: A Layman Thinks About AI
The start-up challenge in Europe
abstract: The start-up scene in the US is the envy of bankers and investors across Europe and the UK. It seems that if you want to scale up, IPO or find any kind of growth capital, you have to go to the US. For years, there has been a dearth of start-up IPOs and even major scale-ups in Europe. To illustrate the problem, I recently came across a LinkedIn post where someone showed the largest VC funding rounds in Europe ever. Mistral’s Series D funding round tops the list with a volume of $3.5bn. Compare this to the US, where a simple Google search (or AI search if you want to waste tokens on something you can get for free) will tell you that the five largest funding rounds were: $122bn for OpenAI in March 2026 $65bn for Anthropic in May 2026 $40bn for OpenAI in March 2025 $30bn for Anthropic in early 2026 $20bn for xAI in Q1 2026 The list goes on. Mistral’s $3.5bn funding round features only in 19 th place. A new analysis by the OECD puts the contrast in sharp light. They looked at the start-ups founded in the EU and the US between 2000 and 2025 and analysed which companies successfully scaled. They distinguished between ‘rising superstars’ (companies that would eventually reach a valuation of more than $11bn) and ‘growth-oriented companies’ (raising at a lead of $50m). The first chart below shows how long it took start-ups in the EU and the US to scale up after filing their first patent. About 40% of EU start-ups took more than seven years from the point of filing their first patent to the point of getting enough funding to scale up. On average, it took 1.5 years longer for EU start-ups to scale up than for US start-ups. Time between first patent filing and scaling Source: OECD The second chart shows that the real difference is at the very top. While the funding collected by EU growth-oriented firms increases at roughly the same rate as in the US, rising superstars and future unicorns clearly have a much easier time in the US. Five or six years after launch, US rising superstars start to attract much, much more capital than their peers in the EU. And if this isn’t bad enough, then wait until Thursday when I will discuss another study that identified another key factor that prevents European start-ups from scaling. Pre-scaling cumulative funding Source: OECD
summary: The start-up scene in the US is the envy of bankers and investors across Europe and the UK.
finding: Time between first patent filing and scaling Source: OECD The second chart shows that the real difference is at the very top.

title: The Gamble of Your Life
abstract: My late grandfather gambled away over $1 million during his lifetime. His wager of choice was horse racing. But if he were alive today, I'm confident he'd be into sports betting. How do I know? Because most other gamblers are. Today, 52% of men aged 18-49 have an online sportsbook account , up from 39% in 2024 . That's over half of all U.S. men this age, not just gamblers. But what really makes this striking is how much they are betting. From 2018 to 2025, the total handle (amount wagered) on U.S. sportsbooks went from $6.6B to $165B, a 25x increase within 7 years. How did this happen? In May 2018, the Supreme Court overturned a law banning sports betting across the United States. The court held that the decision was not up to Congress and the federal government, but up to the states. As a result, 39 states plus Washington, D.C. now have legal sports betting . And as access and volume have grown, so has the house's cut of each dollar. As you can see in the table below, hold (how much sportsbooks keep per dollar wagered) has steadily climbed from 6.7% to 10.1% over this time period: How did sportsbooks manage to increase their hold so much? By promoting parlays, or bets where multiple outcomes need to occur for you to win. One of the most popular ways to do this is a same game parlay (SGP). For example, instead of betting on the NY Knicks to win (a single bet), I could do an SGP where: The Knicks win Jalen Brunson scores over 30 points, and The final game score exceeds 200 points If all three of those things happen, I win the bet, if not, I don't. These parlays are better for sportsbooks because they tend to pay out less than the true odds would suggest. And when you pay out a little less across multiple bets, the house edge shoots up. As Chad Nagel at Sportsboom reported , the house edge for SGPs is 20% to 35%, compared with 4.5% for a standard point-spread bet. And, as SGPs have become a larger share of sportsbook revenue (from under 20% in 2021 to 35%-40% today), the average hold has increased along with them. Given these recent developments, you'd think the sportsbooks would be pretty happy. But they aren't. Because they have competitors who have found a loophole—prediction markets. Companies like Polymarket and Kalshi, which started as prediction markets, now offer event contracts for sports. It's sports betting by another name. However, there are a few big differences between sports betting on prediction markets and on sportsbooks. First, prediction markets are regulated by the CFTC, not the states, meaning they don't have to pay the state gaming taxes that sportsbooks do. Second, prediction markets don't have the same age restrictions as sportsbooks. So 18-to-20-year-olds can place "predictions" on Kalshi though they have to be 21 to place bets on DraftKings or FanDuel. Lastly, many states have self-exclusion lists, where individuals struggling with gambling can voluntarily ban themselves from placing bets. Sportsbooks have to honor these l
summary: My late grandfather gambled away over $1 million during his lifetime.
finding: Because they have competitors who have found a loophole—prediction markets.

title: Talking to the Market: Field Evidence on AI Chatbots, Digital Advice Utilization, and Retail Trading Outcomes
venue: International Journal of Science Strategic Management and Technology
abstract: Background: Conversational AI chatbots are increasingly embedded in retail brokerage applications, yet empirical evidence on how chatbot-based advice influences investor behaviour in real-world trading contexts remains limited. Purpose: This study investigates whether perceived chatbot competence and trust predict digital advice utilisation, and whether such utilisation is associated with self-reported trading outcomes, with financial literacy examined as a moderator. Uniqueness: The study extends prior research by focusing on investor–chatbot interaction and actual utilisation of chatbot guidance among active retail investors, rather than evaluating algorithmic stock-picking performance or purely conceptual advisory models. Methodology: A cross-sectional survey was conducted with 300 active retail investors who had recently interacted with AI-enabled investment chatbots. Multiple regression models were used to test direct relationships and the moderation effect of financial literacy. Findings: Perceived competence (B≈0.32, p<0.001) and trust (B≈0.32, p<0.001) are independently associated with higher digital advice utilisation (R²=0.306). Digital advice utilisation is positively associated with trading outcomes (B≈0.32, p≈0.02). Financial literacy also shows a positive association with trading outcomes (B≈0.30, p≈0.03), while the utilisation×literacy interaction is not statistically significant. Implications: The findings suggest that brokerage chatbots may support more disciplined investing behaviour, though causal interpretation is limited by the survey design. Future work should integrate chatbot interaction logs with objective brokerage trading records to evaluate long-run behavioural and performance effects. Keywords: AI chatbots; Digital advice; Retail investors; Stock trading; Financial literacy; Trading outcomes
summary: The findings suggest that brokerage chatbots may support more disciplined investing behaviour, though causal interpretation is limited by the survey design.
finding: Perceived competence (B≈0.32, p<0.001) and trust (B≈0.32, p<0.001) are independently associated with higher digital advice utilisation (R²=0.306).

title: Influence of ESG and CSR on Indian Investor: Role of Social Media
abstract: Environmental, social and governance (ESG) along with corporate social responsibility (CSR) have become buzz words of the present era. Globalization and internationalization of the world economies have also played a pivotal role in adding momentum to ESG and CSR all the more. India has become the first country to mandate expenditure in the name of CSR for specified companies. Hence, ESG and CSR have become a cause of concern for both investors and companies, former for value investing and security of their funds and later for corporate governance norms. The growing importance of ESG and CSR motivated the authors to investigate the impact of ESG and CSR on Indian investors, specifically if they are aware of and interested in investing in stocks of the companies that follow ESG practices and contribute towards CSR more than the mandate. Furthermore, social media has a tremendous impact on investment decision-making. Therefore, a primary survey is conducted to judge the tendency of Indian investors towards ESG and CSR and the role of social media in directing their preferences. Simple aggregates, mean score and Levene’s T test have been used for the analysis. Findings suggest that Indian investors are more concerned about ESG stocks as compared to CSR stocks. Further, social media was found to have no role in influencing investors’ investment choices, and no difference is found between males and females as regards to investing in stocks of companies pursuing ESG and CSR and with respect to the role of social media too in making their choices.
summary: Environmental, social and governance (ESG) along with corporate social responsibility (CSR) have become buzz words of the present era.
finding: Further, social media was found to have no role in influencing investors’ investment choices, and no difference is found between males and females as regards to investing in stocks of companies pursuing ESG and CSR and with respect to the role of social media…

title: Presidential Address: Human Finance: Incorporating Insights from the Life Sciences
abstract: ABSTRACT Many of the key determinants of human behavior identified in the life sciences, such as stress response, impulse control, and mood regulation, remain absent from standard economic and finance models. This paper illustrates how such insights can enhance economic models in the context of inflation expectations. Combining a retrospective survey that elicits personal inflation histories with an experimental intervention that induces the reexperiencing of historic inflation, I show that physiological, emotional, and cognitive stress markers predict heightened inflation expectations and sharper memory recall, while also shaping personal economic narratives. These findings suggest novel policy tools to counter the persistent scars of economic distress and crisis experiences, for example, by designing experiences to provide predictability and control.
summary: ABSTRACT Many of the key determinants of human behavior identified in the life sciences, such as stress response, impulse control, and mood regulation, remain absent from standard economic and finance models.

title: Fiscal Commitment and the Additionality of Philanthropy: Heterogeneous Donor Purposes in a Shared Public Budget
abstract: Philanthropic donors often value different public services, while a budget authority allocates public spending across a shared portfolio. Policy frameworks frequently seek to ensure that private finance supplements rather than displaces public funding. We distinguish baseline additionality, which preserves pre-gift public funding, from portfolio preservation, which preserves a service's provision after all gifts are pooled under discretionary budgeting. A larger gift to one service raises the discretionary provision of every service and reduces the protection slack available to the others. This cross-donor fiscal externality yields an exact feasibility result: if a service's maximum permissible floor lies below its discretionary post-gift provision, every effective protection reform reduces that service relative to the portfolio reference, including full protection of its own appropriation. Conversely, a reform that expands at least one donor-backed service while preserving all others exists exactly when every maximum floor reaches the reference. The paper characterizes the complete preservation set and its welfare-maximizing element. Under logarithmic preferences, donation shares determine protectability, while heterogeneous donor valuations determine welfare incidence. Baseline additionality may therefore hold while a service loses fiscal benefits generated by other gifts.
summary: Philanthropic donors often value different public services, while a budget authority allocates public spending across a shared portfolio.
finding: if a service's maximum permissible floor lies below its discretionary post-gift provision, every effective protection reform reduces that service relative to the portfolio reference, including full protection of its own appropriation.

title: The AI Trade Deconstructed: AI Builders, AI Suppliers and AI Product firms!
abstract: When I posted my valuation of Anthropic a few days ago, I noted that turbulence lay ahead, both for the company and the market. I did not expect that turbulence to be this forceful and arrive this soon, but markets don't have an obligation to wait until it is convenient for investors, to adjust to new realities. With the election results on November 3 acting as a catalyst, investors initially responded positively with stocks up on Wednesday, but reversed course sharply on Thursday, with the NASDAQ down close to 6% and the S&P 500 declining 4%. This drop has again brought to the forefront questions about the AI trade and whether it has run its course. In this post, I will start by referring to my earlier note on AI as a business, and use the ideas in it to deconstruct the many players that are lumped together as AI companies, from those spending the money building the data centers (hyperscalers) to the firms benefiting from selling the builders the ingredients for these data centers (chip makers, electrical equipment, power and even real estate) to the companies that are spending considerable amounts , leasing these data centers for long periods (with the LLMs in the lead). I will argue that while all of these groups benefit, at least in general, from AI's success at creating large and profitable markets, we are at a point in the AI disruption, where their interests and payoffs will diverge, with implications for both the businesses and investors. I use last week's market carnage in technology and examine how the market treatment of these different groups may be a reflection of a more discerning market, less willing to mark up and mark down all AI companies, and more likely to treat them differently, as their business interests diverge. The AI Transition My journey on AI started with a selfish and narrow intent, which was to evaluate an investment I had made in Nvidia in 2018, for reasons entirely unrelated to AI. I thought that Nvidia, at the time, was a innovative chip company with more pricing power than many in its peer group, and felt that it was undervalued, given its prospects. While the stock outperformed my portfolio early on, it was the ChatGPT debut on November 30, 2022, and the subsequent AI buzz that put its stock price on steroids. That left me with a challenge, albeit a welcome one, of deciding whether I should continue to hold on to a stock that had already become a twenty-bagger or sell some or all of it. Since much of Nvidia's supersized success was being propelled by AI demand, that required me to take my first look at how big the AI market would be, and how well Nvidia was positioned to take advantage of that market. If you have read my multiple posts on Nvidia over the last three years, you may be aware that I sold all my shares in the company in four installments, with the last sale happening earlier this year. As many of you have been quick to point out, my decision to gradually decrease my Nvidia position has led me to leav

finding: I use last week's market carnage in technology and examine how the market treatment of these different groups may be a reflection of a more discerning market, less willing to mark up and mark down all AI companies, and more likely to treat them differently…

title: Cybersecurity and Financial Stability
abstract: Banks have traditionally been concerned with financial risks such as credit losses, liquidity shortages, and market volatility. But as financial institutions become increasingly dependent on digital infrastructure, a different source of vulnerability is emerging: cybersecurity. A cyberattack may initially appear to be a technology problem. Yet when banks rely on interconnected payment systems, cloud services, and third-party technology providers, a disruption affecting one institution can spread to others. What begins as an operational failure may ultimately undermine confidence in the financial system. This raises an important question: Are individual banks investing enough in cybersecurity to protect not only themselves but also the broader financial system? And could the threat of a bank run change how much protection banks are willing to provide? Cybersecurity and Financial Stability Anand, Duley and Gai Review of Finance, 2026 A version of this paper can be found here Want to read our summaries of academic finance papers? Check out our Academic Research Insight category Key Academic Insights Cybersecurity Is a Public Good and the Weakest Link Matters Banks increasingly depend on shared digital infrastructure. While this reduces costs, it also creates vulnerabilities that extend beyond individual institutions. An attacker who compromises one bank may exploit weaknesses in a shared service, potentially disrupting other institutions. Cybersecurity therefore resembles a weakest-link public good . Investments by one bank can protect others, while inadequate defenses at one institution can weaken the entire network. This creates a problem: banks may not fully consider the benefits their cybersecurity investments provide to the broader financial system. Banks Have Incentives to Underinvest in Cybersecurity The authors identify a classic economic problem: free-riding. Because cybersecurity investments benefit other institutions, banks may prefer to rely partly on protection provided by their peers. Individually, this can seem rational. Cybersecurity is expensive, and not all its benefits accrue to the bank making the investment. Collectively, however, these decisions can leave the financial system insufficiently protected. The model shows that decentralized cybersecurity decisions may produce inefficient outcomes. Importantly, the inefficiency does not always involve underinvestment. The Threat of Bank Runs Can Encourage Greater Cybersecurity Investment A surprising finding is that the possibility of a bank run can encourage banks to strengthen their cybersecurity defenses. A successful cyberattack may disrupt operations and undermine creditor confidence. Depositors or other creditors could respond by withdrawing funds or refusing to renew financing. Banks anticipating these consequences have stronger incentives to prevent attacks. The authors therefore identify two opposing forces: free-riding discourages cybersecurity investment, while the threat
summary: Banks have traditionally been concerned with financial risks such as credit losses, liquidity shortages, and market volatility.
finding: The model shows that decentralized cybersecurity decisions may produce inefficient outcomes.

title: UK Equity Exceptionalism
abstract: Over the past 5 years, the exceptional US equity market generated a very healthy total return of 68%. Through the same period, a value-titled UK equity index gained 117%. The most unloved style in one of the most out of favour equity markets trounced the performance of the most in-vogue, technology-dominated region. Very few people would have predicted this 5 years ago, and I don’t think many would believe it now – even after it has happened! Why has this occurred, and why have so few people noticed? The economy is not the stock market: The UK is one of the best examples of the stock market not being a reflection of its domestic economy – this is certainly true of its large cap, high dividend paying companies in energy, health care and banking. The fortunes of the sluggish UK economy are often not that important to UK equity market returns. Despite this, investors cannot seem to stop associating economic views with stock market expectations. This becomes a particularly acute impediment when it is your home market, as it is incredibly hard to separate your lived experience and the constant attention paid to the economy, from what actually drives equity market returns, Starting valuations matter: Whenever an asset class delivers exceptional performance over a meaningful time horizon, everyone scrabbles around for compelling stories to explain it. The right answer is often that starting valuations were exceptionally cheap and the asset was unloved (which was very much the case for UK value stocks in 2021). This is not an exciting narrative and it doesn’t make great copy – but that doesn’t stop it being true. The exact pattern also happens in reverse, poor returns from an asset or stock are frequently a consequence of them having a very expensive starting point, rather than the stories that are told to describe why something has turned sour. It helps to be lucky: Any investment that works well needs a healthy dose of luck. Although an asset class might have delivered very strong returns, that is just one path it could have taken out of many. Over the past five years the (then) cheaper area of the UK market benefitted from tailwinds such as rising energy prices and higher interest rates. In a different world this might not have been the outcome. Although we cannot control luck, buying undervalued assets helps to get luck on our side – because we don’t need much of it for things to work out well. Set the expectation hurdle low : Investors often discuss developments around an asset class in absolute terms – something is either good or bad news – but everything should be set relative to expectations. Back in 2021, value investing was dead and nobody liked the UK market (they still don’t); expectations were so low that surpassing them wasn’t a difficult task. Unbridled pessimism can create an attractive, positive asymmetry. It takes time: One of the many reasons that people dislike buying undervalued assets is that they need to know when something will im
summary: Over the past 5 years, the exceptional US equity market generated a very healthy total return of 68%.
finding: Over the past five years the (then) cheaper area of the UK market benefitted from tailwinds such as rising energy prices and higher interest rates.

title: U.S. Employment Trends Index Edged Down in October, Conference Board Says
Investor Sentiment and Stock Price Dynamics: An Empirical Study on the Casablanca Stock Exchange
venue: Journal d’Economie, de Management, d’Environnement et de Droit
abstract: This study explores investor sentiment, a key concept in behavioral finance, reflecting the collective optimism or pessimism of market participants about future investments. Sentiment can lead to irrational market behaviors like bubbles and crashes. It often deviates from economic fundamentals, influencing asset prices, liquidity, and volatility. Sentiment is considered as positive (optimism), negative (pessimism), or neutral (rational analysis). The research highlights sentiment’s impact on market volatility and its importance for predicting market movements and guiding investment strategies. The study emphasizes the role of investor sentiment in the Moroccan stock market. So, a negative sentiment impacts return and financial risk (variance) differently to the extent that it reduces the former and increases the latter. As for the positive sentiment, it has an opposite effect compared to the negative one, it increases the return and reduces the risk.
summary: This study explores investor sentiment, a key concept in behavioral finance, reflecting the collective optimism or pessimism of market participants about future investments.
finding: As for the positive sentiment, it has an opposite effect compared to the negative one, it increases the return and reduces the risk.

title: Understanding Individual Investment Decisions Through Behavioral Biases: Evidence from Morocco
abstract: Abstract Investment decisions involve a series of choices that can significantly affect the performance of financial investments. Traditional financial theory generally assumes that individuals make decisions through rational analysis, whereas behavioral finance emphasizes the influence of psychological mechanisms and cognitive biases on investors’ choices. Against this background, the present study examines the behavioral determinants of investment decision-making among individual investors operating in the Moroccan stock market. Empirical data were collected through a questionnaire-based survey administered directly to randomly selected retail investors. Of the 300 questionnaires distributed, 112 were fully completed and retained for analysis. The research adopts a positivist epistemological approach and relies on exploratory factor analysis (EFA) and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) to examine the collected data. The findings reveal five underlying behavioral dimensions associated with individual investors’ investment decisions. These results contribute to a better understanding of the psychological and behavioral mechanisms underlying investment choices and may help financial institutions develop investment products and services that more closely reflect the preferences and needs of individual investors. Keywords: Retail investors; equity markets; behavioral biases; investment decisions; behavioral finance.
summary: Investment decisions involve a series of choices that can significantly affect the performance of financial investments.
finding: The findings reveal five underlying behavioral dimensions associated with individual investors’ investment decisions.

title: The Role of SEBI in Protecting Investors in the Indian Stock Market
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Investor confidence is the foundation on which every securities market rests. In India, the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) is the institution charged with sustaining it. This article examines how SEBI protects investors in the Indian stock market through three lenses: its statutory mandate under the SEBI Act, 1992; the preventive, enforcement and remedial tools it deploys; and the judicial and political checks that discipline its power. Drawing on leading Supreme Court decisions and recent regulatory episodes, including the 2024 reforms on retail derivatives trading and the 2025 action against Jane Street Group, the article argues that SEBI has evolved from a reactive watchdog into a rule-maker, investigator and adjudicator of considerable reach. It contends, however, that the concentration of functions, slow adjudication and the persistent vulnerability of retail investors call for continued reform, and it assesses the Securities Markets Code, 2025 against that need.
summary: Investor confidence is the foundation on which every securities market rests.
finding: It contends, however, that the concentration of functions, slow adjudication and the persistent vulnerability of retail investors call for continued reform, and it assesses the Securities Markets Code, 2025 against that need.

title: The sustainable competitive advantage in the digital economy: value creation versus value recognition
abstract: Purpose This study aims to investigate the competitive advantage in the digital economy, focusing on the Standard & Poor’s (Standard & Poor’s Financial Services (S&P) 500 companies. This study uses two measures, the Economic Value Added (EVA), an indicator of value creation and economic excellence, and Total Shareholder Return (TSR), as an indicator of value recognition and financial excellence, integrating business and investment strategy. Design/methodology/approach Recognizing the limitations of TSR as an indicator of corporate effectiveness in allocating capital, it highlights the importance of EVA as a metric of organizations’ economic potency based on a panel data set of 467 S&P 500-listed financial and non-financial companies for the decade 2013–2023. Findings The results indicate that EVA is a good, yet largely overlooked, measure of competitive advantage and capital allocation, serving as a robust antecedent of Wall Street firms’ value creation versus value recognition. Practical implications The study proposes an applied metric that helps business leaders assess how well listed companies create value by allocating capital across business opportunities, and how well that value is reflected in their market valuation. Originality/value The significance of the EVA is particularly evident when considering the competitive advantage of businesses operating at the core of the emergent digital economy and the integration of business and investment strategies in pursuit of superior market returns.

title: Factor Investing in the Age of the Magnificent Seven
Large Funds and Corporate Bond Market Fragility
abstract: Abstract The corporate bond fund industry is characterized by a high concentration of capital, with a substantial portion of assets managed by large funds. We examine the relation between large-fund trading exposure and corporate bond volatility across market conditions. Using a comprehensive sample of U.S. bond funds and corporate bonds, we show that bond return volatility decreases (increases) with trading fund size when market liquidity is high (low). Exploring the underlying mechanisms, we find that large funds are more likely to reach for yield by holding illiquid bonds. Further analysis suggests that while large funds supply liquidity during normal times, their liquidity-supplying activity weakens during market stress. Finally, large funds tend to sell illiquid bonds when facing investor outflows during illiquid markets. Overall, our findings reveal an important yet subtle relation between fund size and bond market fragility, akin to a “dam effect.” JEL Classification: G10, G12, G23
summary: The corporate bond fund industry is characterized by a high concentration of capital, with a substantial portion of assets managed by large funds.
finding: Exploring the underlying mechanisms, we find that large funds are more likely to reach for yield by holding illiquid bonds.

title: Are Value and Momentum Still Everywhere?
abstract: I became insane, with long intervals of horrible sanity. – Edgar Allan Poe (1) We have long regarded value and momentum as the “varsity” factors in stock selection. Decades of academic research, including our own, have shown that, historically, buying cheap stocks and buying winners has been associated with higher average returns. Not always, not guaranteed, but on average and over long periods of time. Arguably, the most robust academic paper on this topic comes via Asness, Moskowitz, and Pedersen’s “Value and Momentum Everywhere.” (2) Notably, the authors went beyond stock selection and provided evidence that these factors also earned positive average returns in equity indexes, bonds, currencies, and commodities over their sample period. The conclusion? Value and momentum appeared far more robust than previously shown. But 2013 was a long time ago. We can look at a decent “out-of-sample” test. Since publication, empirical results have been mixed, or just plain awful, depending on who you ask. Of course, one can expect some level of return decay after publication . But how much decay can one handle before suspecting that a strategy has been “arbed” away, or that it never existed in the first place? title: Weekend Reads – 11/6/26
abstract: Quote for the Week How does one identify risk tolerance? Our thinking on this was that the issue is not so much tolerance for risk as it is tolerance for losses. Tolerance for losses means that you have to know — the individual investor has to know and certainly the advisor has to try to know — how much loss the person will be able to tolerate before he changes his mind about what he is doing. Clearly, changing course by and large is not a good idea, and selling low and buying high is not a good idea… If people are very prone to regret, then you have to help them devise a plan that will minimize their regret. For the very wealthy, emotion is clearly important in determining what policy is appropriate… The main question that I have found useful to ask when someone is very wealthy is how much loss is the individual willing to tolerate? That is, what fraction of their wealth are they actually willing to lose? It turns out that fraction is usually not very large. That’s a very important parameter… Then you have to take steps so that they won’t lose more than they are willing to lose. That’s in effect stop-loss policy… Also, people have to become aware of the fact that by stopping their losses, they are giving up some potential upside. Looking at the trade-off between the upside and the downside gives you a sense of their attitude toward losses and what you should encourage them to do. — Daniel Kahneman ( source ) From the Archives Loss Tolerance Second Guessing the Process Last Call What We Learned From Our Own Mistakes – Reimar Scholz It’s Been a Long Time Since Bonds Looked This Good – J. title: Layered framing: Warren Buffett’s shareholder letters, essays and four Korean editions
abstract: This study traces the framing of Warren Buffett’s shareholder letters across five phases in two parts: their compilation as The Essays of Warren Buffett (1997) and four Korean editions (2001–2022). Joining Baker’s account of framing to Bourdieu’s field concepts, it treats framing as a situated practice through which agents pursue symbolic capital, and the source text as itself a framed product. It compares source and target editions and draws on an interview with the translator of three editions. First, the compilation used labeling, selective appropriation and dechronologization to turn corporate reporting into essays, establishing premises — a genre, an authorship, a thematic frame — that later editions inherited without argument. Second, as value investing became orthodox, Korean agents used capital to reframe the book from popular guide to specialist reference work, contesting those premises. Within editions, naming, arrangement and lexis need not align uniformly, as each is oriented toward legitimacy under distinct, level-specific field expectations.
summary: This study traces the framing of Warren Buffett’s shareholder letters across five phases in two parts: their compilation as The Essays of Warren Buffett (1997) and four Korean editions (2001–2022).
finding: Within editions, naming, arrangement and lexis need not align uniformly, as each is oriented toward legitimacy under distinct, level-specific field expectations.

title: Interdependence and Contagion Between Crude Oil Bubbles and Chinese Stock Market Bubbles
abstract: Studying the interdependence and contagion effects between crude oil bubbles and China’s stock market bubble provides a cross-market perspective for monitoring risks across markets and regulating bubbles. Based on data on West Texas Intermediate (WTI) and China’s Shanghai Composite Index from January 1, 2006, to December 30, 2025, we utilize the Generalized Supremum Augmented Dickey–Fuller method to investigate the crude oil bubble and the Chinese stock market bubble. Furthermore, we use the logistic model to examine the interdependence and contagion effects between the two market bubbles. The results show multiple bubbles in crude oil and Chinese stock markets, accompanied by excessive market volatility. The interdependence and bilateral contagion effect between the two market bubbles in different stages have evolved from weak correlation to strong correlation and then to complex correlation. Finally, we put forward the policy design of crude oil-China stock market linkage governance from the three core dimensions of identification, blocking and buffering.
summary: Studying the interdependence and contagion effects between crude oil bubbles and China’s stock market bubble provides a cross-market perspective for monitoring risks across markets and regulating bubbles.
finding: The results show multiple bubbles in crude oil and Chinese stock markets, accompanied by excessive market volatility.

title: When Factors Sleep and Wake: The Dynamic Nature of Factor Investing in US and European Investment-Grade Credit
China is decoupling from the West
abstract: Ever since the trade war between the US and China started in 2018, the mantra of Western businesses has been to decouple from China and reduce their dependency on Chinese goods. But guess what, the same happens in China, and the result is that Western countries are losing their export markets. Economists at the Bank of Finland measured how Chinese imports have changed between 2015 and 2025. They defined ‘Western’ and ‘Eastern’ blocs in a rather unusual way, namely how the country treats Taiwan. If the country doesn’t recognise Taiwan and follows China’s policy stance, the country is considered part of the Eastern bloc. If the country recognises Taiwan or has diplomatic relations with it, it is considered part of the Western bloc. The charts below show how China’s imports of iron and steel (left-hand chart) and nickel (right-hand chart) have changed rapidly, particularly after the pandemic when the West implemented economic sanctions against Russia and became more focused on decoupling from global suppliers that are geopolitical adversaries. The result is also a small decline in the overall exports of Western-aligned countries as they are replaced by China-aligned countries. Market shares of exports of iron, steel and nickel Source: Kerola et al. (2026) If we look at the change in import origins for all goods between 2015 and 2025, we see in the map below that China mostly pivoted away from the US and towards Brazil and Russia. There, Brazil is mostly driven by soybeans and other agricultural exports, while Russia is obviously driven by exports of oil and gas. But we can see that countries in South America and South Asia in general also exported more to China, creating a larger dependency of these countries on demand from China. Meanwhile, next to the US, Germany, South Korea, and Japan have suffered the largest drop in exports to China. Change in exports to China 2015-2025 Source: Kerola et al. (2026)
