title: Tax management and capital allocation
Do limits to arbitrage and mispricing explain belief heterogeneity? Evidence from an emerging market
abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine whether mispricing and limits to arbitrage explain belief heterogeneity in the Tunisian stock market, while accounting for investor sentiment in an emerging market context. Design/methodology/approach Using portfolio sorting and Fama–MacBeth regressions, this study analyzes stock returns from July 2007 to July 2018. It proposes a new trading–volume-based measure of belief heterogeneity and uses multiple proxies for limits to arbitrage and investor sentiment. Findings The results show that stocks with high belief heterogeneity earn lower expected returns. Limits to arbitrage and investor sentiment do not significantly moderate this relationship. However, belief heterogeneity has a stronger effect on undervalued stocks than on overvalued stocks, providing new evidence beyond traditional overvaluation-based explanations. Research limitations/implications The study is limited by its focus on the Tunisian stock market, and the findings may not be generalizable to markets with different institutional structures and investor behaviors. Practical implications The findings provide useful insights for investors and regulators seeking to better understand how belief heterogeneity and market frictions affect stock returns in emerging markets. Originality/value This study contributes to the literature by developing a novel measure of belief heterogeneity and by providing new empirical evidence on the joint role of mispricing and arbitrage constraints in an emerging market setting.
summary: This study aims to examine whether mispricing and limits to arbitrage explain belief heterogeneity in the Tunisian stock market, while accounting for investor sentiment in an emerging market context.
finding: The results show that stocks with high belief heterogeneity earn lower expected returns.

title: The Potential Repercussions of Psychological Bias and Stock Market Abnormalities on Investor Sentiments
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Behavioural finance is the body of knowledge which helps analyse, understand and improve how ordinary people make financial and investment decisions. And how their psychological, cognitive and emotional factors impact their life, investment and financial choices. In growing economies like India, where retail investor activities are on the rise, the behavioural determinant of investor sentiment is becoming increasingly significant for market practitioners and policymakers. In this study, we address the influence of behavioural or psychological biases on the sentiment of retail investors in the Indian stock market. Furthermore, it highlights the cognitive and emotional factors. A systematically prepared questionnaire was used to collect the primary data with the help of convenience sampling. Based on the empirical findings, it has been recognized that behavioural biases determine investor sentiment and cause them to deviate from a rational decision-making based on information. Overconfidence, herd behaviour, and loss aversion were the most influential behavioural biases, among other which determined investment behaviour affecting investors to be more susceptible to market noise and trading on emotion and making wrong investment decisions. The findings also indicate that retail participation driven by sentiment can improve market liquidity and boost optimistic market trends by rising trading activities. Nevertheless, overreliance on emotion-based investment choices heights volatility and distorts prices. In other words, prices do not behave as normally expected during stressful or uncertain environments. The results below suggest that educating investors about cognitive biases through financial literacy and investor education programs can help in avoiding negative outcomes associated with them and enhance decision quality. The research aids in the understanding of investors’ behaviour by enhancing behaviour awareness and rational investment practices. It has real-world possibilities for investors, public agencies, financial entities, regulators and government authorities that wish to enhance market efficiency, investor welfare and long-term financial stability.
summary: Behavioural finance is the body of knowledge which helps analyse, understand and improve how ordinary people make financial and investment decisions.
finding: The results below suggest that educating investors about cognitive biases through financial literacy and investor education programs can help in avoiding negative outcomes associated with them and enhance decision quality.

title: FINANCIAL ENGINEERING OF TOKENIZED ASSETS: SHAPING THE NEW ARCHITEKTURE OF STOCK MARKET INSTRUMENTS
abstract: The financial system is undergoing a fundamental structural transformation driven by the rapid evolution of digital technologies and the convergence of traditional capital markets with decentralized finance. In this context, the aim of the article is to explore the theoretical and applied foundations of the financial engineering of tokenized assets and to substantiate their role in shaping a new architecture for stock market instruments.The research employs a systematic approach, structural-functional analysis, and abstract-logical generalization to examine the mechanisms of asset tokenization. Comparative analysis was used to assess the efficiency of traditional financial instruments versus their digital tokenized counterparts, while scenario modeling helped identify key regulatory and technological risks.It was found that financial engineering through asset tokenization provides a flexible framework for designing innovative financial products with customized risk-return profiles. The integration of distributed ledger technology and smart contracts into stock market infrastructure enables the automation of trade execution, clearing, and settlement, drastically reducing transaction costs and counterparty risks. It has been proven that tokenizing real-world assets enhances market liquidity, eliminates operational friction, and enables fractional ownership, thereby democratizing access to capital markets for a broader spectrum of institutional and retail investors. Furthermore, the study highlights that hybrid digital securities foster cross-border capital mobility and optimize portfolio management strategies in volatile macroeconomic environments.The scientific novelty lies in the comprehensive systematization of financial engineering methods applied to tokenized assets, as well as the conceptualization of a modernized stock market architecture that integrates traditional regulatory standards with decentralized infrastructure elements.The results obtained can be used by financial regulators, stock exchanges, investment funds, and fintech enterprises to establish robust legal and operational frameworks, design compliant tokenized instruments, and accelerate the digital transformation of national capital markets.

title: The Power and the Glory – 400 Years of Bad Decisions
abstract: If you ever visit Stockholm, I would recommend a trip to the Vasa Museum, which is home to a grand warship that sank little more than a kilometre into its maiden voyage in August 1628. Aside from marvelling at its staggering level of preservation, the Vasa disaster is a vivid and ever-relevant example of why big decisions can go terribly wrong. The Vasa was commissioned by King Gustav II Adolf to project military strength and royal grandeur. It was 69 metres long, with three masts and ten sails. It also carried 64 bronze cannons across two gun decks and close to 700 sculptures and ornaments. Looking at its scale and all it carried, it seems a wonder that it ever floated at all. The design of the ship was the responsibility of Dutch master shipwright Henrik Hybertsson, but he died a year before the ship’s first voyage, which augured poorly for what was to follow. Before departure, a test took place in which 30 men ran from one side of the deck to the other. The roll caused by this activity was so severe that the test had to be abandoned. Although Vice Admiral Klas Fleming witnessed this, he did not report it to the King, who was out of the country. According to testimony at the subsequent inquiry, Fleming exclaimed: “If only His Majesty were at home!” The ship set sail in front of expectant crowds on 10 August 1628. The Vasa almost immediately struggled for stability as winds gusted. Water began to enter through the open lower gunports, and the ship sank. It is estimated that around 30 people died. There are several technical explanations for the Vasa’s sinking: its tall, heavy upper structure, the relatively small hull beneath the waterline and the open gunports. But the choice to sail despite the warning is also a failure of decision making, and one that seems eerily modern. How does such a decision get made? Power and incentives Most decisions reflect the power and incentives at play. Decisions get made by those with power, based on their goals and desires, and the Vasa was no different. The King was the autocratic decision maker and he wanted a glorious and prestigious ship. Those working for him had limited power and were incentivised to please him, or at least not disappoint him. To this day, the best way to predict what decisions will get made in almost any situation is to understand who holds the power and what they want. The consequences of dissent The prospect of disappointing King Gustav II Adolf seems to have carried considerable weight: even the failed test was not reported to him. We cannot know exactly how those involved weighed the consequences of calling out problems or jeopardising the project, but the personal risks of speaking up may have felt more immediate and specific than the general danger of going ahead. title: Can You Count on Social Security in Retirement?
abstract: A few weeks ago, this tweet set off a firestorm on Twitter/X: JUST IN: 🇺🇸 US boomers overwhelmingly support higher taxes on younger workers to maintain current Social Security benefits, poll shows. After the usual boomer bashing, the conversation quickly turned to a question I often get from younger readers: Can I count on Social Security in retirement? It's a fair question. If you're in your 20s, 30s, or 40s, you've probably spent most of your life hearing about how Social Security is going bankrupt. You've been told that the trust fund is running dry. While technically true, does it mean that you should plan as if Social Security won't exist? Not exactly. While the retirement trust fund is projected to run out in 2032, according to the 2026 Trustees Report , benefits will still be paid out, just at a lower percentage. How much lower? 78% of scheduled benefits. That's a 22% reduction, which is real. But it's not a 100% reduction! The average Social Security benefit today is around $2,000/month. So, if the trust fund were to run out tomorrow, the average benefit would be around $1,560/month [78% of $2,000]. That's not great, but it demonstrates that something will continue to be paid even in such an undesirable scenario. Given this, the question isn't whether Social Security will exist in the future (it will), but how much of it can you count on when you hit retirement? Let's take a look at the numbers. What Happens After the Social Security Trust Fund Runs Out of Money? Social Security benefits are paid out from two sources: taxes on existing workers (i.e., payroll taxes) and the trust fund. Well, technically, there are two trust funds. The main one is Old-Age and Survivors Insurance (OASI), which pays retirement and survivor benefits. And the other is Disability Insurance (DI), which pays disability benefits. The DI fund is in good shape, projected to pay full benefits through the end of the 75-year projection window in 2100. But OASI isn't. That's the one estimated to run dry in 2032. While these two funds are often quoted together as OASDI, money can't move between them without Congress passing a law. Let's assume that doesn't happen, so OASI is what we will focus on for retirement benefits. And OASI has been running out of money since 2021 . That was the first year where benefits paid to retirees exceeded the total payroll taxes collected from workers plus interest income on OASI. As a result, principal had to be withdrawn from the OASI trust fund. This will continue until the trust fund runs out in 2032. What happens then? Since Social Security can't borrow funds, it can only pay out what it takes in. So once the trust fund is empty, benefits would have to be brought down to whatever payroll taxes can cover. Right now that estimate is 78% of scheduled benefits in the first year . After that, the percentage declines as the ratio of workers to retirees continues to fall. title: Market perspectives
How Wise Is the Crowd? Timing and Selection Skill of Retail Social-Trading Portfolios
abstract: Social-trading platforms publish every trade of thousands of private investors. Aggregating such trades into a "crowd signal" is an old idea; whether the crowd actually knows something is an empirical question. We study 313,302 trades of 82 top-ranked portfolios on wikifolio.com (June 2012 to 23 February 2026; data cutoff 1 March 2026) and separate market timing from stock selection. Four results stand out. (i) Net crowd buying is a reaction variable: it follows past index weakness and rising volatility, and none of 54 predictive regressions on future DAX or S&P 500 returns has a Newey–West |t| above 1.7. (ii) Stock selection looks positive for buys (60-day alpha +0.79%, cluster t=2.3, return measured from the close of the day after the trade) and the buy-minus-sell difference is significant (+1.04 pp, t=3.3). A panel baseline of all days of the same stocks shows that the spread of buy returns is mostly proximity to the 52-week high, a known anomaly; after controlling for it, buys keep a modest increment of +0.92 pp over 60 days (t=2.9), sells none (+0.15 pp, t=0.4), gross of costs. (iii) Since 2020 the edge sits on the sell side: stocks sold in 2020–26 underperformed by 1.12% over 60 days (t=-2.3) while buy alpha at 60 days is indistinguishable from zero (+0.05%, t=0.1); sells after strong run-ups are too early. (iv) Very short holdings earn nothing (1–5 days: 36.8% win rate). We then report what happened when these facts were turned into a signal generator ("Maximale Crowd"): a contribution-weighted aggregation of traders (Budescu and Chen), a binomial consensus gate and a stop-loss hybrid. The system suffered from sparse trader overlap, a concentrated effective crowd (about 10 of 71 qualified traders carry the weight), tuning on 165 trading days, and a look-ahead bug that invalidated every backtest. We therefore claim no tradable edge. The paper documents data, methods, discarded ideas and pitfalls so that the work can be audited or continued.Read next: The look-ahead bug described here motivated the leak-resistant point-in-time backtesting. For event signals beyond the crowd, see the negative results on event-driven signals. Crowd-based candidates were later judged in a pre-registered out-of-sample test.This preprint is part of an eight-paper series on retail equity research from public data by Christopher Helm, covering German and Nordic small caps, backtesting methodology, data sources and AI-assisted research. title: Defining, Measuring, and Comparing Short-Termism
abstract: This chapter defines, measures, and compares corporate short-termism and sets out the empirical strategy used in the book’s large-N analysis. It specifies the book’s central empirical question: whether the existence and extent of short-termism varies among publicly listed firms across national contexts once structural and economic differences are controlled for, and whether coordinated market economies are converging towards the Anglo-American model in capital allocation. It defines short-termism primarily as relatively high shareholder payout and treats real investment as a related but distinct outcome that cannot be straightforwardly equated with long-termism or short-termism in all contexts. It then justifies the selection of Germany, Japan, the United States, and the United Kingdom and explains the treatment of the United States and the United Kingdom as an Anglo-American benchmark while still analysing them separately. The chapter describes the data source, sample construction, accounting comparability, and the study period, and it outlines the main measures for shareholder payout and real investment, including alternative operationalisations. It details the use of ratios, growth rates, common-currency comparisons using purchasing power parity, inflation adjustment, and winsorisation to address outliers. Finally, it presents the matching procedure used to compare public firms across countries by industry and size and previews how matched comparisons are applied in the empirical chapters that follow.
summary: This chapter defines, measures, and compares corporate short-termism and sets out the empirical strategy used in the book’s large-N analysis.
finding: Finally, it presents the matching procedure used to compare public firms across countries by industry and size and previews how matched comparisons are applied in the empirical chapters that follow.

title: Zen and the Art of Financial Risk Management: A Behavioral Framework Synchronizing
abstract: Modern financial markets are characterized by high volatility, information asymmetry, and intense emotional catalysts. While standard economic theory relies on the Rational Expectations Hypothesis (REH), empirical evidence from behavioral finance demonstrates that cognitive biases and emotional reactivity consistently drive market inefficiencies and systematic investor underperformance. This paper introduces an interdisciplinary paradigm by integrating Zen Buddhist epistemology—specifically the tenets of mindfulness (sati), non-attachment (anatta), and impermanence (anicca)—into the operational mechanics of derivative options, macroeconomic futures speculation, and fundamental value investing. We present a quantitative framework showing how Zen cognitive strategies systematically mitigate pervasive behavioral anomalies such as loss aversion, herd behavior, and overconfidence. Finally, we model this through a proposed Zen-Equanimity Index (ZEI) regression design and provide a comparative critique of institutional algorithmic high-frequency trading (HFT) versus human Zen trading systems. By replacing ego-driven utility maximization with detached observation and process-oriented execution, market participants can achieve structural equanimity, optimizing risk management and decision-making utility within highly volatile financial environments.
summary: Modern financial markets are characterized by high volatility, information asymmetry, and intense emotional catalysts.
finding: By replacing ego-driven utility maximization with detached observation and process-oriented execution, market participants can achieve structural equanimity, optimizing risk management and decision-making utility within highly volatile financial environments.

title: AI-Augmented Behavioural Finance Pedagogy: Transforming Undergraduate and Postgraduate Classrooms through Simulation-Based Learning
publisher: Journal of Asia Entrepreneurship and Sustainability
venue: Journal of Asia Entrepreneurship and Sustainability
abstract: The rapid integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into higher education has transformed how business and management subjects are taught and learned. In finance education, traditional teaching methods often emphasize numerical calculations and theoretical frameworks while offering limited opportunities for experiential and behavioral learning. In this case study, the authors present a real classroom-based pedagogical intervention implemented in a course for undergraduate and postgraduate students at Commerce and Management Institutes in India, where AI tools and behavioral finance simulations through games were integrated into teaching practices to improve student engagement, analytical thinking, and practical decision-making skills. This case study emerged from observations by the teaching faculty who taught Behavioural Finance courses to undergraduate and graduate students, who frequently struggled to connect financial theories with real-world investment behaviour and market psychology. In an attempt to make students show their interest in learning this kind of course, which requires understanding the fundamentals of Psychology, which is a prerequisite for this course. To address these challenges, AI-assisted simulations, AI-generated market scenarios, interactive case discussions, and behavioural finance activities were introduced into the classroom in the form of a game. Students were exposed to emotionally driven financial decision-making situations, such as panic selling, herding behaviour, overconfidence bias, and speculative investment trends, through AI-generated business narratives and stock market simulations. The teaching faculty made an attempt through gamification as an intervention by adopting a simulation-based learning framework. Based on the authors' experience in teaching behavioural finance courses, a simulation was created using AI. This AI-generated investment simulation scenario was used as a pilot study in the real classroom. The students actively participated in games and were able to make decisions rather than absorb theoretical content. AI tools were used to generate realistic market situations, investment dilemmas, and personalised learning prompts that encouraged critical analysis and collaborative problem-solving. The results demonstrated and presented active classroom participation, improved conceptual understanding, enhanced critical thinking abilities, and greater student interest in finance subjects. Students reported that the integration of AI made finance learning more relatable, practical, and interactive. This case also discusses ethical concerns, faculty adaptation challenges, limitations of AI-generated learning environments, and recommendations for responsible AI integration in finance education. This case study contributes to the growing discourse on gamification through AI-enabled pedagogy by demonstrating how behavioural finance and AI can be combined to create immersive and mock experiential learning experiences in management education.
summary: The rapid integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into higher education has transformed how business and management subjects are taught and learned.
finding: In an attempt to make students show their interest in learning this kind of course, which requires understanding the fundamentals of Psychology, which is a prerequisite for this course.

title: Risk-Adjusted Performance Ranking and Clustering Analysis of NIFTY 50 Stocks on the Financial Metrics and Time-Series Forecasting
abstract: Stock market analytics is a vital part of systematic investment decision-making, portfolio management, and risk management. Conventional price-based evaluation procedures do not consider volatility, downside risk, and liquidity limitations, resulting in inappropriate stock selection. This paper suggests a combined risk-adjusted analytical framework that is applied to the constituents of the NIFTY 50 index based on historical data from 2015 to 2025. The dataset contains historical data for 52 unique companies that were constituents of the NIFTY 50 index during the study period (2015-2025). Although the index consists of 50 companies at any point in time, constituent changes over the study period resulted in a total of 52 unique companies being included in the analysis. This approach is a combination of the Compounded Annual Growth Rate (CAGR), annualized volatility, Sharpe ratio, Sortino ratio, and Maximum Drawdown to create a composite performance score. To ensure feasible tradability, liquidity screening is included. K-means clustering (K = 3) is used to carry out structural market segmentation based on growth and risk dimensions, and predictive power is determined through AutoRegressive Integrated Moving Average-based time-series forecasting. According to the empirical evidence, the top five risk-adjusted performers include TITAN, HINDUNILVR, BAJFINANCE, KOTAKBANK, and HDFC, with composite scores ranging from 0.833 to 1.829. The clustering results show three different performance regimes, with high-CAGR stocks (~26%) exhibiting better Sharpe ratios (~0.66) and lower volatility (~32%), while underperforming groups show negative growth and extreme drawdowns (-89%). The research adds a unified and quantitatively reliable stock assessment paradigm that balances growth, risk, and liquidity. In practice, the method aids robust stock ranking and provides a foundation for improving portfolio allocation strategies and predictive modeling.
summary: Stock market analytics is a vital part of systematic investment decision-making, portfolio management, and risk management.
finding: The clustering results show three different performance regimes, with high-CAGR stocks (~26%) exhibiting better Sharpe ratios (~0.66) and lower volatility (~32%), while underperforming groups show negative growth and extreme drawdowns (-89%).

title: A Critical Exploratory Study on the Method of Value Investing (Warren Buffett's Portfolio Management Strategy) as Opposed to Diversified Quantitative Models of Modern Portfolio Theory
venue: International Journal of Economics and Management Studies
abstract: Modern Portfolio Theory and Value Investing are widely treated as competing investment frameworks, with debate centering on which delivers superior risk-adjusted returns. This paper challenges that framing, arguing that the two are not rival frameworks, but complementary tools applied at different stages of the investment process. It compares how each framework defines risk, diversification, and portfolio construction, drawing on a conceptual review of the literature and case studies of leading practitioners — Warren Buffett and Peter Lynch as value investors, and Ray Dalio's Bridgewater and Dimensional Fund Advisors as quantitative, MPT-based managers. To test whether this complementarity holds in practice, the study conducts a primary survey on Indian investment practitioners, including individual investors, fund managers, and wealth advisors. The findings indicate that pure forms of either framework are rarely practiced: institutional approaches retain MPT's mathematical framework while building on it with factor models and risk parity. Most surveyed practitioners reported using a combination of both philosophies — MPT to guide portfolio construction and diversification, and value investing’s margin-of-safety concept to select individual securities. Practitioners tilt towards the value investing definition of risk as permanent loss of capital rather than volatility, as in MPT, and most consider markets to be only moderately efficient. The study concludes that an optimal approach for investors lies not in choosing between the frameworks but in pragmatic diversification using the two, offering insights highly relevant to retail and emerging-market investors navigating between these methods themselves.
summary: Modern Portfolio Theory and Value Investing are widely treated as competing investment frameworks, with debate centering on which delivers superior risk-adjusted returns.
finding: The study concludes that an optimal approach for investors lies not in choosing between the frameworks but in pragmatic diversification using the two, offering insights highly relevant to retail and emerging-market investors navigating between these methods…

title: Realized semi-coskewnesses and the cross-section of expected stock returns
The Rise of Alternatives
abstract: Abstract Since the 2000s, U.S. public pension funds have actively shifted their risky investments away from public equities and toward alternative assets like private equity and hedge funds—some much more than others. We explore a range of possible explanations for these trends and argue that beliefs about the risk-adjusted return of alternatives have played a central role. Pension beliefs are shaped by investment consultants, peers, and experience in the 1990s. Other demand-side channels related to risk-seeking motives, spending needs, and fund governance have weaker empirical support. We also consider supply-side factors and agency interpretations of the data.
summary: Since the 2000s, U.S. public pension funds have actively shifted their risky investments away from public equities and toward alternative assets like private equity and hedge funds—some much more than others.
finding: We also consider supply-side factors and agency interpretations of the data.

title: The economics of data unions: optimal data sharing and coordination
abstract: Abstract We develop a model of data-driven competition in which product quality depends on users’ data contributions and firms’ investments in data infrastructure. Users’ inability to internalize the value generated by their data, together with firms’ strategic investment incentives, can lead to data underinvestment—limiting quality—or overinvestment—concentrating market power. We introduce a data union that coordinates users’ contributions and can be implemented through a data trust or intermediary that aggregates user data. By shaping data compensation, the union enables users to capture and internalize more of their data’s value, enhancing user welfare, especially when combined with data sharing among firms. We apply these insights to financial data, digital payments, and Open Finance. Our analysis shows that data portability can strengthen competition but, without coordination, may leave data investment too low or excessive.
summary: We develop a model of data-driven competition in which product quality depends on users’ data contributions and firms’ investments in data infrastructure.
finding: Our analysis shows that data portability can strengthen competition but, without coordination, may leave data investment too low or excessive.

title: Financial Context-Rich Strategy for Actor-Critic based Agents: A Deep Reinforcement Learning Approach for Stock Trading
abstract: In modern financial markets, more than 3/4th of the large volume trade is executed by algorithmic trading based on advanced trading strategies to attain higher precision and speed than traditional human traders. The conventional strategies focused on price-based indicators are inadequate in capturing the market dynamism arising from real-world events such as social sentiments, political instability, or sudden economic shifts. With the rise of Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) and data availability, there is a requirement for more efficient algorithms that can incorporate these external factors in trading strategies. DRL has shown potential in simulating real-world scenarios and in simplifying complex decision-making since DRL agents can automate the trading process i.e. executing trades in a manner comparable to human traders. They have shown reliable performance since they can update their policies based on risk and quantitative factors. In this paper, we propose a DRL approach based on partial and deep-infusion of sentimental analysis. It features distinct policy designs of actor-critic-based agents: only policy optimization (A2C & PPO) and policy optimization along with Q-learning principles (DDPG, TD3 & SAC). Our findings reveal, that the agents based on policy optimization combined with Q-learning, significantly and consistently demonstrate improved performance upon sentiment deep-infusion in profit maximization as well as risk-averse trading.
summary: In modern financial markets, more than 3/4th of the large volume trade is executed by algorithmic trading based on advanced trading strategies to attain higher precision and speed than traditional human traders.
finding: Our findings reveal, that the agents based on policy optimization combined with Q-learning, significantly and consistently demonstrate improved performance upon sentiment deep-infusion in profit maximization as well as risk-averse trading.

title: Private Equity Valuation Dynamics in the Generative Artificial Intelligence Sector: A Case Study of OpenAI
venue: Advances in economics, business and management research/Advances in Economics, Business and Management Research
abstract: This study examines valuation mechanisms and phased differences in the generative artificial intelligence (AI) industry. Taking OpenAI as the core case and comparing it with private leading firms such as Anthropic and listed peers, including NVIDIA and Microsoft, this research uses case analysis, cross-firm comparison, and multi-model valuation to build a two-dimensional framework that combines financial indicators and non-financial core assets. This study develops phased valuation models for the seed stage (comparable transaction method + real option method), growth stage (average revenue per paying user (ARPU) multiple method + user value method), and mature stage (discounted cash flow (DCF) method + price-to-earnings (PE) method + comparable company method). This study subsequently benchmarks the computational outcomes against market valuations, analyzes the causes of deviations, and proposes directions for model optimization. Empirical evidence suggests a fundamental shift in GenAI valuation logic, transitioning from a “financial statement-driven” approach to “technological asset pricing”. The three-stage model proposed in this paper successfully captures the premium fluctuations of OpenAI in empirical analysis, demonstrating that quantifying non-financial indicators can notably correct the issue of traditional models underestimating the valuation of high-growth AI companies. The model elevates the private equity valuation system in the generative AI industry, providing a more granular reference perspective for primary market pricing.
summary: This study examines valuation mechanisms and phased differences in the generative artificial intelligence (AI) industry.
finding: The model elevates the private equity valuation system in the generative AI industry, providing a more granular reference perspective for primary market pricing.

title: Analysis of the Valuation Evolution and Driving Factors of Minimax From the Perspective of Private Equity Investment
venue: Advances in economics, business and management research/Advances in Economics, Business and Management Research
abstract: The valuation challenges in the Artificial Intelligence (AI) large model industry have highlighted the limitations of traditional valuation methods, while the construction of a valuation system with Chinese characteristics has provided a new logical dimension for the valuation of emerging technology enterprises. This study takes MiniMax, a leading domestic large language model (LLM) enterprise, as a case to examine its full financing and listing trajectory from angel round to Initial Public Offering (IPO) between late 2021 and January 2026. Using a combination of case analysis and comparable company valuation, it systematically traces the evolution of private equity valuation logic, core driving factors, and the enabling role of the “China Special Valuation” policy. The findings reveal the inherent logic of valuation transition from private to public equity in China’s LLM industry, emphasizing the valuation support from localized scenario adaptation and policy empowerment for growth-oriented tech firms. This research provides a reference for PE investment valuation, corporate financing, and listing strategies in the LLM sector, and offers an empirical case for understanding the practical effects of the “China Special Valuation” policy in emerging technology industries.
summary: The valuation challenges in the Artificial Intelligence (AI) large model industry have highlighted the limitations of traditional valuation methods, while the construction of a valuation system with Chinese characteristics has provided a new logical dimension for the valuation of emerging technology enterprises.
finding: The findings reveal the inherent logic of valuation transition from private to public equity in China’s LLM industry, emphasizing the valuation support from localized scenario adaptation and policy empowerment for growth-oriented tech firms.

title: Investor Sentiment and Stock Return Prediction: Evidence from Machine Learning and VAR Models
venue: Advances in economics, business and management research/Advances in Economics, Business and Management Research
abstract: In the context of rapid information technology development and improved data acquisition capabilities, traditional linear-assumption-based asset pricing models gradually face challenges in short-term return forecasting. As an important behavioral factor affecting stock prices, investor sentiment is of increasing concern about its role in irrational volatility. Taking China’s A-share market as the research object, this paper constructs a multi-dimensional factor system covering fundamentals, trading characteristics, and investor sentiment within a unified data framework, and applies a multifactor linear model, a random forest model, and an XGBoost model to predict stock returns separately. At the same time, the vector autoregressive model is introduced to characterize the dynamic relationship between investor sentiment and stock returns. Empirical results show that machine learning models outperform traditional linear models in out-of-sample prediction and portfolio performance, with the XGBoost model performing the best. After the inclusion of sentiment factors, the predictive power and risk-adjusted returns of the models are significantly improved. Further analysis shows that investor sentiment has a significant but short-term impact on stock returns. The results of this paper show that investor sentiment has a certain explanatory power in short-term earnings forecasting and improves the performance of the model to a certain extent.
summary: In the context of rapid information technology development and improved data acquisition capabilities, traditional linear-assumption-based asset pricing models gradually face challenges in short-term return forecasting.
finding: Further analysis shows that investor sentiment has a significant but short-term impact on stock returns.

title: Excess Movement in Option‐Implied Beliefs
abstract: ABSTRACT We derive bounds on the rational variation in option‐implied beliefs about market returns. While risk preferences distort option‐implied (or risk‐neutral ) beliefs away from subjective beliefs, one can nonetheless bound risk‐neutral belief movement under a general assumption on the stochastic discount factor. The resulting test requires no knowledge of the objective distribution and allows significantly more flexibility in discount rates than standard volatility tests. Implementing our test empirically using index options, we find that there is so much movement in risk‐neutral beliefs that the bounds are routinely violated. Our results imply significant excess index‐price volatility.
summary: ABSTRACT We derive bounds on the rational variation in option‐implied beliefs about market returns.
finding: Our results imply significant excess index‐price volatility.

title: Intraday Forecasting Ability and Liquidity Provision of Institutional Traders
abstract: This study uses a high-frequency dataset from a stock exchange to examine how forecasting ability and liquidity provision relate to institutional traders' proprietary intraday profitability. We discover persistent forecasting abilities among traders. Specifically, we demonstrate that hypothetical flow-following strategies based on the execution flows of these skillful traders yield annualized Sharpe ratios ranging from 16 to 63 across various trading frequencies. We match buy and sell executions into positions, linking realized profit and loss (P&L) to horizon-matched forecasting proxies and the liquidity roles of both executions. Our findings indicate a direct correlation between improved forecasting ability and profitability, where a one-standard-deviation increase in the forecasting ability proxy is associated with 1.02 -- 1.19 currency units higher P&L per matched position. Additionally, we measure liquidity-provision intensity within a matched position by its number of passive executions: zero, one, or two. In these regressions, P&L is 1.28 -- 1.31 currency units higher for one passive execution than for none, and a further 3.79 -- 3.82 higher for two than for one, underscoring the significant financial benefits of liquidity provision.
summary: This study uses a high-frequency dataset from a stock exchange to examine how forecasting ability and liquidity provision relate to institutional traders' proprietary intraday profitability.
finding: In these regressions, P&L is 1.28 -- 1.31 currency units higher for one passive execution than for none, and a further 3.79 -- 3.82 higher for two than for one, underscoring the significant financial benefits of liquidity provision.

title: From Eyeballs to Annual Run Rates (ARR): Buzzy Pricing Metrics and the Anthropic Trade!
abstract: I was in San Francisco last week to talk to NYU Stern Alumni on October 15, and it was the day that Anthropic had a pre-IPO meeting with prospective investors. While I was not at the meeting, the focus of teh gathering was laying a foundation for its upcoming IPO, with the company reporting third-quarter revenue of $16.8 billion, which news reports described as surging 45% over the previous quarter's revenues, and positive profits, albeit on an adjusted basis. During the meeting, Anthropic also reported an annual revenue run rate (ARR) of $67 billion, a metric that those in the AI space have adopted with gusto, with an estimate that the ARR would exceed $100 billion by the end of the year. The nature of ARR, where choices on how revenue is calculated (gross versus net) and on annualization periods (daily, weekly or monthly) can make a significant difference, has led investors to be skeptical about comparing these numbers across time and companies. While I share some of that skepticism, it is worth remembering that young businesses are often priced on inventive metrics, some with more basis than others. In the late nineties, dot.com companies were priced not just on the number of visitors to their websites, but on eyeballs , where Mary Meeker argued that ad spending at these companies was correlated with time that these visitors spent on websites (eyeballs), rather than with total visitors. In the last decade, you saw social media companies priced based upon the number of users and subscription-based companies on subscriber numbers. In this post, I will try to lay out the rationale for why pricing supplants valuation in young companies and why that pricing almost always has to be built around messy metrics like eyeballs, users and ARR, rather than more conventional metrics like earnings, book value or cash flows. Young Companies in a Corporate Life Cycle All businesses, no matter how large and established they might be today, started as young businesses and matured. With that perspective in mind, I will start this discussion by placing young businesses in a corporate life cycle in the figure below: One of the first steps in analyzing a company is placing it in the right stage of the life cycle, and there are three choices that you can use in making this placement: Chronological age : The first and simplest choice is to look at the age of a business, putting companies that have been in operation for short periods into the young company grouping and classifying those that have been in operation for longer as mature. While this approach is easy to use, and for the most part, effective, it can be misleading in businesses like infrastructure, where it can take decades to get established, and in technology, where the lack of capital intensity can allow a company can go from start-up to mature in a few years. A stretchable liquid-metal bioelectric catheter for active management of catheter-associated urinary tract infections
abstract: Catheter-associated urinary tract infections (CAUTIs) continue to be a major clinical complication of indwelling catheterization, sustained by persistent bacterial colonization and dysregulated local immune responses. Most antimicrobial coatings provide passive protection and have limited capacity to address both bacterial persistence and the host response at the catheter-tissue interface. This study presents a stretchable urological catheter for electrical stimulation (SUCES) based on a liquid metal composite. SUCES consists of a stable gallium-10 vol% silver (Ga-Ag) circuit encapsulated within a silver-doped (5 vol%) polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS-Ag) layer. SUCES delivers low-voltage electrical stimulation (1.5 V for 5 min) in combination with sustained Ag release, resulting in effective combined antibacterial activity. In vitro testing demonstrates bacterial killing efficiencies of approximately 95% for E. coli and 94% for S. aureus. The same electrical input also promoted an M1-associated macrophage response. In a rabbit CAUTI model, seven days of treatment reduced the viable urinary bacterial burden by 93% (>1-log reduction). SUCES-treated tissues also showed less infection-associated inflammation and better-preserved urothelial barrier integrity. These findings support SUCES as an active bioelectric catheter interface that integrates antibacterial treatment with macrophage-associated immune modulation for catheter-associated infection management.
summary: Catheter-associated urinary tract infections (CAUTIs) continue to be a major clinical complication of indwelling catheterization, sustained by persistent bacterial colonization and dysregulated local immune responses.
finding: SUCES-treated tissues also showed less infection-associated inflammation and better-preserved urothelial barrier integrity.

title: Financial Performance, Valuation, and Stock-Market Behavior of Selected Philippine Hotel and Leisure Companies
abstract: Financial performance and stock-market behavior may provide different assessments of companies operating within the same industry. This study examined the financial performance, valuation, and market characteristics of four Philippine Stock Exchange-listed hotel and leisure companies: Acesite (Phils.) Hotel Corporation (ACE), Boulevard Holdings, Inc. (BHI), Grand Plaza Hotel Corporation (GPH), and Waterfront Philippines, Inc. (WPI). A descriptive-comparative design was employed using secondary financial and stock-market information reported in a September 2026 company analysis. The investigation integrated profitability, valuation, liquidity, leverage, historical stock-price returns, trading activity, and technical indicators. Results revealed substantial company-level differences. ACE continued to report losses despite favorable recent stock returns. BHI exhibited inconsistent profitability alongside a current ratio of 2.71 and a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.13. GPH experienced declining revenue, negative earnings, and a reported three-year stock-price return of -49.40%. WPI maintained relatively stable revenue and returned to positive quarterly earnings during the first half of 2026, although its year-to-date and one-year returns remained negative. Negative trailing earnings limited conventional price-to-earnings comparisons, while technical indicators frequently produced mixed signals across observation horizons. The findings support an integrated assessment that distinguishes earnings performance, balance-sheet condition, valuation, and market behavior. Unequal reporting periods, incomplete indicator coverage, and the ownership relationship between ACE and WPI limit comparability. The conclusions remain specific to the selected companies and do not establish causal relationships or predictive investment performance.
summary: Financial performance and stock-market behavior may provide different assessments of companies operating within the same industry.
finding: The conclusions remain specific to the selected companies and do not establish causal relationships or predictive investment performance.

title: Key behavioral factors of participant groups in the Ukrainian stock market
venue: Management and Entrepreneurship Trends of Development
abstract: The article is devoted to developing new scientific solutions regarding the determination of key behavioral factors of participant groups in the Ukrainian stock market. The study proved that the development of effective stimulating measures for the development of Ukraine's stock market is possible only on the basis of identification and consideration of the behavioral factors influencing the main groups of stock market participants in the country. The article aims to identify the key behavioral factors influencing groups of participants in the Ukrainian stock market based on a review of scholarly works by foreign and Ukrainian researchers, an analysis of the country’s stock market development, and an examination of the actions of major groups of stock market participants under wartime challenges. Methodology: A set of general and special methods was applied at the empirical and theoretical levels, including critical literature analysis to evaluate academic research in the field of behavioral finance; historical comparative quantitative analysis to examine the development of the Ukrainian stock market in 2021–2025; logical generalization to identify the key behavioral factors affecting the defined groups of participants in the Ukrainian stock market; synthesis to identify the key groups of participants in the Ukrainian stock market; and systematization, grouping, and logical generalization to systematize information and formulate the conclusions and scientific proposals of the study. Results: The study allowed for the identification of the key behavioral factors influencing the defined groups of participants in the Ukrainian stock market, such as Ukrainian issuers, excluding the state and municipal authorities; the state; municipal authorities (local self-government bodies); professional investors, including institutional investors; private investors, households; and foreign investors. Practical significance: The practical implementation of the proposals and conclusions of this article should be considered in the context of their importance for developing ways to stimulate the development of Ukraine’s stock market amid the wartime and post-war transformation of the country’s economic system. Uniqueness/value: The scientific study, based on the author's definition of the term "behavioral finance," proposed expanding the range of behavioral factors that influence the stock market by incorporating behavioral factors associated with the digitalization of the market. It also suggested identifying behavioral factors according to the key groups of stock market participants, based on an analysis of the development of a specific stock market, namely the Ukrainian stock market. What is the Average Net Worth by Age? [2025 Latest Data]
abstract: Do you want to know how you are doing relative to your peers financially? Then this is the article for you. The Federal Reserve recently released its 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances , the gold standard of wealth data for American households. I've decided to take this data and calculate the average net worth by age so you can get a better handle on how you stack up financially. Of course, we know that "comparison is the thief of joy," but this doesn't mean that benchmarking can't be useful. This is especially true when it comes to benchmarking your wealth, something that is still taboo to discuss openly. And since it isn't discussed, most people can only infer how they are doing by looking at what people buy as a signal to their wealth. Unfortunately, this isn't the clearest picture of someone's finances. This is why we must rely on aggregated financial data (i.e. net worth). More importantly, we must break this net worth data down by age for it to be useful to us. Why? Because age is positively correlated with how long you've worked, which is positively correlated with your savings and wealth. After all, would it be fair to compare the wealth of someone with three decades of work experience against someone who just graduated from college? Of course not! Though that older person probably has more money, the younger person has more time (which can be used to create money). This is why comparing net worth by age is essential if we want to have a better understanding of our financial well-being. But, before we dig into the data on net worth, let's do a quick refresher on what it shows and how to interpret it. What is Net Worth? Net worth is the total value of an individual's assets minus their liabilities: Net Worth = Assets – Liabilities In other words, it's everything you own (i.e. house, car, bank accounts, stocks, ETFs, rental properties, etc.) minus everything that you owe to others (i.e. credit card debt, student loan debt, mortgage, etc.). After netting the differences, we get a financial measure that we can use to compare across households. One other thing to note is that all of the net worth figures used in this article are inflation-adjusted to 2025 dollars. This means that I am showing real dollar changes when showing any year before 2025. With that being said, let's look at the average net worth and why this measure has its limitations. What is the Average Net Worth (and What Are its Limitations)? The average net worth of U.S. households in 2025 was $1,231,997. This is an inflation-adjusted increase of $72,550 (6%) from the average net worth of $1,159,447 in 2022. If these figures seem high to you, it's because they are. The typical American household is not walking around with $1 million in wealth. The problem with the average net worth is that it tends to be heavily skewed by outliers (i.e. the superrich).
