title: The Rise of Passive Investing in India: Performance, Risk and Market Efficiency of Index Funds and Actively Managed Mutual Funds
abstract: Purpose – The paper aims to explore if the speedy migration of Indian investors to index funds/Exchange Traded Funds (ETFs) can be explained by the comparative performance, risk and cost character is tics of passive and active equity mutual funds and how far it is indicative of informational efficiency of Indian equity markets. Design/methodology/approach – AMFI provides industry-level data to us in the AMFI-CRISIL Factbook 2026, combined with the S&P Indices Versus Active (SPIVA) India scorecards for the period ending December 2025. We evaluate performance by benchmark-relative underperformance rates over 1-, 3-, 5- and 10-year horizons, asset- and equal-weighted returns, risk-adjusted comparisons and survivorship. We analyze the evidence through the lens of the Efficient Market Hypothesis, the Grossman-Stiglitz paradox and the Sharpe’s arithmetic of active management and specify a fund-level multi-factor model for replication. Findings – Passive assets reached ~₹13.7 lakh crore by March 2026, increasing industry share of passive from 9.8% to 18.6% in five years. Over 10 years (2006-17), 76.3% of active large cap funds, 82.9% of ELSS funds and 79.0% of mid/small-cap funds underperformed benchmark, and 27% of funds failed to survive a decade. Shorter-horizon findings vary substantially by segment: active mid/small-cap fund beat the benchmark at a high rate in 2025, whereas active large-cap fund failed to do so. The pattern is in line with a near semi-strong-form efficient large cap segment, and a relatively inefficient, illiquid small-cap segment. Originality/value – The article provides fresh, India-specific, 2017 alternative insights on the passive-active debate following SEBI’s move to recategorize the scheme in 2017, and positions the passive growth as an efficiency story not just an investor-cost one.
summary: Purpose – The paper aims to explore if the speedy migration of Indian investors to index funds/Exchange Traded Funds (ETFs) can be explained by the comparative performance, risk and cost character is tics of passive and active equity mutual funds and how far it is indicative of informational efficiency of Indian…
finding: Originality/value – The article provides fresh, India-specific, 2017 alternative insights on the passive-active debate following SEBI’s move to recategorize the scheme in 2017, and positions the passive growth as an efficiency story not just an investor-cost…

title: Physical AI Adoption and Corporate Valuation: Examining How Investment in Autonomous Technologies Influences Firm Performance, Capital Allocation, and Long-Term Shareholder Value
Physical AI Adoption and Firm Valuation: Examining How Investment in Robotics and Autonomous Systems Influences Corporate Performance, Capital Allocation, and Long-Term Shareholder Value
Optimal Information and Security Design
abstract: Abstract An asset owner designs an asset-backed security and a signal about its value. After experiencing a liquidity shock and privately observing the signal, he sells the security to imperfectly competitive buyers. With flexible information design, the security’s informational sensitivity is a blessing, not a curse. Among double-monotone securities, the issuer prefers to sell the asset in combination with an appropriate signal rather than design more complex securities. Within the class of monotone securities, live-or-die securities are optimal and strictly dominate asset sales. When signals are restricted to be sufficiently informative about the upside, debt and additional-tier-1 debt become optimal.
summary: An asset owner designs an asset-backed security and a signal about its value.
finding: When signals are restricted to be sufficiently informative about the upside, debt and additional-tier-1 debt become optimal.

title: Aligning Investment Managers and Clients through Utility-Based Performance Measurement
Insurance and assurance: government interventions and depositor behavior in crisis
abstract: Abstract We examine how different forms of government intervention—explicit deposit insurance, implicit guarantees from nationalization, and assurance effects from re-privatization—shape depositor behavior during a banking crisis. Using proprietary monthly account-level data, we show that depositors respond to formal insurance limits even in an environment of broad state support, but adjust only partially. Stabilization is markedly stronger after the takeover by a financially strong private bank than during state ownership, despite unchanged statutory coverage. These patterns are inconsistent with a strong bailout-expectations view in which explicit insurance is largely irrelevant and instead point to credibility as a key determinant of depositor behavior. We further show that political trust amplifies the effectiveness of government guarantees. Overall, our findings highlight that the form and credibility of government backstops, rather than coverage levels alone, are central to retail deposit funding stability during crises.
summary: We examine how different forms of government intervention—explicit deposit insurance, implicit guarantees from nationalization, and assurance effects from re-privatization—shape depositor behavior during a banking crisis.
finding: We further show that political trust amplifies the effectiveness of government guarantees.

title: Explaining Drawdowns: An ADCC Framework for Communicating Losses with Clarity and Trust
Long-Term Thinking
abstract: Why should we adhere to long-term thinking in investment? Because investment inherently involves sacrificing current consumption in pursuit of higher returns in the future. The legendary investor Benjamin Graham once made a classic remark: “ In the short run, the stock market is a voting machine, but in the long run, it is a weighing machine .” The implication of this statement is that capital markets in the short term can be irrational, and the price of a company’s stock may deviate significantly from its intrinsic value. Even if an investor’s assessment of value is correct, the economy and markets can remain on an irrational trajectory for quite a long time. Yet in the long run, a company’s stock price ultimately aligns with its fundamental value.
summary: Why should we adhere to long-term thinking in investment?
finding: Because investment inherently involves sacrificing current consumption in pursuit of higher returns in the future.

title: Deep Sentiment, Deeper Insights: LSTM and GRU Models for Reliance Stock Price Forecasting
venue: Advances in computational intelligence and robotics book series
abstract: In this research, the impact of financial news sentiment on enhancing stock price forecasting is analyzed by incorporating sentiment features with market historical data and applying deep learning models. With a representative example of Reliance Industries Limited, LSTM and GRU are implemented to analyze nonlinear temporal pattern in stock prices. A lexicon-based and a domain-specific method have been applied to measure sentiment from financial news. The findings show that sentiment-augmented models consistently outperform price only models on a variety of performance measures such as forecasting accuracy and directionality prediction. The models are evaluated on their performance, and GRU outperforms the other models, especially in cases of fluctuations in the stock market data, suggesting its ability to deal with noisy financial information. The results of this study validate the theory of behavioral finance and point to the need to include qualitative data into quantitative forecasting models to be useful in financial decision making.
summary: In this research, the impact of financial news sentiment on enhancing stock price forecasting is analyzed by incorporating sentiment features with market historical data and applying deep learning models.
finding: The findings show that sentiment-augmented models consistently outperform price only models on a variety of performance measures such as forecasting accuracy and directionality prediction.

title: Momentum, Commentary Tone, and Earnings Surprise in LLM Financial Forecasts
abstract: Which inputs drive a language model's financial forecast? We construct synthetic earnings announcements that independently reverse 20-day momentum, non-informational commentary tone, and whether fixed actual EPS beats a manipulated consensus. Six instruction/chat checkpoint conversions from four families (0.49-7.61B base parameters) receive 2,016 prompts each under a direct-answer Q8_0 protocol. The design includes 24 numerical blocks, six commentary pairs, profits and losses, rising and falling annual EPS, and two surprise sizes. Both A/B answer assignments and U/D cover all 384 primary scenarios per conversion. We estimate matched changes in conditional answer-prefix scores, not calibrated market probabilities. Across these checkpoints, the primary EPS contrast ranges from -0.19 to 86.80 percentage points. The magnitude of the primary signed tone contrast exceeds that of EPS in 5 of six models, and momentum exceeds it in 5. Natural-word numerical diagnostic accuracy ranges from 51.0 to 95.8 percent. Answer-encoding, wording, context, and conversion controls qualify these results. The experiment measures observable input reliance and numerical recognition; it establishes neither an internal reasoning mechanism nor realized return predictability. Public benchmark prompts, recorded scores, and an interactive recorded-results explorer accompany the study.
summary: Which inputs drive a language model's financial forecast?
finding: The experiment measures observable input reliance and numerical recognition; it establishes neither an internal reasoning mechanism nor realized return predictability.

title: ESG Integration and Risk-Adjusted Returns: Evidence from the S&P 500 (2019–2024)
publisher: International journal of research and scientific innovation
venue: International journal of research and scientific innovation
abstract: This study investigates the relationship between Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) integration and risk-adjusted returns among S&P 500 constituent firms over the period 2019–2024. Employing a comparative analysis of the S&P 500 Index and the S&P 500 ESG Index, we examine whether ESG screening enhances portfolio performance after controlling for standard risk measures. Our findings reveal that the S&P 500 ESG Index delivered a cumulative outperformance of approximately 17.5 percentage points over the benchmark during the sample period, driven predominantly by stock selection effects rather than sector rebalancing. Risk-adjusted performance metrics including Sharpe ratios, Sortino ratios, and maximum drawdown statistics consistently favor the ESG-screened portfolio. Quintile analysis by ESG score demonstrates a monotonically increasing relationship between ESG ratings and annualized returns, accompanied by declining portfolio volatility. These results contribute to the growing body of evidence suggesting that ESG integration does not impose a performance penalty and may, under certain market conditions, provide a modest risk-return advantage. Policy implications for institutional investors and asset managers are discussed.
summary: This study investigates the relationship between Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) integration and risk-adjusted returns among S&P 500 constituent firms over the period 2019–2024.
finding: Our findings reveal that the S&P 500 ESG Index delivered a cumulative outperformance of approximately 17.5 percentage points over the benchmark during the sample period, driven predominantly by stock selection effects rather than sector rebalancing.

title: SOCIAL MEDIA SENTIMENT, HERDING BEHAVIOUR AND RETAIL INVESTOR ACTIVITY IN THE INDIAN STOCK MARKET: A SECONDARY DATA ANALYSIS
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Externalities of Responsible Investments
abstract: ABSTRACT We develop a model to study the efficiency of socially responsible investing (SRI) as a mechanism to control firms' externalities. When SRI is not too popular, responsible investors favor strategies that lead to a concentration of SRI in a subset of firms in the economy. This concentration can mitigate coordination issues in adopting green technologies, but it can also crowd out the green investments of excluded firms and increase the price of green products. In equilibrium, responsible investors continue to favor concentration even as SRI becomes more popular, and concentrate the most when concentration is least desirable.
summary: ABSTRACT We develop a model to study the efficiency of socially responsible investing (SRI) as a mechanism to control firms' externalities.
finding: In equilibrium, responsible investors continue to favor concentration even as SRI becomes more popular, and concentrate the most when concentration is least desirable.

title: Lessons from the Masters: Communicating Investment Wisdom to Clients, Boards, and Regulators
Data-Driven Dynamic Portfolio Selection with Vine Copula Simulation and Reinforcement Learning
abstract: We develop a data-driven approach to dynamic portfolio selection that combines vine-copula simulation with reinforcement learning. The investor has constant relative risk aversion and maximises expected terminal utility with a running penalty on the conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) of one-period losses. We estimate a conditional vine model from historical returns and use it to generate joint scenarios for CVaR evaluation and conditional paths for training a recurrent portfolio policy. Under uniform local derivative bounds, we propagate edgewise pair-copula parameter errors through the conditional transforms to obtain power-law stability bounds in Hellinger distance and total variation. In a finite-horizon investment model, we combine these estimates with a marginal and structural approximation budget to bound policy values, optimal values and the true-market loss of policies selected under a fitted model, with separate simulation and numerical optimisation terms. On a seven-asset panel comprising US and Chinese equities and gold, the selected ensemble of ten trained policies achieves a compound annual growth rate of 34.13% and a Sharpe ratio of 2.31 over 22 complete monthly holding periods, exceeding the corresponding values of six classical and vine-based benchmarks. Combining simulated and historical training data reduces monthly target-to-target turnover by 41.5% relative to training on historical data alone, while maintaining comparable growth.
summary: We develop a data-driven approach to dynamic portfolio selection that combines vine-copula simulation with reinforcement learning.
finding: Combining simulated and historical training data reduces monthly target-to-target turnover by 41.5% relative to training on historical data alone, while maintaining comparable growth.

title: Price efficiency and equity risk premiums: A multicountry examination
The Triadic Law of Infrastructure Resilience: De-Risking Capital Allocation via the Three-Point Architecture Principle
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Large-scale infrastructure investments routinely suffer from severe stranded asset risk and mispriced capital due to fragmented, highly customized, project-by-project engineering designs. To address this structural vulnerability, this paper introduces a novel infrastructure risk-assessment framework grounded in Charles Sanders Peirce’s metaphysical theory of "Thirdness" and the cybernetic Input-Process-Output (IPO) model, proving that an infrastructure asset’s long-term resilience depends entirely on the structural protection of its Intermediate element. By operationalizing the Three-Point Architecture Principle (End 1 → Intermediate → End 2), we demonstrate that a true, stable system only exists when two terminal nodes are mediated by an independent structural interface. We establish that while the endpoints represent highly variable, modular technologies, the Intermediate element represents the capital-intensive core that dictates overall systemic longevity. From this triadic law, we derive a practical Dual-Question Screening Protocol for institutional investors, requiring assets to satisfy a rigorous Segregation Test and a Lifecycle Continuity Mandate before capital allocation. Finally, we demonstrate how critical secondary underwriting risks—including counterparty insolvency, technological obsolescence, regulatory spillover, and CapEx volatility—can be directly diagnosed and neutralized by evaluating the boundary rules of the intermediate interface. Ultimately, this framework shifts infrastructure due diligence from chaotic, project-level engineering reviews to a systematic, boundary-enforced protocol that unlocks embedded real options and compresses equity risk premiums for long-term institutional capital.
summary: Large-scale infrastructure investments routinely suffer from severe stranded asset risk and mispriced capital due to fragmented, highly customized, project-by-project engineering designs.
finding: Ultimately, this framework shifts infrastructure due diligence from chaotic, project-level engineering reviews to a systematic, boundary-enforced protocol that unlocks embedded real options and compresses equity risk premiums for long-term institutional…

title: AI Washing and Stock Returns: Evidence from Chinese A-Share Firms
publisher: Advances in Economics Management and Political Sciences
venue: Advances in Economics Management and Political Sciences
abstract: Artificial intelligence has become increasingly prominent in corporate disclosure, yet firms' AI-related narratives may not always be supported by observable investment in technology or human capital. Using AI-related keywords from annual reports, AI patents, and AI-related job postings of Chinese A-share firms from 2020 to 2025, we construct a firm-year measure to examine this disclosure-investment gap. We classify a firm as an AI washer when its AI-related disclosure is above the industry-year median, while both AI patent activity and AI-related recruitment remain below their corresponding medians. Firms meeting this definition are associated with lower annual stock returns, and the result remains qualitatively unchanged when we use alternative methods to identify AI patents. Additional tests point to two related market responses: AI washing is accompanied by more negative media coverage and weaker investor sentiment. The return discount is also more pronounced among firms with higher institutional ownership and among firms in regions with stronger local AI policy support. These results suggest that investors do not treat AI-related disclosure independently of observable corporate activity. Instead, the impact of AI narratives on stock returns appears to depend partly on whether firms can support those narratives with technological development and hiring.
summary: Artificial intelligence has become increasingly prominent in corporate disclosure, yet firms' AI-related narratives may not always be supported by observable investment in technology or human capital.
finding: These results suggest that investors do not treat AI-related disclosure independently of observable corporate activity.

title: Business Portfolio Diversification and AI-driven Growth Strategy: Case Study of Microsoft
publisher: Advances in Economics Management and Political Sciences
venue: Advances in Economics Management and Political Sciences
abstract: With the rapid development of artificial intelligence, large-scale technology firms generally face the challenge of balancing the stability of mature businesses with new growth opportunities. Taking Microsoft as an example, this paper discusses the relationship between business portfolio diversification and AI-driven growth strategy. This article focuses on how Microsoft can maintain revenue stability through its business segments—such as productivity software, cloud computing, personal computing, and gaming—while also creating new growth opportunities through AI-related businesses. This paper uses a case study approach, along with Microsoft annual reports, investor information, and public market data, to analyze business-segment revenue, AI-related growth, stock returns, volatility and market risk characteristics. This article does not regard AI as an independent product, but analyzes how it is embedded in Microsoft's overall business portfolio through Azure, Microsoft 365, GitHub and other channels. The results show that Microsoft's diversified business segments provide a relatively stable revenue base for AI‑driven growth, while cloud computing and AI-related businesses further enhance the company's growth potential. From 2021 to 2025, Microsoft's cumulative return and annualized return were 131.53% and 18.33%, respectively, higher than the S&P 500's 84.98% and 13.12%; however, Microsoft's annualized volatility was also higher. The research results show that business diversification can support Microsoft's AI-driven growth, but this higher growth potential is accompanied by more pronounced market risks. Therefore, Microsoft's future portfolio optimization needs to maintain a balance between AI investment, profitability, cash flow stability and risk exposure.
summary: With the rapid development of artificial intelligence, large-scale technology firms generally face the challenge of balancing the stability of mature businesses with new growth opportunities.
finding: The research results show that business diversification can support Microsoft's AI-driven growth, but this higher growth potential is accompanied by more pronounced market risks.

title: Risk, Specialization, and Covered‐Interest Parity
abstract: ABSTRACT Prevailing theories of financial intermediation assume an integrated financial sector with frictionless risk‐sharing. However, we identify substantial risk‐sharing frictions linked to intermediary specialization using currency derivatives markets as a laboratory. Using confidential supervisory data covering $25 trillion in daily bank exposures, we document imperfect hedging in banks' FX‐swap intermediation: banks rarely hedge their synthetic dollar lending with maturity‐matched foreign safe assets. Intermediaries specialize in markets in which they have expertise in managing the associated exposures, giving rise to cross‐market variation in deviations from covered‐interest parity. Our results highlight the importance of intermediary specialization and its impact on risk premia.
summary: ABSTRACT Prevailing theories of financial intermediation assume an integrated financial sector with frictionless risk‐sharing.
finding: Our results highlight the importance of intermediary specialization and its impact on risk premia.

title: Momentum in the Cryptocurrency Market: A Comprehensive Analysis under Realistic Assumptions
abstract: Abstract Prior studies on cryptocurrency momentum overlook liquidation risk and other real-world frictions and inadequately assess its profitability. We evaluate time-series and cross-sectional momentum addressing these issues. When portfolios are marked to market daily, many cross-sectional momentum portfolios are liquidated, and those with statistically significant mean returns often earn negative profits. The mean return is insufficient for testing profitability in the cryptocurrency market, where returns are heavily skewed and fat-tailed. Evidence of time-series momentum is strong, whereas evidence of cross-sectional momentum is almost nonexistent. Investor overconfidence and the disposition effect appear to be important drivers of cryptocurrencies’ price dynamics. Received: 7 October 2025Editor: Zhiguo HeAuthors have furnished an Internet Appendix, which is available on the Oxford University Press Web site next to the link to the final published paper online.
summary: Prior studies on cryptocurrency momentum overlook liquidation risk and other real-world frictions and inadequately assess its profitability.
finding: When portfolios are marked to market daily, many cross-sectional momentum portfolios are liquidated, and those with statistically significant mean returns often earn negative profits.

title: Risk Measures for the Climate Transition Age: Why Symmetric Risk Budgets are unlikely to mitigate two-dimensionally asymmetric Climate Change risks
abstract: The most widely used investment risk measures - variance, standard deviation, and tracking error - treat upside deviations as equally undesirable as downside losses. In stable markets with assumed symmetric return distributions, this simplification is potentially harmless. In the climate transition age, it is not. Climate risk is two-dimensionally asymmetric, across assets and over time. Both dimensions are negatively skewed against investors. Hence, climate transition investment strategies deliberately deviate from benchmarks that reflect an insufficiently decarbonising global economy. When fiduciaries enforce tracking error budgets that penalise outperformance just as heavily as underperformance, they inadvertently constrain exactly the portfolio return opportunities that climate-aware investing seeks. We argue that replacing symmetric deviation-based risk measures with their downside-only counterparts - semi-variance, standard risk and trailing error - resolves this conflict without sacrificing any fiduciary discipline. The distinction is not merely semantic: as the gap between climate transition trajectories and market benchmarks widens over the coming decades, symmetric risk budgets will become binding constraints on transition strategies well before actual investment risk warrants it. We propose specific changes to mandate design that would allow institutional investors to pursue climate transition opportunities within genuinely risk-aware (rather than deviation-averse) frameworks.
summary: The most widely used investment risk measures - variance, standard deviation, and tracking error - treat upside deviations as equally undesirable as downside losses.
finding: We propose specific changes to mandate design that would allow institutional investors to pursue climate transition opportunities within genuinely risk-aware (rather than deviation-averse) frameworks.

title: When Do Fundamentals Matter?
abstract: When people describe the reason for share price moves or shifts in bond yields, it is almost always in fundamental terms. As if every time a new piece of market-relevant information is released, investors are hurriedly updating their valuation models. This gives a pleasing sense of order to the fluctuations of financial markets, but is a poor explanation for what is really happening. Most market moves are about investors guessing what other investors are going to do. Let’s say there is a weak employment number in the US, and the S&P 500 drops by 1%. Is that a result of investors reassessing the fair value of US equities due to an increasing risk of slower growth? Maybe. But it is more likely to be investors reacting to how they think other investors will respond to this new information. Markets – particularly over the short term – are much like what was traditionally called a ‘Keynesian Beauty Contest’ or a guessing game where you win not by guessing the right answer, but what you think others will say the right answer is. Does this behaviour have anything to do with changes in the fundamental worth of an asset? Yes and no. If investors are predicting how other investors will react to new fundamental information, then they indirectly care about fundamentals. However, they don’t have to. If they are just trying to predict other investors’ actions, they care about whatever signals those investors might respond to at that time. These could be relevant to the asset’s long-term value or not at all. Also, if most people are involved in the same guessing game, then it is not necessary to predict how other investors will react to new information, but what other people in the game expect other people in the game to be doing. (It can get very circular.) We can easily end up with a market where nobody is paying any attention to fundamentals; everyone just acts as if everyone else is. While a lot of market activity has little to do with genuine fundamental changes in the value of an asset and even if it does it is indirect. This type of ‘guessing game’ behaviour can, however, impact fundamentals, if we bring in Soros’ concept of reflexivity. Here significant movements in price (whatever the cause) can affect fundamentals or ‘reality’. Imagine French government bond yields are being pushed higher by investors guessing that other investors will react to a worsening fiscal situation and higher inflation. This investor-led price move can morph into a profound fundamental problem as these higher yields create higher debt service costs and increasing political pressure. Although they can often feel entirely distinct, asset prices and fundamentals are not entirely independent of each other. The Fundamentals Will Out If most fluctuations in markets are not driven by investors changing their views on the fundamental value of an asset, does that mean they don’t matter? I don’t think so, they are important in a variety of different ways and over different horizons: To
summary: When people describe the reason for share price moves or shifts in bond yields, it is almost always in fundamental terms.
finding: This investor-led price move can morph into a profound fundamental problem as these higher yields create higher debt service costs and increasing political pressure.

title: Who Got Richer Since 2022?
abstract: Last Friday, the Federal Reserve released the results of its 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances (SCF) , which takes a detailed snapshot of American households' finances every three years. And the big takeaway from this year's release is clear—older Americans got richer while younger Americans got poorer. From 2022-2025, the median net worth of households 75 and older went up 38%, while the median net worth of households under 35 fell by 23% (adjusted for inflation): Households in between saw far smaller changes, with no other age cohort seeing more than a 6% shift in median net worth in either direction. [Author's Note: the SCF surveys only a few thousand households, so changes within smaller groups (like a single age bracket) can be noisy. What caused the wealth of older Americans to surge as younger Americans fell behind? That's what this post is about. So let's take a look at who got richer since 2022 and why. Are the Rich Getting Richer? When the mainstream financial media reports that older Americans are getting richer while younger Americans are falling behind, it's tempting to simply say that "the rich are getting richer." While this isn't wrong, it's not quite right either. For example, if we were to look at the percentage change in real net worth from 2022 to 2025, we would see that the richest households saw net worth gains while the poorest households saw net worth losses: Since those at the 20th percentile experienced a net worth decrease of 11% while those at the 70th percentile (and above) experienced a net worth increase of ~11% (or higher), it seems like the rich got richer while the poor got poorer. This is the classic "K-shaped economy" story, where the top moves up and the bottom moves down. But once you examine this by age, the relationship breaks down. title: Is SpaceX Worth $1.75 Trillion or More?—A Value Investing Perspective
abstract: In its 2026 initial public offering, SpaceX sought a market “valuation” of up to $1.75 trillion and ultimately achieved a market capitalization of approximately $1.77 trillion. Strong investor demand subsequently pushed its market capitalization above $2 trillion before a sharp correction, after which the share price remained highly volatile. This raises the question of whether SpaceX is intrinsically worth $1.75 trillion or even more. The case illustrates the broader challenge of valuing New Space companies, where technological uncertainty and substantial future growth opportunities make conventional valuation approaches difficult to apply. However, valuing New Space companies does not require reinventing the wheel. Rather, established valuation methods must be carefully selected and adapted to distinguish intrinsic value from market expectations and speculative narratives. Using SpaceX as a case study, this article develops a value investing framework for the valuation of New Space companies.
summary: In its 2026 initial public offering, SpaceX sought a market “valuation” of up to $1.75 trillion and ultimately achieved a market capitalization of approximately $1.77 trillion.
finding: Using SpaceX as a case study, this article develops a value investing framework for the valuation of New Space companies.

title: Arbitrage Risk
abstract: The market for a security is semistrong form efficient if the price of the security reflects all publicly available information. Prices of securities reflect, to varying extents, all publicly available information; therefore, markets for securities are efficient in varying degrees. Correction of mispricing of a stock primarily occurs through arbitrage activity. Since arbitrage is not a cost-free activity, whether in the form of transaction costs, idiosyncratic risk, or other costs and risks associated with trading securities, pricing anomalies may persist. As a result, a stock’s market efficiency is negatively related to its arbitrage risk. Thus, we refer to arbitrage risk as a negative proxy for market efficiency. Consider an arbitrageur whose information suggests that a stock is underpriced. The arbitrageur will then go long on that stock and, the arbitrageur will also hedge its risks. The risk of this optimal arbitrage portfolio is the arbitrage risk of the stock, our negative proxy for market efficiency. We apply this methodology to calculate, on a yearly basis, the arbitrage risk for each U.S. exchange-listed common stock, and we also perform a series of simple reduced form regressions of arbitrage risk on factors identified by courts in securities class actions.
summary: The market for a security is semistrong form efficient if the price of the security reflects all publicly available information.
finding: We apply this methodology to calculate, on a yearly basis, the arbitrage risk for each U.S. exchange-listed common stock, and we also perform a series of simple reduced form regressions of arbitrage risk on factors identified by courts in securities class…

title: The Impact of Investor Sentiment on Earnings Management and Financial Disclosure Behavior: Evidence from China’s A-Share Market
The impact of corporate information disclosure ambiguity on investor sentiment: Evidence from stock forum text analysis
Carbon Footprints and Indonesia Market Dynamics: The Risk-Mitigation Role of Artificial Intelligence Innovation
venue: Business Innovation Management and Entrepreneurship Journal (BIMANTARA)
abstract: Climate transition has increased investors' concerns about carbon risk, yet evidence remains limited on how firms' technological capabilities shape market responses, particularly in emerging markets. This study examines the effect of carbon risk on stock performance and the moderating role of AI innovation among non financial companies listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange during 2016 - 2024. Drawing on Asset Pricing Theory, Signaling Theory, and Stakeholder Theory, this study argues that AI innovation reduces investors' uncertainty by enhancing firms' environmental management and signaling stronger technological capability. Indonesia provides a relevant setting because its carbon regulation, sustainability reporting, and AI adoption are still evolving. The results show that carbon risk is marginally associated with lower stock returns and increases stock volatility, while AI innovation significantly weakens the positive effect of carbon risk on stock volatility but has no direct effect on stock returns. This study contributes to the climate finance literature by providing evidence from an emerging market and demonstrating that AI innovation serves as a strategic mechanism for mitigating the financial impact of carbon-transition risk. The findings offer implications for managers, investors, and policymakers in supporting a more resilient low-carbon transition
summary: Climate transition has increased investors' concerns about carbon risk, yet evidence remains limited on how firms' technological capabilities shape market responses, particularly in emerging markets.
finding: The results show that carbon risk is marginally associated with lower stock returns and increases stock volatility, while AI innovation significantly weakens the positive effect of carbon risk on stock volatility but has no direct effect on stock returns.

title: Social media sentiment, behavioral biases, and abnormal returns: evidence from Indonesian Non-Cyclical Consumer Stocks
abstract: Social media has become an important source of information for investors, while stock price anomalies continue to challenge market efficiency. However, evidence on the combined role of social media sentiment, overconfidence, and herding behavior in the Indonesian stock market remains limited. This study examines the associations of social media sentiment and behavioral biases, particularly overconfidence and herding, with abnormal returns (AR) of Indonesia’s non-cyclical consumer sector stocks listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange (IDX) during 2021–2025. Through a quantitative approach, this study employs panel data gathered from 119 firms selected through purposive sampling, comprising daily abnormal returns, a social-media-based sentiment index, overconfidence and herding proxies, and firm size as a control variable. The proposed model is tested using fixed-effects panel regression selected through Chow and Hausman tests. The reported main model shows positive and statistically significant associations for social media sentiment and herding, while firm size is also significant while included as a control variable. In contrast, overconfidence shows no statistically significance results after the reported robust standard-error adjustment. An alternative treatment is provided which excludes no-comment days yields consistent positive directions for sentiment and herding, but reduces the sample from 129,457 to 3,955 firm-day observations. The findings indicate statistically significant associations between social media sentiment, the herding proxy, and abnormal returns; they do not establish causal effects or a ranking of economic importance.
summary: Social media has become an important source of information for investors, while stock price anomalies continue to challenge market efficiency.
finding: The reported main model shows positive and statistically significant associations for social media sentiment and herding, while firm size is also significant while included as a control variable.

title: Competing digital money
abstract: Abstract We study competition between two payment instruments: bank deposits and digital platform tokens. Using a Hotelling model that integrates the theory of two-sided markets and payment economics, we assess how this competition is affected by a public payment infrastructure that makes private payment instruments interoperable. We show that interoperability, whether implemented as a fast payment system or a central bank digital currency, may eliminate payment access exclusion and increase trade volumes and social welfare, but at the cost of some disintermediation. When new payment service providers (PSPs) enter and compete for consumers, they soften competition for merchants: incumbent intermediaries then charge merchants higher fees and earn higher profits. This contrasts with the entry of PSPs on the merchant side, which instead disciplines incumbent fees.
summary: We study competition between two payment instruments: bank deposits and digital platform tokens.
finding: When new payment service providers (PSPs) enter and compete for consumers, they soften competition for merchants: incumbent intermediaries then charge merchants higher fees and earn higher profits.

title: The depositary of last resort
abstract: Abstract What are the consequences of making central bank deposits accessible to actors beyond the banking sector? We collect novel microdata on deposit accounts historically held with the Bank of England by individuals and firms other than banks to study their role in the financial panic of 1866. We document that the use of deposit accounts at the central bank soared during the crisis, while commercial banks permanently lost funding. The expansion in the number of active accounts was fueled by individuals, but the intensive margin increase in balances came almost entirely from firms. Recourse to central bank deposits was heterogeneous and persisted well beyond the panic, reflecting easy access, low opportunity costs, and positive network externalities. At the same time, retail borrowers seeking liquidity support from the Bank during the crisis preferred receiving loan proceeds in the form of cash rather than deposits.
summary: What are the consequences of making central bank deposits accessible to actors beyond the banking sector?
finding: At the same time, retail borrowers seeking liquidity support from the Bank during the crisis preferred receiving loan proceeds in the form of cash rather than deposits.

title: Safety Research and the Allocation of Frontier Compute
abstract: During a frontier takeoff period, an AI lab splits a committed stock of compute among capability research, safety research, and customers, and a regulator limits both the services customers lose and how long any capability can be delayed. Extra safety compute can then come from customers or from capability research. Funding from capability research delays the end of the takeoff period, so the cheaper source depends on how much finishing raises customer services: customers above a threshold, capability research as well below it. Customer funding leaves capability dates unchanged, while research funding gives safety knowledge more time at the cost of later capability and customer services. The threshold is evaluated at a given allocation under a common continuation. Varying the calibration shows how delay costs, additional safety learning, and service valuation move it; in the baseline, it rises with the service budget. Customer-funded safety is front-loaded relative to customer use under the baseline timing conditions. Within the tested constant-share rules, commitment before the safety technology is known costs little unless safety work also advances capability. At the baseline budget, front-loaded customer-funded safety cuts catastrophe probability from 75 to 51 percent when full-speed catastrophe has a 75 percent probability, and from 25 to 14 percent when it has 25 percent. Either way it comes within one point of the best tested rule that also cuts capability research, and the funding threshold does not move.
summary: During a frontier takeoff period, an AI lab splits a committed stock of compute among capability research, safety research, and customers, and a regulator limits both the services customers lose and how long any capability can be delayed.
finding: Varying the calibration shows how delay costs, additional safety learning, and service valuation move it; in the baseline, it rises with the service budget.

title: Is the business of frontier AI companies selling tokens? Value capture and equity prices
abstract: We examine business models that could support frontier AI companies' valuations and the public evidence of plans to earn income beyond selling model access. Reverse cash-flow calculations for OpenAI and Anthropic yield combined year-ten revenue requirements of \$2.79 trillion or \$733 billion, depending on financial assumptions. Public documents identify proposed payments and ownership interests that could supply additional income, such as through partnerships on pharmaceuticals, robotics, or materials science. We discuss how these arrangements relate to firm boundaries and value capture.
summary: We examine business models that could support frontier AI companies' valuations and the public evidence of plans to earn income beyond selling model access.
finding: We discuss how these arrangements relate to firm boundaries and value capture.

title: Stock Market Liberalization and Institutional Investor Clique Behavior: Evidence from China
publisher: International Journal of Advanced AI Applications
venue: International Journal of Advanced AI Applications
abstract: This study examines how stock market liberalization affects the clique behavior of domestic institutional investors, distinguishing hotspot clustering from value clustering. Using panel data on Chinese listed firms from 2011 to 2019 and a difference-in-differences design, we identify institutional cliques with the Louvain community detection algorithm, and we apply large language models to cross-validate clique measurement and to construct a cross-border thematic similarity index. We find that stock market liberalization significantly reduces hotspot clustering while promoting value clustering. The inhibitory effect on hotspot clustering is more pronounced for speculative stocks, whereas the promotion of value clustering is stronger among industry leaders. These effects operate through improved market efficiency, optimized institutional holding structures, and enhanced cross-border narrative alignment. Institutions that prioritize fundamental analysis achieve superior investment returns. This study advances research on institutional cliques by integrating large language models into clique measurement and identifies a channel through which foreign investors mitigate short-term speculation in emerging liberalizing markets.
summary: This study examines how stock market liberalization affects the clique behavior of domestic institutional investors, distinguishing hotspot clustering from value clustering.
finding: We find that stock market liberalization significantly reduces hotspot clustering while promoting value clustering.

title: A Comparison between Estimating the Required Rate of Return in Market Value and Within the Framework of (ROI) and its Impact on the Fair Value of Shares - A Comparative Study of Iraqi Industrial Companies for the Period (2015-2024)
venue: Global Academic Journal of Economics and Business
abstract: This research aims to assess the effectiveness of using the book value and market value frameworks to estimate the implied required rate of return (Ke), examining their subsequent impact on determining the fair value of common stocks and comparing their effects. Traditional valuation models, primarily based on the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM) and market-based metrics, often suffer from increased volatility and conflicting prices in public stock markets. This distorted environment negatively impacts the reliability of cost of equity estimates. To address this vulnerability, this research shifts its analytical focus to a data-driven framework for a group of 10 Iraqi industrial companies over the period 2015-2024. This framework applies the best solutions and models to support the implied rate of return (RM), specifically using the return on investment (ROI) of the companies in the research sample and comparing it to the same implied ROI using earnings per share (EPS) for the same companies over the same period (book value and earnings). The goal is to determine the best approach for estimating the required rate of return and its role in the fair value of the stock, while also controlling for the degree of systematic risk, company size, and earnings quality to understand the direct impact of the two models. Their impact on the accuracy and comparability of fair value. Through periods of macroeconomic distress or systemic market shocks, the first model framework provides a more stable and reversible required rate of return compared to the second model. Consequently, derived fair values exhibit a tighter convergence with long-term intrinsic values, effectively reducing valuation errors resulting from market movement. The analysis highlights a critical gap in the valuation literature by demonstrating that accounting metrics are not merely retrospective reporting requirements, but rather structural anchors capable of stabilizing equity valuations. Its most important findings have profound implications for institutional investors, financial analysts, and regulatory bodies seeking robust valuation methodologies less susceptible to anomalies in temporary market movements.
summary: This research aims to assess the effectiveness of using the book value and market value frameworks to estimate the implied required rate of return (Ke), examining their subsequent impact on determining the fair value of common stocks and comparing their effects.
finding: Its most important findings have profound implications for institutional investors, financial analysts, and regulatory bodies seeking robust valuation methodologies less susceptible to anomalies in temporary market movements.

title: Generative AI and Firm Values
abstract: ABSTRACT How do recent advances in Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) affect firm value? We construct the first measure of firms' workforce exposures to Generative AI and show that an “Artificial‐Minus‐Human” portfolio earned 5% in the two weeks following the release of ChatGPT. The labor‐exposure effect is more pronounced for firms with greater data assets and is distinct from the effect of firms' product exposures to AI. We assess whether exposed workforces are substituted or complemented by Generative AI based on whether their exposed tasks are core or supplemental. Examining firms' labor demand and profitability following the release of ChatGPT supports a labor‐technology substitution channel.
summary: ABSTRACT How do recent advances in Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) affect firm value?
finding: We construct the first measure of firms' workforce exposures to Generative AI and show that an “Artificial‐Minus‐Human” portfolio earned 5% in the two weeks following the release of ChatGPT.

title: The Financial Premium
abstract: ABSTRACT We show that bonds issued by financial firms have higher spreads than bonds issued by industrial firms with the same rating and maturity, a difference that we refer to as the financial premium. Over the period 1987 to 2020, in the United States, this premium is 43 basis points on average, with the premium higher for lower ratings, higher during financial crises, and increasing in bond beta. We derive a model that explains the financial premium: banks hold diversified portfolios of nonfinancial debt, and bank debt therefore reflects more systematic risk than nonfinancial debt.
summary: ABSTRACT We show that bonds issued by financial firms have higher spreads than bonds issued by industrial firms with the same rating and maturity, a difference that we refer to as the financial premium.
finding: Over the period 1987 to 2020, in the United States, this premium is 43 basis points on average, with the premium higher for lower ratings, higher during financial crises, and increasing in bond beta.

title: Feedback and Contagion through Distressed Competition
abstract: ABSTRACT Firms tend to compete more aggressively when facing financial distress. This intensified competition reduces profit margins, pushing them further into distress and adversely affecting their industry peers. To study such feedback and contagion effects, we incorporate strategic competition in a dynamic model with long‐term defaultable debt, exploring various peer interactions such as predation and price wars. The feedback effect represents a novel source of financial distress costs associated with leverage, which helps explain the negative profitability‐leverage relation across industries. Owing to the contagion effect, firms' optimal leverage is often excessively high from an industry perspective, undermining the industry's financial stability.
summary: ABSTRACT Firms tend to compete more aggressively when facing financial distress.
finding: The feedback effect represents a novel source of financial distress costs associated with leverage, which helps explain the negative profitability‐leverage relation across industries.

title: Stock Prices, Earnings and Cashflows: The AI Effect plays through!
abstract: In a post at the end of August 2026, I talked about interest rates in 2026 and marveled at the capacity of equities to keep rising in the face of rising rates. I argued that the resilience of stocks during the year could be traced to higher-than-expected earnings being reported by companies in 2026, and a concurrent increase in expected earnings in 2027 and 2028. Now that September 2026 is one for the record books, it is time to take stock and dig a little deeper, especially since the month brought about one of the largest increase in treasury yield rates in recent memory, and stock prices still held their own. In particular, I want to examine the earnings at US companies, in the aggregate and by sector, trying to trace out where the earnings increase is coming from, and how that increased earnings is playing out on corporate balance sheets and cash flows. Stock Prices and Rates In my earlier post on interest rates, I had looked at treasury rates by day through the end of August, and I will begin this section by updating that chart to include a tumultuous September: I had described the rise in rates between January and August as gradual, but the rise in rates in September was anything but, as the ten-year rate rose from 4.75% at the start of the month to 5.29% at the end. In fact, to put the 54 basis point rise in the ten-year rate in context, take a look at the distribution of monthly rate changes in the ten-year treasury in the chart below: The September rise in rates would put in the top ten percent of 770 monthly rate changes that we have seen between 1962 and 2026. In the face of the mark up in rates, stocks held their own in September, at least in the aggregate, and you can see that in the chart below, where I look at aggregate market values, by month, and by sector: = The market added $2.5 trillion in market capitalization across all stocks in September 2026, but almost $1.5 trillion of that came from technology As you look across the entire year, broken down by quarters, here is what you see in the aggregate market caps: Only companies listed at the start of 2026 included I excluded firms that were not listed at the start of 2026 from the list since including them will give a misleading sense of returns to investors; adding SpaceX, for instance, which was listed in June 2026, will increase the value of communication service companies by more than $2 trillion, but it was listed at roughly that value. There are many who have pointed to the fact that US equities, while up for the year, have seen divergence in performance, and you can see that phenomenon play out in two statistics. The first is that three sectors - technology, energy and materials have carried the market, with technology being the biggest contributor to market gains. The second is that the percent of companies within each sector that are up for the year is about 50% across the market, and in the third quarter, about 65% of all listed stocks saw dropping stock prices. summary: In a post at the end of August 2026, I talked about interest rates in 2026 and marveled at the capacity of equities to keep rising in the face of rising rates.
finding: I argued that the resilience of stocks during the year could be traced to higher-than-expected earnings being reported by companies in 2026, and a concurrent increase in expected earnings in 2027 and 2028.

title: Investor Sentiment and Stock Market Returns in Nigeria
venue: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ECONOMICS AND FINANCIAL MANAGEMENT
abstract: The Nigerian bourse is characterized by continual volatility and unpredictability that traditional macroeconomic models have failed to sufficiently explain this phenomenon. It is against this backdrop that this study examines the impact of investor sentiment on stock market returns in Nigeria. To achieve this, the study built an investor sentiment index (IVSI) using a Principal Component Analysis (PCA). It relied on the ex post facto research design to collated 38 observations of annual time series data spanning 1986 to 2024. Econometric analysis was conducted using descriptive statistics, the Augmented Dickey-Fuller unit root test, and ARCH/GARCH models, with a significance level of 5%. The results indicated that investor sentiment significantly affected stock market returns. Nevertheless, the GARCH model showed positive and significant volatility persistence, implying that past volatility contributed to current market volatility. The study concludes that investor sentiment was not an important factor in stock returns but did play a role in volatility. The study recommends enhanced market transparency and implementing risk management strategies based on volatility. The study contributes to the body of knowledge by integrating behavioural finance with volatility modelling in the Nigerian context.
summary: The Nigerian bourse is characterized by continual volatility and unpredictability that traditional macroeconomic models have failed to sufficiently explain this phenomenon.
finding: Nevertheless, the GARCH model showed positive and significant volatility persistence, implying that past volatility contributed to current market volatility.

title: The Impact of Social Media Influence on Investor Behavior and Purchase Intention in the Indian Stock Market
venue: International Journal of Creative and Open Research in Engineering and Management
abstract: In spite of the fast rise in participation of retail investors in the Indian stock market through social media, the available body of literature on the topic has not tried to disentangle which of the above-mentioned elements of 'social media influence' drive investment actions. The purpose of this study was to analyze how social media affects investors and, more precisely, to find out which of the social media-related elements are strong predictors of purchase intention among retail investors in the Indian stock market. A descriptive-cum-analytical approach was used for this study and primary data were collected from 202 retail investors using structured five-point Likert scale questionnaire employing non-probability or convenience purposive sampling method. Social Media Exposure, Perceived Content Credibility, Trust, Social Media Engagement and Herding Behaviour were considered as independent constructs while Purchase Intention was considered as the dependent construct. The data collected in SPSS software underwent analysis based on descriptive statistics, Cronbach's Alpha, Exploratory Factor Analysis, Pearson correlation and multiple linear regression analysis. It was found that all six constructs had acceptable-to-good reliability and each of the independent constructs had positive and significant correlation with Purchase Intention. However, the regression analysis revealed a model to be significant with F(5,196)= 25.410, p < .001, which accounted for 39.3 percent of the variance in Purchase Intention. Among independent constructs, Trust and Social Media Engagement emerged as the two significant individual predictors while Exposure, Credibility and Herding, though having positive correlation with Purchase Intention, lost their significance when other variables were controlled for. Thus, platforms and regulators can expect more benefits out of developing verifiable trust and engaging investors than just increasing exposure of investment content. Keywords: Social Media Exposure; Perceived Content Credibility; Trust; Social Media Engagement; Herding Behaviour; Purchase Intention; Retail Investors; Indian Stock Market t.
summary: In spite of the fast rise in participation of retail investors in the Indian stock market through social media, the available body of literature on the topic has not tried to disentangle which of the above-mentioned elements of 'social media influence' drive investment actions.
finding: However, the regression analysis revealed a model to be significant with F(5,196)= 25.410, p < .001, which accounted for 39.3 percent of the variance in Purchase Intention.

title: When Do Treasuries Earn the Convenience Yield?—A Hedging Perspective
abstract: ABSTRACT We document that the convenience yield of U.S. Treasuries exhibits properties consistent with a hedging perspective of safe assets, that is, Treasuries are valued highly if they appreciate with poor aggregate shocks. In particular, the convenience yield tends to be low when the covariance of Treasury returns with the aggregate stock market returns is high. A decomposition of the aggregate stock‐bond covariance into terms corresponding to the convenience yield, the frictionless risk‐free rate, and default risk reveals that the covariance between stock returns and the convenience yield itself drives the effect in a substantive capacity.
