title: Value investing in emerging markets: The effectiveness of the Piotroski F-score strategy in Poland as a Central and Eastern European case study
abstract: Objective: The aim of this article is to verify the investment effectiveness of a long-only strategy based on the Piotroski F-score indicator on the Polish equity market, relative to the passive ‘buy and hold’ strategy tracking the broad WIG index. Research Design & Methods: The study used data from the Warsaw Stock Exchange for the full investment cycle covering the years 2006-2025. The study deployed a long-only strategy variant (selection of companies with a score of 7-9 points), incorporating real trading frictions: brokerage commissions (0.39%), capital gains tax (19%) with a loss deduction mechanism, and annual rebalancing deferred to 31 May to preclude look-ahead bias. The non-parametric Wilcoxon signed-rank test verified the repeatability of the market advantage. Findings: The F-score-based strategy generated a CAGR of 15.22% compared to 4.36% for the WIG index, yielding a cumulative return of 1 376.19% (compared to 124.78% for the WIG). Although the Wilcoxon test did not confirm the statistical regularity of excess returns year-on-year, the portfolio exhibited a highly right-skewed payout profile and a risk-adjusted return (Sharpe ratio of 0.37) almost four times higher than the broad market’s. Implications & Recommendations: The lack of unconditional statistical regularity does not negate the high economic utility of the model. The results prove that investors on the Polish market should accept increased portfolio volatility and a lack of return linearity in exchange for an asymmetric risk premium. The Polish capital market still exhibits the characteristics of an emerging market, favouring classic value investing strategies. Treating Poland as a representative case study for the Central and Eastern European (CEE) region, these results provide useful guidance for international investors allocating capital in markets with lower informational efficiency. Contribution & Value Added: Including rigorous transaction and tax costs significantly improves the realism of the results compared to the existing literature. The article first demonstrates the option-like payoff profile of Piotroski’s payout strategy over a long, twenty-year horizon on the Polish market, confirming that simple fundamental filters have not yet eroded here, as is typical of highly developed markets.
summary: The aim of this article is to verify the investment effectiveness of a long-only strategy based on the Piotroski F-score indicator on the Polish equity market, relative to the passive ‘buy and hold’ strategy tracking the broad WIG index.
finding: The F-score-based strategy generated a CAGR of 15.22% compared to 4.36% for the WIG index, yielding a cumulative return of 1 376.19% (compared to 124.78% for the WIG).

title: Socio-Economic Heterogeneity and Mutual Fund Investment Patterns among Investors in Thiruvananthapuram District
venue: International Journal of Advanced Research in Commerce Management & Social Science
abstract: Mutual funds have become an increasingly important investment option for individual investors by providing diversification, expert management, liquidity, and flexible investment opportunities. However, investors differ considerably in their scheme selection, investment mode, amount committed, investment horizon, and frequency of investment, reflecting variations in financial capacity and investment orientation. Despite the growing participation in mutual funds, limited regional evidence explains how socio-economic and demographic characteristics shape distinct investment patterns. Addressing this gap, the present study examines mutual fund investment patterns and their determinants among investors in Thiruvananthapuram District, Kerala. A structured questionnaire was used to gather primary data from 263 mutual fund investors employing a quantitative research approach. The findings revealed a significant association between scheme preference and investment horizon and identified three distinct segments: Systematic Growth-oriented Investors, Conservative Stability-Oriented Investors, and Active High-Value Investors. Systematic Growth-oriented Investors represented the largest segment (39.2%). Significant differences in investment patterns were observed across occupation, gender, monthly income, age, and investment experience. Monthly income and investment experience emerged as the most influential determinants of investor-cluster membership. The findings provide practical insights for mutual fund institutions and financial advisors to develop differentiated investment products, communication strategies, and advisory services aligned with heterogeneous investor profiles.
summary: Mutual funds have become an increasingly important investment option for individual investors by providing diversification, expert management, liquidity, and flexible investment opportunities.
finding: Significant differences in investment patterns were observed across occupation, gender, monthly income, age, and investment experience.

title: Temporal Ordering of AI Policy Communication and Market Attention: A SER-M Perspective from Korea and the United States
publisher: Korean Operations Research and Management Science Society
abstract: Government artificial-intelligence (AI) policy has intensified in both Korea and the United States, yet how policy communication and market attention are ordered over time remains unexamined in the mechanism-based (SER-M) tradition, which has relied on qualitative single-country case studies. This study asks whether the temporal ordering among government AI-policy communication, investor attention, and AI-stock returns differs between the two countries. Using a five-year daily panel (April 2021 to April 2026) of AI-stock baskets, government AI-news counts, and abnormal trading volume as an attention proxy, we apply the Toda-Yamamoto procedure with macroeconomic controls, supplemented by an equivalence (TOST) test, structural VAR, an event study, and multiplicity and measurement robustness checks. In Korea, investor attention precedes policy communication at the five-day horizon while the reverse direction is not significant; in the United States, no precedence appears in either direction, and the equivalence test indicates this null is unlikely to reflect low power alone. The asymmetry holds at daily but not monthly frequency, and the direct price effect of U.S. AI policy on Korean AI stocks is not robust. Because no test survives multiple-testing correction and orthogonalizing volume against volatility weakens the pattern, the results are exploratory. The contribution is a quantitative, cross-country observation of policy-attention ordering within the SER-M framework: an attention-led pattern in Korea versus decoupling in the United States.
summary: Government artificial-intelligence (AI) policy has intensified in both Korea and the United States, yet how policy communication and market attention are ordered over time remains unexamined in the mechanism-based (SER-M) tradition, which has relied on qualitative single-country case studies.
finding: In Korea, investor attention precedes policy communication at the five-day horizon while the reverse direction is not significant; in the United States, no precedence appears in either direction, and the equivalence test indicates this null is unlikely to…

title: The Psychology of Stock Market Bubbles: A Conceptual Review of Why Intelligent Investors Repeat the Same Mistakes
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Stock market bubbles are often described as episodes of greed or irrational speculation, yet such explanations do not fully account for participation by educated and informed investors. This conceptual review examines how behavioral and social-psychological mechanisms interact across the life cycle of a market bubble. Using a narrative synthesis of foundational research on market efficiency, financial instability, informational cascades, conformity, confirmation bias, selective exposure, prospect theory, overconfidence, and narrative economics, together with recent evidence on social-media-driven trading and Indian retail participation, the article develops an integrated behavioral account of bubble formation and collapse. The review argues that bubbles are reinforced through a sequential mechanism: persuasive narratives create emotional commitment; herd behaviour and social proof normalize risk; confirmation bias and selective exposure weaken corrective information; loss aversion delays exit; and overconfidence and leverage encourage continued risk-taking. Digital trading platforms and online communities can accelerate these mechanisms by reducing transaction friction and amplifying attention. Evidence from the Indian context illustrates how rapid growth in retail participation and reliance on financial influencers may intensify these behavioral pressures. The article concludes that investor protection should complement disclosure with behavioral education and choice architecture designed to slow impulsive decisions and make risk more salient. The central implication is that market rationality is incomplete without attention to the emotional and social processes that shape investor judgment.
summary: This conceptual review examines how behavioral and social-psychological mechanisms interact across the life cycle of a market bubble.
finding: Stock market bubbles are often described as episodes of greed or irrational speculation, yet such explanations do not fully account for participation by educated and informed investors.

title: Investor Sentiment and Stock Market Volatility: A Study Using Social Media Data and Financial Indicators
publisher: Minnesota Journal of Business Law and Entrepreneurship
venue: Minnesota Journal of Business Law and Entrepreneurship
abstract: The study analyzes the correlation between the sentiment and social-media attention toward the stock and the stock price movement by examining daily data from Twitter and the stock market for 25 stocks selected for one year starting from September 2021 to September 2022. The study accounts for the direction as well as the size of the following day's price change. Sentiment scores, proportions, and probabilities measure sentiment; tweet volume is the main indicator of attention. Descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, lagged analysis, attention-group comparisons, robust regression, stock fixed-effects models, and machine-learning methods with a strict chronological train-test procedure are used for the analysis. The results show that sentiment from social media is only marginally and inconclusively associated with later stock returns. The predictive power of classification models was found to be under the 55.12% majority class baseline and XGBoost did not perform well. By contrast, social-media attention showed a weak and positive correlation with the size of future price changes. The magnitude of absolute next-day returns rose from 2.05% in the low-attention observations to 2.38% in the high-attention observations. The relationship between tweet volume and absolute returns was positive and the relationship was robust to controlling for market variables and stock fixed effects. The results indicate that the attention paid by social media might be more indicative of the magnitude of stock-price movements than of their direction. But these findings suggest association, not causation.
summary: The study analyzes the correlation between the sentiment and social-media attention toward the stock and the stock price movement by examining daily data from Twitter and the stock market for 25 stocks selected for one year starting from September 2021 to September 2022.
finding: But these findings suggest association, not causation.

title: A Comparative Performance Analysis of Machine Learning Models for Predicting Technology Sector Stock Returns Using Global Macroeconomic Indicators
venue: NOLEGEIN-Journal of Financial Planning and Management
abstract: The financial markets do not depend on a single factor but are the result of interaction of macroeconomic, investor sentiment, and efficient company-specific factors. It is also difficult to predict the stock market especially in the technology industry because they are nonlinear and highly dynamic. The past few years have seen machine learning methods become effective tools in the analysis of financial data and the identification of implicit relationships that cannot be captured by standard statistical models. This study explores whether machine learning models can be effective in daily returns of the technology industry based on macroeconomic indicators and market variables. The data used in this study is the Kaggle dataset known as “Tech Giants and Global Macroeconomic Indicators” ,which is a dataset that comprises financial and macroeconomic data between March 2015 and March 2026. The data is comprised of 2762 trading days and 44 financial indicators that are stock prices, market indices, volatility, and macroeconomic variables. Three prediction models based on machine learning were tested and compared in terms of predictability: Random Forest Regressor, XGBoost Regressor with support of a GPU, and a neural network of a Multi Layer Perceptron. To assess the models, Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), R-squared score, and training time were used. The outcome of experiments suggests that the Random Forest model has the largest predictive accuracy, whereas XGBoost has a much higher training time and is still competitive. Its findings point to the promise of machine learning methods in financial predictions and how macroeconomic predictors can give valuable clues on predicting returns in the technology sector.
summary: The financial markets do not depend on a single factor but are the result of interaction of macroeconomic, investor sentiment, and efficient company-specific factors.
finding: The outcome of experiments suggests that the Random Forest model has the largest predictive accuracy, whereas XGBoost has a much higher training time and is still competitive.

title: INVESTMENT DECISION-MAKING IN IPO AND STOCK MARKETS: THE MEDIATING INFLUENCE OF FEAR OF MISSING OUT
venue: BEMJ Business Entrepreneurship and Management Journal
abstract: This study investigates how behavioral biases and financial literacy shape investors’ decisions in the stock market. The proposed model integrates herding behavior, loss aversion, and financial literacy while incorporating Fear of Missing Out (FOMO) as a mediating mechanism linking behavioral tendencies to investment decisions. Data were collected from 331 Indonesian capital market investors, with the sample predominantly consisting of young adults and students, and analyzed using (PLS-SEM). The results reveal that loss aversion and financial literacy significantly influence investment decisions, whereas herding behavior does not demonstrate a significant direct effect. However, the indirect analysis shows that FOMO mediates the relationships between both herding behavior and loss aversion and investment decisions. These results suggest that investors’ decisions are shaped not only by financial knowledge and individual cognitive tendencies but also by emotional responses arising from social influences and perceived investment opportunities. By integrating cognitive, financial, social, and emotional factors within a single framework, this study provides further insight into investment decision-making from a behavioral finance perspective
summary: This study investigates how behavioral biases and financial literacy shape investors’ decisions in the stock market.
finding: The results reveal that loss aversion and financial literacy significantly influence investment decisions, whereas herding behavior does not demonstrate a significant direct effect.

title: From Tweets to Trades: Analyzing the Influence of Public Mood over Stock Market Performance in Turkiye
abstract: Purpose: This study examines whether domain-specific public mood is associated with stock-market dynamics and whether these relationships vary across communication domains and market conditions. It distinguishes public mood from investor sentiment and investigates whether heterogeneous sources of public communication exhibit different relationships with market behaviour. Design: The study analyses 610,422 posts published by 176 curated X accounts between January 2022 and December 2023, covering Politics and Government, Economy and Finance, and Media and Society. Posts are classified using fine-tuned Turkish transformer models under three domain-specific and one pooled regime. Public mood measures are constructed at daily, weekly, and monthly frequencies and examined alongside BIST100 and BIST30 market measures using correlation, Granger causality, vector autoregression, and impulse response analyses across the full period and selected market conditions. Findings: Public mood is not associated with the direction of stock-market returns but is associated with the magnitude of price movements, particularly for Media and Society and pooled communication. These relationships become stronger at longer aggregation frequencies. Predictive relationships are concentrated in Economy and Finance communication, while their magnitude and direction vary across market conditions, particularly during the 2023 election period. The pooled measure largely reflects the most active communication domain. Originality: The study contributes to behavioral-finance research by incorporating communication - domain heterogeneity into the analysis of public mood and market dynamics. It also demonstrates how aggregating heterogeneous sources can obscure domain-specific relationships between public communication and financial markets.
summary: This study examines whether domain-specific public mood is associated with stock-market dynamics and whether these relationships vary across communication domains and market conditions.
finding: Public mood is not associated with the direction of stock-market returns but is associated with the magnitude of price movements, particularly for Media and Society and pooled communication.

title: To What Extent Does Herd Behaviour Among Retail Investors on Platforms Like Zerodha and Groww Contribute to Stock Market Volatility in India?
publisher: Journal of Economics Finance and Management Studies
venue: Journal of Economics Finance and Management Studies
abstract: Indian retail investors have been increasingly active in the last few years largely due to the emergence of digital brokerage firms such as Zerodha and Groww. These platforms are beneficial to use as they decrease the costs of investment and simplify the process of trading. Meanwhile, social media, financial influencers and online communities have begun to influence the decision of many investors. Instead of relying solely on fundamentals, retail investors now use market trends and mimic the actions of other market players, also referred to as herd behaviour. This behaviour can boost price swings and possibly worsen market volatility, particularly when there is uncertainty and sentiments running hot. However, stock market volatility is not homogenous and is also affected by institutional trading, macro-economic factors and global events. The paper will try to understand the extent to which the herd behaviour of the retail investors on Zerodha and Groww influences stock market volatility in India. It also delves into the causes of this behaviour, the patterns it exhibits in market movements and the role that digital platforms as well as social media have on investor sentiment. Herd behaviour by retail investors is overall concluded to meaningfully add to the volatility at the short end, but not the only strand on the Indian capital market that affects the price movements of the stock (Shiller, 2000).
summary: Indian retail investors have been increasingly active in the last few years largely due to the emergence of digital brokerage firms such as Zerodha and Groww.
finding: Herd behaviour by retail investors is overall concluded to meaningfully add to the volatility at the short end, but not the only strand on the Indian capital market that affects the price movements of the stock (Shiller, 2000).

title: Retail Investor Prediction in India’s Stock Market Using Complex-Value Spatio-Temporal Graph Convolutional Neural Network for Demographic Analysis and Risk Assessment
venue: Journal of Circuits Systems and Computers
abstract: Retail investor participation in India’s stock market has been increasing, driven by improved access to digital platforms and rising financial literacy. However, this surge leads to higher volatility and exposes investors to significant risks if they lack proper knowledge or experience in market dynamics. To overcome this problem, in this paper, retail investor prediction in India’s stock market for demographic analysis and risk assessment (RIP-ISM-CVSTGCNN) is proposed. The model utilizes financial time-series data from the Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) stock dataset, integrated with investor demographic and behavioral attributes to enable comprehensive analysis. The data are pre-processed utilizing implicit unscented particle filter (IUPF), which is employed to clean the data. Then the pre-processed data are fed into a complex-value spatio-temporal graph convolutional neural network (CVSTGCNN) to forecast demographic factors along with a quantitative risk score that reflects the investor’s financial risk level. The proposed model is evaluated using multiple performance metrics, including precision, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, F1-score and AUC. Results show that the RIP-ISM-CVSTGCNN method achieves an accuracy of 97.3%, precision of 96.3%, sensitivity of 96.3%, specificity of 96.3%, F1-score of 96.6% and an AUC of 0.97. Comparative analysis with existing methods, including multi-granularity spatio-temporal correlation networks for stock trend prediction (MGSTCN-STP-GNN), Black Swan event-based hybrid model for Indian stock markets’ trend prediction (ISMT-1DCNN) and series decomposition transformer with period-correlation for stock market index prediction (SDTPC-SMI-RNN), demonstrates that the proposed model significantly outperforms all baseline approaches across all evaluation metrics. These outcomes confirm that the proposed framework provides a robust and effective solution for integrated demographic prediction and risk assessment, enabling improved financial decision-making in stock market analysis.
summary: Retail investor participation in India’s stock market has been increasing, driven by improved access to digital platforms and rising financial literacy.
finding: However, this surge leads to higher volatility and exposes investors to significant risks if they lack proper knowledge or experience in market dynamics.

title: Supranational Banking Supervision, Credit Supply, and Risk‐Taking: European Evidence from Multi‐Country Credit Registers
abstract: ABSTRACT Using a novel data set of multi‐country credit registers and an institutional change from national to supranational supervision, we show that supranational banking supervision can increase credit supply while mitigating excessive risk‐taking. Supranational supervision increases credit supply only in financially stressed countries while reducing the credit supply to the riskiest (zombie) firms. These improved lending effects stem from weaker national institutions, differential national supervisory incentives, lower national supervisory abilities, and weaker national insolvency laws. Moreover, improved access to external finance from wholesale and bond markets as well as lower risk‐weighted assets allow supranationally supervised banks to expand the supply of credit. Overall, despite some supranational supervisory arbitrage, supranational supervision decreases firm‐level credit to the riskiest firms while increasing firm‐level credit availability in stressed countries without reducing it in nonstressed countries.
summary: ABSTRACT Using a novel data set of multi‐country credit registers and an institutional change from national to supranational supervision, we show that supranational banking supervision can increase credit supply while mitigating excessive risk‐taking.
finding: Moreover, improved access to external finance from wholesale and bond markets as well as lower risk‐weighted assets allow supranationally supervised banks to expand the supply of credit.

title: Mind the App: Mobile Access to Financial Information and Consumer Behavior
abstract: ABSTRACT We study whether easier monitoring of personal finances affects consumer spending. We use transaction data from an account aggregation company to study consumers who installed the mobile app after using the same service on a personal computer for several months. We utilize the staggered release of the apps on different devices (iPhone, iPad, and Android) to identify a causal effect conditional on adoption of the mobile app. Consumers decrease their discretionary spending following the installation of the mobile app. The decrease is larger during evening hours and among individuals with lower proxies of self‐control, patterns consistent with a monitoring/self‐regulation channel and with benchmark models of costly self‐control.
summary: ABSTRACT We study whether easier monitoring of personal finances affects consumer spending.
finding: The decrease is larger during evening hours and among individuals with lower proxies of self‐control, patterns consistent with a monitoring/self‐regulation channel and with benchmark models of costly self‐control.

title: The Politicization of Social Responsibility
abstract: ABSTRACT Institutional investors are less likely to support shareholder proposals on environmental and social issues for firms headquartered in Republican‐led states. The decline in support has become more pronounced in recent years, aligning with politicians emphasizing companies’ social responsibility efforts, and among firms receiving state‐level subsidies and tax breaks. Investor support also varies with shifts in state leadership, dropping by 12 percentage points in the same state when Republicans are in control instead of Democrats. The findings indicate that institutional investors prioritize maximizing shareholder value and that politicians can influence investor votes by altering the value implications of shareholder proposals.
summary: The decline in support has become more pronounced in recent years, aligning with politicians emphasizing companies’ social responsibility efforts, and among firms receiving state‐level subsidies and tax breaks.
finding: ABSTRACT Institutional investors are less likely to support shareholder proposals on environmental and social issues for firms headquartered in Republican‐led states.

title: The Real Channel for Nominal Bond‐Stock Puzzles
abstract: ABSTRACT We document that the nature of aggregate consumption dynamics changes when the bond‐stock correlation switches sign. We identify three regimes in a real‐time, sequential learning framework: two highly persistent regimes where permanent or transitory consumption shocks are more dominant, and a largely transitory disaster regime. We study the implications for asset prices. The transition from the second to the first regime in the late 1990s makes the correlation between equities and real bonds switch from positive to negative as in the data, providing an explanation from the perspective of real consumption dynamics. The findings extend to the international setting.
summary: ABSTRACT We document that the nature of aggregate consumption dynamics changes when the bond‐stock correlation switches sign.
finding: The findings extend to the international setting.

title: From Model Output to Portfolio Authority: A One-Page Decision Record for Investment Committees
Comparative Study of Value Investing vs. Growth Investing
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This paper presents a comparative review of value investing and growth investing, two dominant equity strategies distinguished by their conceptual foundations, valuation methodologies, and risk–return profiles. Drawing on peer-reviewed literature published between 2015 and 2026, the study synthesises evidence on the persistence and volatility of the value premium, the cyclicality of style performance across macroeconomic regimes, and the practical application of both philosophies through case studies of Berkshire Hathaway, Apple, Amazon, Microsoft, and Nvidia. The review identifies a research gap concerning the post-pandemic structural break in value–growth return dynamics and the blurring of style boundaries among mega-cap technology firms. Findings suggest that while growth investing has delivered superior absolute returns during low-interest-rate, innovation-driven cycles, value investing continues to offer risk-adjusted resilience and downside protection during inflationary and rate-tightening periods. The paper concludes that strategy selection should be contingent on investor time horizon, risk tolerance, and macroeconomic regime rather than treated as a permanent ideological choice.
summary: This paper presents a comparative review of value investing and growth investing, two dominant equity strategies distinguished by their conceptual foundations, valuation methodologies, and risk–return profiles.
